# COMPREHENSIVE PLAN FOR FRANKEN_ROBOTICS

> **FrankenRobotics** is a robot proving ground, a robot design studio for AI agents, and a mission-query engine,
> built as one mathematical instrument. It simulates legged, wheeled, tracked and hybrid robots in terrain and
> interior scenes with physics supplied by FrankenSim, runs thousands of worlds and hundreds of different robots at
> once on CUDA and Metal GPUs, and exposes a command line and an MCP server through which agents design a robot, test
> it, read what happened and improve it. It answers questions about families of designs and not only about single
> designs: which bodies can do this mission, which cannot and why, and which experiment would settle the rest. It
> searches for the worlds that break a design, shrinks each failure to a minimal counterexample world, and explains a
> failure by intervening on a replay of it. It carries a path from simulation to calibration against measured reality
> and to manufacturable output. Every layer is formulated in Lie theory and abstract algebra: configurations are group
> elements, joints are subgroups, contact is a cone program in the dual Lie algebra, symmetry is a finite group acting
> on the design, and the hot kernels are derived from that algebra instead of being typed in by hand. Repo
> `franken_robotics`; crate prefix `frob-`; binaries `frob` (CLI), `frobd` (job daemon), `frob-mcp` (MCP server),
> `frob-verify` (offline certificate auditor) and `frob-tui` (terminal dashboard).

# PART 0. DOCUMENT CONTROL

## 0.1 Normative language, evidence labels and tiers

MUST, MUST NOT, SHOULD and MAY carry their RFC 2119 meanings. Five labels say what kind of statement a sentence is. A
number in this plan without one of these labels, or without an obvious label from its table header, is a defect in the
plan.

| Label | Meaning | Who may change it |
|---|---|---|
| **FACT** | Observed on 2026-11-21 in a sibling repo, on this machine, or in a cited public source. Code facts cite `repo/path`; web facts cite a URL in Appendix H. | New evidence only |
| **DESIGN** | A decision of this plan. It carries its reason. | An architecture decision record (ADR) |
| **HYPOTHESIS** | Believed, not established. It names the test that would confirm or kill it. | The named test |
| **TARGET** | A number we intend to hit. It is not a measurement until a gate records the measured value. | The gate that measures it |
| **OPEN** | Undecided. It has an owner, a deadline expressed as the gate it blocks, and a fail-closed default (§42). | The owner |

Three rules govern numbers that come from outside this repository.

1. **An external number is a FACT about its source, not about this system.** Every external figure is registered in
   Appendix H with its URL or path, the version or tag it was read at, how it was read (raw text, a rendered figure
   read by eye, or a derivation from published inputs), and the phrase "to be re-read from the primary source before a
   gate cites it". The phrase is not repeated in each sentence that uses the figure.
2. **A reported defect in a foundation is a FACT to recheck.** Where a review reported a defect in a sibling crate and
   this program has not reproduced it at a pinned commit, the statement is written "FACT (to recheck)", and it becomes
   an admission test and an upstream work item (§33, Appendix F) before anything depends on it.
3. **No number is written as a result.** Nothing in this plan was measured on FrankenRobotics. A ratio, a rate or a
   coverage figure that describes this system is a TARGET, or a HYPOTHESIS with the range the evidence supports.
   Headline multipliers do not appear.

Ambition is calibrated with the three tiers the suite already uses (FACT:
`frankensim/COMPREHENSIVE_PLAN_FOR_FRANKENSIM.md` §0). Every mechanism in this plan carries one.

- **[S] Solid**: established mathematics and engineering. The risk is implementation quality.
- **[F] Frontier**: published research that mainstream robot simulators have not productized, or a narrowed form of a
  mechanism whose strong form failed review (§0.8). Real engineering risk.
- **[M] Moonshot**: a synthesis proposed here. It lives behind a feature flag and never sits on the critical path.

The spine of this plan is [S]. The features that make it worth building are [F]. The [M] items are what would make it
unlike anything else, and the plan works without every one of them. Two obligations attach to the upper tiers (DESIGN;
the reason is in §0.7):

- Every [F] and [M] item names a **paper-scale pilot with a falsifier** that must run before its work package is
  funded, and states the **ceiling of its benefit** before any speed test is run.
- Every [F] and [M] item has a **kill gate with a fallback named in advance**. The fallback is a mechanism of a lower
  tier that the plan already contains, so that losing the item costs a capability and never the critical path.

Every mechanism, at any tier, states: what it is (types, data layout, algorithm); which crate owns it (§34); the verb
that exposes it (Appendix J); a known-answer or negative-control test (§38, Appendix M); and a gate with a numeric
threshold (§40). The word "verified" is not used for results anywhere in this plan or in the product's output. A
result is proved, certified, tested or estimated (§12), and it says which.

## 0.2 What "implemented" means

A capability is implemented only when all eight hold. Otherwise it MUST be described as partial, and the missing items
named.

1. Code exists in the crate this plan maps it to (§34).
2. The crate ships a `CONTRACT.md` with ten sections: purpose, inputs, outputs, invariants, refusals, determinism
   class, evidence class of outputs, validity domain, oracles, known gaps.
3. Known-answer tests pass against a pinned oracle that was never regenerated from the candidate (§38).
4. Outputs that cross the agent boundary carry the claim product of §8: the kind of claim, the evidence class set by
   the weakest input, a tier, a determinism class, a model identity, a seed, and the no-authorization flags. No naked
   numbers reach an agent (§29).
5. A CPU reference path exists. Where a GPU path is claimed, a retained differential check against the CPU path exists
   for the same kernels (§21).
6. The capability is reachable through `frob --json` with a documented schema and exit code, and, where the verb
   registry exposes it to agents, through `frob-mcp` (§32).
7. Cancellation is tested: request, drain, finalize, with no leaked device resources (§38).
8. Its gate has a recorded PASS carrying the measured values, not the targets, in a receipt that names the commit, the
   hardware fingerprint and the seed (§40).

Two riders apply to particular kinds of capability.

- **Family certificates.** A capability that emits a certificate about a family of designs or worlds (§25) is
  implemented only when the certificate travels in a `.frobcert` bundle and the independent offline auditor
  `frob-verify` accepts it on a machine with neither the agent nor a GPU, and rejects the registered mutations of it
  (§12).
- **Upper tiers.** An [F] or [M] capability is implemented only when its pilot and its kill-gate decision are on
  record (§0.7). A capability that fell back at its kill gate is described by the name of the fallback.

Gates are written `GATE-<SUBSYS>-NN`. The subsystem codes carried from version 0.2 are MARROW, LEMMA, SKEL, SINEW,
KIN, FID, TRAC, HAB, SENS, REFLEX, CORTEX, SPARK, ARENA, ATEL, CHRON, TETHER and GAUNT. This version adds AUGUR,
PHYLUM, NEMESIS, AUTOPSY, GROUND, FOUNDRY, SHIELD, GAIT, QUAL (the blinded qualification lane) and TENFOLD (the

Three reading paths are supported. The short path is the header, §1.5, §2, §3 and §43. The decision path, for the

## 0.6 How this plan was produced

This plan was produced in four stages. Each left artifacts under `planning/` in the repository; this section says
what was done, and Appendix K gives the counts and what each review changed.

1. **Study of the exemplars.** The plan documents named by the owner were read: FrankenSim's main plan and its four
   companion plans, FrankenTextiles, FrankenMining, FrankenThreeD, FrankenLean and FrankenSymPy. Their structural
   devices are reused on purpose: evidence labels and the definition of "implemented"; claims that are never
   conflated; ambition tags and the layer discipline; kill gates with fallbacks named in advance; a first
   implementation session and a definition of done; an idea-pass appendix.
2. **Audits of the foundations.** Seven code audits reported what the sibling projects contain in code as opposed
   to in plans (FrankenSim's workspace, multibody, contact and GPU policy; FrankenTextiles; FrankenMining;
   FrankenThreeD and the adjacent 3D projects; FrankenLean with FrankenSymPy; the numeric siblings and the MCP
   library). The load-bearing facts were then checked directly in source, and a public-source pass covered GPU
   simulators, Rust-to-GPU routes, geometric robotics, scene assets and benchmarks. Later stages re-read sibling
   code many times; every sibling fact in this plan is stated as FACT with a path, or as FACT-to-recheck where it
   was reported and not re-read.
3. **Version 0.2 and the ambition pass.** A first complete plan (3,666 lines) was written with an idea pass of
   thirty ideas winnowed to fifteen. The owner then asked for a far more ambitious plan and a ten-fold advance
   over every existing system. Five exercises followed, each run to its own method:
   - *An analysis by distinct modes of reasoning.* A neutral case file with an evidence ledger; five independent
     passes (an Amdahl accounting of where design time goes, an adversarial audit of what incumbents already do, a
     transfer of mechanisms from other fields with their breakpoints, hardware envelopes, and a backcast with a
     pre-mortem); 94 atomic claims; independent audit of 76 of them against primary sources and by recomputation.
   - *An adversarial idea duel.* Three agents of different model families each proposed thirty ideas for the plan,
     scored the others' ideas, and reacted to the scores they received, including steelman and blind-spot rounds.
   - *A hypothesis session in the style of Brenner.* A question of record with a falsifier; twenty-four hypotheses,
     two of them deliberate third alternatives; four investigators working refuter-first; a verdict register; then
     a challenge round in which agents of two other model families attacked the register, and an adjudication
     that changed sixteen of its rows.
   - *A harvest of neglected computer-science primitives* against thirteen anticipated hot spots, with the rule
     that every hot spot is anticipated until the first profile.
   - *A compilation of eleven decision problems* (promotion, allocation across evaluation rungs, rank fidelity,
     rare failures, the next experiment, attribution, calibration, solver effort, scheduling, scene selection,
     kernel rewriting) into mathematical families with runtime artifacts, proof obligations and fallbacks.
4. **The blend.** Two other complete plans of this project, written independently
   (`COMPREHENSIVE_PLAN_FOR_FRANKEN_ROBOTICS__ASTRA.md` and `COMPREHENSIVE_PLAN_FOR_FRANKEN_ROBOTICS__NEON.md`),
   were digested in full and compared with version 0.2 without sparing it: where each was better, where version
   0.2 was better, where they conflict, and which of their claims should not be inherited. A catalog merged 112
   distinct ideas from every exercise, with the calculations that killed some of them. An integration charter
   fixed names, tiers and sixteen binding decisions; this document was then written chapter by chapter against
   that charter. The owner's instruction for the blend was maximalist: include every sound mechanism, at the tier
   its evidence supports. The evidence of stage 3 decides the tier (§0.8).
5. **Review of the blend.** A mathematical review of the spine and the physics chapters; a coherence review across
   all chapters; two completeness audits against the two other plans and the idea catalog; a reconciliation pass;
   and a final audit of the two other plans' latest revisions, which changed while this document was being
   written. Appendix K lists the findings and the revisions integrated.

What has **not** happened: no FrankenRobotics code exists; nothing in this plan was compiled, run or measured as
FrankenRobotics; no incumbent simulator was run by this program (every statement about one is a documentation
finding at a pinned version, or a published figure); the external review rounds the planning method calls for have
not been run on this version; and the plan has not been converted to beads. Paper-scale pilots were run at plan
time by one of the two other plans' authors; they are recorded in Appendix K and in §25, and none of them used
FrankenSim dynamics, contact or a real sensor pipeline.

## 0.7 Plan hygiene rules

The first eight come from what the sibling plans recorded about their own mistakes. The rest come from the reviews,
audits and paper-scale pilots behind this version (§0.8).

- **The delivery log lives in `docs/delivery/`, never in this plan.** FrankenTextiles' §25 grew to 82% of its plan
  (FACT: Mining §0.7). This document states decisions; crate contracts and beads state progress.
- **A closed bead is not acceptance.** FrankenMining found 87 beads closed within 12 seconds with one shared close
  reason, serving figures from a stand-in (FACT: Mining App. K.2). Here a bead closes with a typed reason that cites
  its own test, and gates require a live-dependency proof (§38).
- **Process is never the product.** FrankenMining's `xtask` reached about 27% of its code (FACT: audit of
  `franken_mining`). `xtask` here has a hard scope: six checks, listed in §34. A new check needs a named defect class
  it would have caught. The same rule covers every registry, ledger and receipt this version adds: each exists because
  a named verb reads it or a named gate checks it, and one that nothing reads is deleted.
- **Line counts are scope caps, never schedules.** Per-crate figures in §34 are caps that trigger a scope conversation
  at 115%. FrankenTextiles set a ceiling and retired it at 1.9× (FACT: audit of `franken_textiles`).
- **Every number carries a label** (§0.1). Performance numbers also carry the disclosure block of §36, and any ratio
  against an incumbent carries the measurement protocol of §39.
- **The seven claims are never conflated** (§8), and each gate names exactly one of them.
- **Mathematics is written in Unicode, without LaTeX**, and every symbol is defined in §11 or Appendix D.
- **Sibling repos are the owner's, and this program changes them.** A limitation, defect or mismatch in a sibling
  is fixed in that sibling's repository, under its own `AGENTS.md`, gates and conventions, as an upstream work item
  (Appendix F): a bead in this program's graph with the label `upstream`, mirrored as a bead in the sibling's
  tracker. Every upstream work item carries an interim posture and a switch-over rule, so no milestone waits on a
  sibling change landing.
- **Every Frontier and Moonshot item needs a paper-scale pilot with a falsifier before it is funded.** A pilot is
  small enough to run on a CPU in a day, uses exact or hand-checkable arithmetic where it can, is registered before it
  runs, and has an outcome that is not known in advance. A pilot that cannot fail is not a pilot. Its result,
  including a negative one, is recorded in the review log (Appendix K) and its mechanism's tier and scope are revised
  to match.
- **The ceiling is computed before any speed test.** Before a speed comparison is locked, the ceiling implied by the
  work both arms share (authoring, checking, serialization, review) is computed, and the test is refused if the
  ceiling is below the claimed ratio. One pilot behind this version measured a specialized solver at 1.345× a composed
  one warm and 1.088× cold, with a residual of 575.7 µs that the solver does not touch (parsing, assembly, checking,
  serialization and harness, not separately timed), so that no solver could have shown more than about 1.46×
  (842.8 ÷ 575.7; FACT, Appendix K): the test could not have confirmed the claim it was run to test.
- **A frozen decision rule is enumerated before sampling.** For every fixed-n rule the set of reachable verdicts at
  that n is listed first. One pilot rule with 64 pairs could return three of its four verdicts; the fourth was first
  reachable at 86 pairs (FACT, Appendix K).
- **Counterexamples are first-class.** Where a plausible shortcut is wrong, the plan gives the smallest hand-checkable
  case that breaks it, and the case enters the negative-control registry (§38) and the counterexample catalogue
  (Appendix N). A rule that ships without such a case has not been thought through.
- **Killed ideas stay on the page with the calculation that killed them** (Appendix C). A mechanism whose strong form
  was refuted is not built in that form, and its narrowed form is written with the claim that survived (§0.8).
- **Mechanisms are named plainly.** A label from a richer theory is used only when the mechanism uses that theory's
  theorems. A least-squares pose graph is a least-squares pose graph.
- **A gate needs only what a simulator has.** A gate that needs a physical board, a bench measurement, a building scan
  or a human review panel is written as an import lane with a recorded `no-claim` until the data exists (§30).
- **The incumbent is measured before a mechanism is funded against it.** Versions are pinned, the strongest warm
  configuration is recorded, and the phase ledger of the incumbent loop is taken on `trj` before any ratio is written
  (§39).

## 0.8 How evidence from the planning exercises binds the plan

Before this version was written, the load-bearing hypotheses of the program were put to refutation on paper: published
results were re-read at pinned versions, arithmetic was redone, sibling code was inspected, and a small number of
exact, small pilots were run, on CPUs and, for one boundary-classifier kernel, on the three GPUs (§21.8). No
hypothesis was tested by running FrankenRobotics code. Each hypothesis received one of four verdicts, and the verdict
binds what this plan may say and build.

| State | Meaning | What the plan text may say | What is in scope |
|---|---|---|---|
| **ACTIVE** | Unrefuted and untested. Nothing narrows it yet. | The hypothesis, labelled HYPOTHESIS, with its test. No number as a result. | The test is scheduled early. Work that depends on the hypothesis is gated on it, and the plan states what it does if the test goes against it. |
| **NARROWED** | The strong form failed on evidence. A stated weaker claim survives. | Only the surviving claim, with the surviving numbers as HYPOTHESIS ranges. The strong form appears once, in Appendix C, with the refuting calculation. | The narrowed mechanism, at the tier its evidence supports, with a falsifier and a kill gate. |
| **REFUTED** | A calculation or an executed check shows the mechanism does not deliver what was claimed. | The strong form is not written as a goal, a bet or a target. What survives, often as hygiene, is named. | The strong form is not built. It may be reopened only by the reversal condition recorded with the verdict. |
| **DEFERRED** | Real, but not an answer to the question that was asked of it (here: time to a decision). | What it does deliver, under its own heading. It is not counted in the thesis of §2. | Built off the critical path, at [F] or [M], or not at all. |

The register follows. Numbers in the "what survives" column are ranges read from published work or computed from it
(sources in Appendix H). Each is a HYPOTHESIS about this system until the gate of the named section records a
measurement.

| ID | Hypothesis | State | What survives | Where it binds |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| H-01 | Sampling control with zero training | NARROWED | A screening rung and an out-of-distribution fallback, at about 0.3–1 GPU-minute per quadruped episode and 1–5 per humanoid episode: cheaper than one training run up to about 30 episodes per quadruped design and 60 per humanoid design at a 20 ms planning step (6 and 12 at 4 ms). The published successes are legged robots with hand-built swing or stepping references; there is no success rate over a varied corpus and nothing for tracked robots. It never stands in for a trained policy as acceptance evidence. Where the sampling controller is itself the delivered controller, its own episodes are the evidence; the break-even against training once is 2.0 GPU-seconds per 20 s episode for a quadruped and 12 for a humanoid, which published settings miss by 10× and 5×. | Reflex has a sampling controller as a screening rung, a fallback and a demonstration source, and a delivered-controller lane with a frozen planner record (§22.8; BET-27). |
| H-02 | A universal policy prior | NARROWED | Within one morphology class, on flat or mildly varied ground with fixed actuation: zero-shot at 70–85% of specialist return; fine-tuning at about 2–25% of a from-scratch run stopped at matched return (1–10% against the fixed budget one source used). Across topology-diverse designs at affordable pretraining: zero-shot at 10–40%, a fine-tuning gain of 2–3× at best and none on flat ground. Within a class on interior terrain, with payload or actuator-card changes: no published figure. | Family policies per morphology class, not one universal policy. A gated experiment on interior terrain, against an early-stopped from-scratch control, that needs an owner-approved compute envelope (§23; BET-15). |
| H-03 | Topology as data | NARROWED | Mixed-topology populations with few worlds per design, in size buckets. One incumbent solver publishes a mixed batch of three body plans at 0.86 of the harmonic mean of its homogeneous rates. That solver is maximal-coordinate, is documented as not deterministic, and is reported as slower than the reduced-coordinate solvers of its framework. Three differentiators are left: measured mixed-batch throughput, the time from an edit to the first GPU step, and run-to-run replay and forks inside a mixed batch, which no incumbent document read claims. | Per-world model variants inside padded capacities; a head-to-head experiment with a per-family-template control arm and a digest check inside the mixed batch (§17; BET-18). |
| H-04 | Supercompiled kernels | REFUTED for recursion-only specialization | The Lie-algebraic recursions are 16–20% of two incumbent step traces, so the ceiling is about 1.2× and reaching it needs the recursions more than five times faster. Derived derivative kernels for CPU solvers survive. Reversal condition: a specializable share of at least one third on our own profile. | Specialization only for survivors, and only past the reversal condition. Derivation stays, for correctness, certificates and CPU solvers (§21; BET-01). |
| H-04b | Structure-exploiting constraint assembly and solve | ACTIVE | Constraint assembly and the solve are 62% of the same incumbent trace: a ceiling of 2.6× if both vanished and 1.7× at a three-fold reduction. Ancestor-sparse rows and a tree-ordered factor cut operation counts 2.6× to 4.1× for the factor and 3.8× to 8.1× per foot row. The shares of those operations inside the solve stage are unmeasured, fewer operations do not imply a faster device step, and the sparsity is carried as data, not compiled per design. | An operation ledger on the CPU tier and a device measurement at M2, with a kill gate. Not counted in the thesis of §2 (§16). |
| H-05 | Gait continuation | NARROWED | Full-order orbit solves take about 4–260 s of CPU at 20–68 states: a screening signal for periodic gaits on regular ground, at about 1% to 63% of a 410 s training run. Not a referee-ready controller. | A gait-orbit analysis with continuation in design parameters, labelled screening (§22; BET-26). |
| H-06 | Region certificates | NARROWED | Certificates per constraint. Bisection is confined to a split set of about six sensitive parameters; the others are enclosed at full range, and a box of any dimension is admitted when that enclosure is narrower than the constraint's margin. Isotropic paving of a 10–20 dimensional box is out of reach. Whether robot constraints have narrow weak-variable enclosures is unmeasured. | Family answers are built from per-constraint certificates, monotonicity and witnesses, not from brute paving (§12, §25; BET-20). |
| H-07 | A rare-event engine | NARROWED | Search finds failures; a bound comes from a proposal frozen before the confirming draws, with bounded weights, or from crude sampling. Published measured gains are 2–20× and about 5× in mean-square error; 10–100× at 10⁻⁴–10⁻⁵ is a TARGET. Proposals may act on static scene parameters as well as per-step disturbances; only snapshot reuse needs per-step noise. A failure mode the proposal misses costs up to 1/ε times crude sampling, so absence is never certified more cheaply. | Nemesis separates exploration from certification, and its bound claims refutation and tightening (§26; BET-32). |
| H-08 | Counterfactual autopsy | NARROWED | Interventional contrasts reported with a flip rate under perturbations at or above round-off scale. Temporary interventions fork from the snapshot; design-parameter interventions re-run from the episode start. Precision follows measured sensitivity: at the published exponent, single-precision round-off stays below 4 × 10⁻⁵ of state scale over fork windows up to about 1 s and reaches 2% at 2 s. Double precision is the default for one failure and the escalation for marginal cases. | Autopsy reports the stability of each attribution, uses a placebo fork, and may attribute on the originating tier under an admission rule (§27; BET-23). |
| H-09 | Incremental evaluation | REFUTED for exact reuse | Exact reuse of rollouts after a mass or geometry edit is at most about 10% of compute. Training avoided by warm starts is a different quantity; it belongs to H-21 and is counted once. A memo graph for analyses, step plans, kernels and scene compiles survives as hygiene. Dependency-directed revalidation of verdicts survives as an evidence rule. | The memo graph extends past model identity; "which verdicts survive an edit" is a verb; a reuse ledger keeps exact reuse, carried evidence and avoided reacquisition apart (§28; BET-33). |
| H-10 | Value of information | NARROWED | 2–5× from stopping and elimination when candidates are separated; about 1× otherwise. | Experiment planning is used at the finalist stage and for choosing measurements (§28). |
| H-11 | An always-on referee | NARROWED | A sampled snapshot referee on any backend. A correctness guard that saves no compute. Its coverage is unmeasured and scales with referee speed: about 0.1–2.4% of GPU world-seconds if the referee runs at 0.2–1.0× real time per core on 24 cores, and more if it is faster. Its samples, drawn with recorded inclusion probabilities, also serve the paired tier correction. | A background referee sampler that reports its coverage and detection delay per hardware and backend pair (§16; BET-34). |
| H-12 | Generative structure | DEFERRED as a decision-time lever | Links 7–30% lighter than engineered parts: 2–8% of robot mass on the one quadruped with a published mass breakdown, and no figure for humanoids. It improves the output, not the time to a decision. | Foundry is an output-quality subsystem (§31; BET-29). |
| H-12b | Member sizing inside screening | ACTIVE | A closed-form check that a declared link wall survives the design's own loads keeps screening from rewarding links that cannot be built. How often it changes the winning actuator or gear ratio is unmeasured. | The beam rung runs at preflight and blocks promotion of under-built designs (§31, §14). |
| H-13 | Requirements replace rewards | NARROWED | Bounded-time requirements as the acceptance metric and as a falsification score. Not a replacement for shaped rewards. | Missions are requirements; training keeps reward terms (§24; BET-24). |
| H-14 | Conformal reality bands | NARROWED | Coverage within one calibrated robot and task family, varying by about six points at n = 20. Nothing for designs that were never built. | Ground issues bands per calibrated family and refuses elsewhere (§30; BET-28). |
| H-15 | Half precision | REFUTED | The condition number times half-precision round-off is at or above one in 37–64% of sampled contact states, and refinement alone costs more than the single-precision factorization. | Not built. Single precision with diagonal scaling (§35; BET-08). |
| H-16 | Living multiphysics in every world | REFUTED as stated | Full-room fluid is out of memory by orders of magnitude, and coupled cloth and cable at batch speed are out of reach on present foundations. A contact-level film-friction law and rigid proxies are the [S] substitutes; whether they reproduce the failures of coupled models is untested. | The film law and the proxies are [S]. The proxy-adequacy pilot decides the proxies' claim and whether a coupled island is ever funded; islands are [M] (§19; BET-36). |
| H-17 | From mission to design by solving | NARROWED | Trajectory optimization with design variables as local refinement (about 12 degrees of freedom, up to 17 parameters, 4–10 minutes). Polynomial synthesis only inside the symbolic library's caps. Monotone catalog selection of actuators, batteries and compute, with no measured timing. The pass rate of synthesized designs under independent closed-loop evaluation is unknown. | A bounded exact synthesis lane, a refinement lane and catalog selection; continuation is [M], on the CPU; every synthesized candidate passes the ordinary ladder (§25). |
| H-18 | Information, not the engine, is the lever | ACTIVE | No instrumented design session exists. Where every candidate is trained, training is about 96% of an illustrative campaign and information features that do not remove training cap near 1.04×. Once controller acquisition is amortized, agent turns are about two thirds of elapsed time. Which regime a mission is in is a measurement. | The ten-fold test measures decisions, with a phase ledger and three single-change ablations (§2, §39). |
| H-19 | A thin layer over an incumbent would do | ACTIVE | Decided by a measured recovery ratio, not by a count of gaps. Documented engine-internal gaps: a mixed-topology batch with run-to-run replay; a Metal tier. Unverified: replay of one world outside its batch; solver-internal certificates. In the incumbent documents read, run-to-run determinism, heterogeneous worlds and the fastest solver sit on different solver paths, so each is available and their conjunction is not shown. | The ten-fold test has three arms and reports how much of the gain a composed incumbent recovers; the plan says what it does if that arm ties (§39; BET-14). |
| H-20 | Proof-guided control | NARROWED | Reduced-order barrier shields with a statistically measured margin. No full-order certificates. | An energy-budget tier and runtime filters, classed Tested (§22, §12; BET-25). |
| H-21 | Policy inheritance | NARROWED | No published figure measures a small typed parameter edit from parent to child. Transfer from a multi-embodiment prior to a similar body costs about 2–25% of a from-scratch run stopped at matched return; the one parent-to-child figure is about 50%. Single-limb topology edits: 33–100%. Chained inheritance risks loss of plasticity and narrows morphological diversity. | Inheritance for parameter edits must beat an early-stopped from-scratch control per edit class before it is the default. Resets follow a measured regression of an audit twin, with a depth schedule as fallback (§23; BET-16). |
| H-22a | Rank fidelity between rungs | ACTIVE | No published rank agreement between a shared policy and specialists was found. The nearest figure, 0.40, compares a critic with its own policy. A high rank correlation does not protect the winner: with 40 designs and the true best at cheap rank 3, τ is 0.91 on the top ten and a cut to two discards it. | The rank-agreement experiment is the decisive early experiment of the program, and it reports containment and regret beside τ (§23, §28; BET-17). |
| H-22b | The fast tier as a paired control | ACTIVE | A paired correction gains 1/(1 − ρ²) before cost: 2.0× at 0.7, 2.8× at 0.8, 5.3× at 0.9. The correlation is unmeasured and is reported separately for continuous metrics and for binary outcomes. | The tier-correction ledger of §16 and §29. |
| H-23 | A family per dispatch | NARROWED | Fewer rounds are plausible; measured compute gains in published population methods are about 3–4×. Paired finite-difference gradients are unproven over long contact-rich horizons. | Families per dispatch, with short-horizon paired differences (§17, §28). |
| H-24 | A geometric-algebra tree policy | NARROWED | Invariance to heading and to description conventions is necessary, and augmentation recovers most of it. There is no locomotion evidence for the geometric-algebra specifics: expect 0–1.3×. | An [M] experiment with a plain morphology transformer as the control arm (§23; BET-30). |
| H-25 | Brackets on what a body can achieve | ACTIVE | A controller-independent upper bound and an achieved lower bound on task utility; controller effort stops only when a checked upper bound falls below a competitor's lower bound. The bound is often vacuous for contact-rich full-order tasks. | §25.32, §28. |
| H-26 | Common randomness compiled from the task | ACTIVE | Separate address domains for world fields, absolute time and task-triggered events keep paired draws paired across retiming and topology changes. A paired contrast's variance scales with 1 − ρ. Any change in a marginal distribution is a failure of the mechanism. | §24.22, §35. |
| H-27 | Step adjoints with short-horizon joint training | ACTIVE | Implicit-function adjoints through the converged contact solve are exact for a fixed active set and cheap. Several incumbents differentiate their step, so this is no differentiator. Gradients say nothing about outcomes decided by a change of contact sequence. | [M], off the critical path (§16.21, §23.29). |
| H-28 | Placement and sizing along a prescribed motion | ACTIVE | Inverse dynamics is linear in inertial parameters and contact forces for a fixed motion, so placement and sizing is one cone program. Its certificate excludes a motion, not a design; gear ratios are enumerated; link lengths are not variables. | §25.33. |
| H-29 | Visibility and observability in sensor placement | ACTIVE | Visibility along a motion with the robot's own limbs and payload as occluders is a cheap, missing analysis. The observability index is exact only without bias states. The share of estimated-state failures it explains is unknown. | §20.24. |

The question the program was asked is open: no matched mission has been run on any pipeline. No single mechanism
delivers ten-fold, and no conjunction has been shown to. §2 states the candidate conjunction and the two
comparators it must be measured against. The register above was challenged after it was first adjudicated, and
sixteen of its rows were corrected; the corrections are in the rows as printed. These disagreements remain open,
and each has a test that settles it:

- **Whether a thin layer over an incumbent recovers the gain.** Settled by the recovery ratio of §39 (BET-14).
- **Whether design missions are dominated by training or by agent turns and diagnosis.** Settled by the phase
  ledger and the three ablations of §39.
- **Whether cheap rungs rank designs as specialists do, and how well tiers correlate.** Settled by the
  rank-agreement experiment (§23, §28; BET-17).
- **Whether a family policy holds within a class on interior terrain, and what an inherited edit costs.** Settled
  by BET-15 and BET-16 against early-stopped controls (§23).
- **Whether a sampling controller is more than a screen.** Settled by BET-06 and BET-27 on the design corpus, and
  by the delivered-controller lane (§22).
- **Whether a structure-exploiting solve beats parity, and whether per-design code adds to it.** Settled by the
  operation ledger and our own M2 profile (§16, §21, §36).
- **Whether rigid proxies reproduce the failures of coupled models.** Settled by the pilot of §19.10.7.
- **Whether formal certificates change any design decision.** There is no evidence either way. Lemma records, for
  every certificate consumed by a decision, whether the decision would have differed without it (§12; BET-11,
  BET-20).

The same evidence binds three further things. Differentiators that the incumbent audit withdrew are not claimed
anywhere in this plan; §1.3 lists them. Numbers that the audit corrected replace the numbers of version 0.2 wherever
they appear; §2 and §36 carry the corrected figures. A verdict changes only on new evidence of the kind that produced
it: a pilot, a measurement at a gate, or a primary source re-read at a pinned version. The register is append-only,
and a changed verdict keeps its history.

# PART I. THESIS

## 1. What exists, what is missing, what this is

This chapter is an audit before it is a thesis. It states what the strongest existing systems already do, what they
document as absent, what this plan therefore does not claim, and only then what FrankenRobotics is and where it may
differ. The incumbents were read in their own files at pinned versions: MuJoCo and MuJoCo Warp 4.0.1, Newton 1.8.0,
Warp 1.19.0, Isaac Lab 3.0.0 with Isaac Sim 6.2.0, Genesis 1.4.7, Drake 1.58.0 and ManiSkill 3.0.1 (FACT, Appendix H).
No incumbent GPU simulator was run (the one executed incumbent measurement is CPU MuJoCo on this Mac, §36.3 row 13):
a capability listed here is documented, not demonstrated, and where a search found nothing the text says "not found",
which is absence of evidence and not evidence of absence. The audit is repeated with execution at M0, when the
incumbents are installed on `trj` and their strongest warm configurations are frozen (§39).

### 1.1 What the strongest existing systems already do

Every row is a FACT about its source (Appendix H). The third column is the consequence this plan draws.

| Capability | What is documented or published | Consequence for this plan |
|---|---|---|
| Training speed | A quadruped joystick policy trains in about 410 s on one RTX 4090 and about 325 s on two, compile time included (MuJoCo Playground, a figure read by eye, ± 20 s; the text says "within 5 minutes" on two). Humanoid policies train in under 15 to 30 minutes on two RTX 4090. A default rough-terrain humanoid run takes about 1 h on one RTX 4090 (derived from Isaac Lab's published configuration and frame rate). | The training rung is a parity requirement. The 15-minute target of version 0.2 was slower than the published run on the same card and is replaced (§36). Narrative denominators are minutes to about an hour. |
| Physics throughput | About 2.55 M humanoid (G1) world-steps/s at 8,192 worlds on an RTX 6000 Ada on flat ground, and 1.68 M on a heightfield (MuJoCo Warp nightly benchmark). Physics-only 4.8 M physics steps/s for a quadruped at 4,096 environments on an RTX 5090, with 71% of the full environment step spent outside physics (mjlab nightly). CPU MuJoCo runs the classic humanoid at 650 k steps/s on an M3 Max and 1.8 M on 64 cores. | Throughput targets are restated as ratios to the incumbent measured on `trj` under the disclosure block (§36). No order-of-magnitude headroom per step is assumed anywhere. |
| Determinism | Opt-in bitwise run-to-run determinism on the same GPU model, driver, toolkit, build, model, inputs and step sequence: Newton 1.8.0 for five solvers, and Isaac Lab 3.0.0 on PhysX for rigid bodies and articulations. | Deterministic GPU replay as such is not a differentiator. §1.2 says what is documented as absent. |
| Different robots in one batch | ManiSkill 3.0.1 merges articulations with different link and joint structures, padded to the largest. Newton 1.8.0 documents heterogeneous worlds for two solvers and labels the support experimental. One paper trains a single policy across three-, four- and five-legged bodies and reports the mixed batch at 86 k samples/s at 2,048 environments, 0.86 of the harmonic mean of its homogeneous rates. | Not a capability differentiator. Only two measured numbers can differentiate (§17, N11). |
| Per-world parameters and assets | MuJoCo Warp 4.0.1 documents batched model fields and per-world assets. | Per-world parameter variants within one topology are parity, and are [S] here. |
| Structural editing | CPU MuJoCo's `mj_recompile` "updates an existing mjModel and mjData pair in-place, while preserving the simulation state", including adding or removing bodies during simulation. On the GPU a model edit needs a host compile and a new graph capture. | Editing structure is prior art on the CPU. No edit-to-first-GPU-step latency is published, so that is a number to measure, not to assume. |
| Forking state | CPU MuJoCo copies integration state so that source and copy step identically, and its batch API is bit-identical at any thread count. No GPU fork verb was found. | Counterfactual replay is established on the CPU. |
| Control with no training | Sampling-based predictive control with about 30 sampled trajectories and three iterations on a desktop CPU runs a real quadruped at 50 Hz, and a simulated humanoid with 60 to 70 samples. A GPU variant uses 2,048 samples. Each published controller uses cost weights chosen per task and robot. | "No training needed" is not a claim of this plan. The roles of baseline synthesis and sampling control are separated (BET-06, BET-27). |
| Differentiability | Available in MJX on JAX, Brax, Newton and Genesis; gradient quality through contact was not audited. | Not a differentiator. Contact gradients remain deferred (§6.2). |
| Actuator physics | MuJoCo's DC-motor actuator has optional inductance, cogging torque, thermal resistance variation, LuGre friction and a winding-temperature state, on the CPU and, in MuJoCo Warp 4.0.1, on the GPU. | Electrical and thermal actuator modelling is parity, not novelty (GOAL-12). |
| One kernel source, several backends | Warp compiles one kernel source for CPU and CUDA. Genesis's compiler lowers one source to CUDA, ROCm, Metal, Vulkan, x86 and ARM64. | Conceded. N1 claims only the derivation and the stored disagreement record. |
| Several solvers on one model | Newton documents a solver matrix over one model; Isaac Lab 3.0 introduces a multi-backend architecture over PhysX and Newton. | Conceded. N3 claims only the promotion rule. |
| Sequential comparison | Anytime-valid sequential comparison of two robot policies on binary, partial-credit and bounded continuous outcomes is published (arXiv 2603.13616). An earlier sequential test needs a maximum sample size fixed in advance (arXiv 2503.10966). | N4 claims only the application to paired design comparisons inside the studio. |
| Certificates | Drake 1.58.0 certifies collision-free polytopes in configuration space with sum-of-squares programs. | Kinematic certificates are prior art. N5 is narrower and says so. |
| Apple GPU | Genesis 1.4.7 lowers kernels to Metal. No published rigid-body throughput on Apple silicon was found. | The Metal tier is a number, not a first (BET-09, N10). |
| Interior scenes | Homes and kitchens (one project ships 2,500 or more kitchen scenes; others generate interiors from text or procedurally, with articulated fixtures). Two published retail-store generators. A warehouse builder that turns a 2D plan into a scene and has a headless interface. | GOAL-06 claims the grammar system and the two archetypes for which no generator was found (N12). |
| Agent access | Isaac Sim 6.2.0 ships an MCP server for documentation lookup. A community server exposes 42 tools that drive the simulator. | MCP access to a simulator is prior art. What remains is in N9. |
| One policy across bodies | One policy trained on 16 legged robots (1.6 × 10⁹ steps), on 50 robots (5 × 10⁹ steps, about 40 A100-hours) and on about 1,000 embodiments (over 2 × 10¹² steps on 160 GPUs for five days), with zero-shot transfer to withheld robots that resemble the training set. | Family policies per morphology class (BET-15). The third compute scale is out of reach of two cards. |
| Population co-design | Sharing specialist policies across candidates cut co-design wall-clock by 67.4%, about 3.1×, in design spaces of at most four dimensions. Clustering similar morphologies explored about 780 times more designs with 78% fewer simulation steps, at slightly lower best fitness. | Order-of-magnitude gains are published for designs evaluated per unit of simulation, not for the time or the quality of the best design. |
| Agent-driven design loops | Published loops spend about an hour of reinforcement learning per round of 16 candidates on eight GPUs, and train 80 to 1,600 candidates per campaign at 7.5 to 30 GPU-minutes each. | This is the denominator of the ten-fold test (§2). |
| Co-design theory and search | Grammar-based robot search, monotone co-design theory and language-model design loops all exist. | None is open ground. |

### 1.2 The fossils, corrected

Version 0.2 listed eight "fossils" of robot simulation. The incumbent audit showed that several described incumbents
wrongly. The table below keeps only what an incumbent documents as absent or limited, quotes or cites the
documentation, and names what this plan does about it and what must pass before the plan may say so.

| Stage | What incumbents document as absent or limited | Where | What this plan does, and the condition on claiming it |
|---|---|---|---|
| Replay | Bitwise agreement between a CPU run and a GPU run. Results "usually differ ... between the CPU and CUDA backends"; the kernel compiler defines only run-to-run and GPU-to-GPU determinism modes. | Newton 1.8.0 determinism guide; Warp 1.19.0 | Any world is re-run alone on the CPU from its address, bit for bit where the device reaches class D1 (N6). A hypothesis until GATE-SPARK-01 and GATE-SPARK-02 pass. |
| Replay | Independence of a world's trajectory from the batch it ran in. One solver's own tests hold a world equal to its isolated run only to 10⁻⁵–10⁻⁴; no guarantee is documented. | Newton 1.8.0 test suite | A batch-composition invariance test is part of the determinism program (§35). Until it passes, replay of a world taken out of its batch is a tolerance replay. |
| Determinism | GPU determinism in one leading engine: "Is MJWarp on GPU deterministic? No." | MuJoCo Warp 4.0.1 documentation | A determinism class is typed on every result and tested (GOAL-20). |
| Design | A topology change inside a running GPU batch. One engine keeps one model per batch and varies only fields and assets per world; one binding requires identical links and joints; heterogeneous worlds elsewhere are experimental, and "not all solvers are able to simulate them". | MuJoCo Warp 4.0.1; Isaac Lab 3.0.0; Newton 1.8.0 | Per-world model variants inside padded capacities and size buckets (§17). Claimed only as two measured numbers (N11). |
| Energy | Constraint energy: "potential and kinetic energy in constraints is not accounted for". | MuJoCo 4.0.1 XML reference | An energy ledger that closes to a stated residual with dissipation attributed per contact (N8), claimed only once the residual is measured. |
| Apple GPU | Metal acceleration in the Warp and JAX stacks: macOS wheels "support CPU execution but not Metal acceleration"; "macOS (CPU only)"; "not supported on Mac/OSX GPU". | Warp 1.19.0; Newton 1.8.0; JAX installation notes | A Metal tier measured against the one incumbent that does lower to Metal, on the same machine (N10). |
| Symmetry | Automatic symmetry: the reference library takes each robot's symmetry group from a per-robot configuration file. | MorphoSymm documentation | The symmetry group is computed from the design; a declared symmetry is an assertion that is checked (§13, §28). |
| Control | Automatic cost synthesis: each published sampling controller uses cost weights chosen per task and robot. | The controller papers (Appendix H) | A baseline controller synthesized from the model per morphology class (N7), conditional on BET-06. |
| Statistics | Paired comparison of designs on common random numbers. The published sequential tests compare policies, and one of them needs a fixed maximum sample size and binary outcomes. | arXiv 2503.10966; arXiv 2603.13616 | The published tests, applied to paired design comparison on common world addresses (N4). |
| Agents | Execution under budgets. The vendor MCP server is lookup, not execution, and neither it nor the community server documents compute budgets, provenance or a typed refusal taxonomy. | Isaac Sim 6.2.0 documentation; the community server's description | Every verb carries a compute budget, provenance and a typed refusal (N9). |
| Transfer | Policies for bodies far from the training set: the authors of the multi-embodiment results report that transfer "completely out of the training distribution is still problematic". | The multi-embodiment papers (Appendix H) | Family policies per class with an out-of-distribution check and a fallback (§23). |
| Gradients | Differentiation on the newer GPU back end of one engine: "not currently available in MJX-Warp". | MuJoCo 4.0.1 MJX documentation | Nothing. Listed for completeness; contact gradients are deferred here too. |

A second, weaker list holds what was **not found** after a bounded search. Each item is an absence of evidence. None
is called a gap in an incumbent, and each has a line in the M0 audit that tries again with the software installed.

- Checked certificates attached to the kernels of a GPU engine, or enclosures of simulated quantities.
- Pre-simulation design analyses built into an engine (static sizing toolkits for serial arms exist outside engines).
- A promotion rule between solvers or tiers, or a cross-tier disagreement ledger.
- A generator for manufacturing plants or for commercial kitchens.
- An integrated GPU tool for rare-event or adversarial failure search (research methods exist).
- Structural analysis, topology optimization or fatigue inside an agent's design loop (one co-design framework has an
  automated finite-element filter).
- A published latency from a topology edit to the first GPU step.
- A published end-to-end phase ledger of a design loop on the late-2026 software stack.
- A published rank agreement between a shared policy and per-design specialists.
- A published ten-fold gain in end-to-end time to a qualified legged-robot design against a comparable baseline.
- A rigid-body throughput figure for the one Metal-capable incumbent on Apple silicon.

### 1.3 What this plan does not claim

The following statements appeared in version 0.2 or follow from a careless reading of it. They are withdrawn (DESIGN;
the reason for each is the row of §1.1 or §1.2 that contradicts it).

1. Deterministic GPU replay as such. Two incumbents document opt-in bitwise run-to-run determinism.
2. "The CPU version is a different code base." One kernel compiler emits CPU and CUDA code from one source, and one
   engine runs on its CPU device.
3. Different robot topologies in one GPU batch, as a capability. One environment suite and two solvers of one engine
   document it.
4. The combination of mixed topologies, determinism and articulated contact as an incumbent gap. One experimental
   solver documents all three, and its tests exercise the combination on small chains.
5. Electrical and thermal actuator modelling as a novelty.
6. "No training needed" for baseline control.
7. Anytime-valid comparison as a novelty of the field.
8. One kernel source for several backends, and simulation on several tiers, as novelties.
9. Apple-GPU support as a first.
10. Interior scenes for homes, kitchens, retail stores and warehouses as a novelty.
11. An agent interface to a simulator as such.
12. The humanoid throughput target of version 0.2 as parity, and its note that no absolute incumbent figure was found.
    Published figures exist and the target was about five times below one of them.
13. Any ten-fold claim that rests on per-step throughput, on sampling control as the evaluator, or on a published
    ten-fold in time to a qualified design. None is supported.
14. "Morphology is fixed before the simulator starts." State-preserving recompilation on the CPU contradicts it.
15. That an imported model with an impossible inertia "loads without complaint" everywhere. One incumbent's compiler
    rejects physically impossible inertias.
16. That an incumbent loop teaches an agent its mistake "six hours later". Published training takes about seven
    minutes for a flat-ground quadruped task, under 15 to 30 minutes for humanoids, and about an hour for a default
    rough-terrain humanoid run.

### 1.4 What is already solved, and what nobody has composed

Each of the following exists and works (sources in Appendix H):

- Linear-time articulated-body dynamics in spatial algebra (Featherstone), and its Lie-group formulation (Park,
  Bobrow, Ploen).
- Convex, compliant contact that scales to thousands of GPU worlds (MuJoCo's formulation in MuJoCo Warp and Newton;
  Drake's SAP and its successors on the CPU).
- Lie-group and variational integrators with discrete conservation laws (Iserles et al.; Marsden and West; Lee, Leok,
  McClamroch).
- Invariant filtering for legged state estimation (Barrau and Bonnabel; Hartley et al.).
- Morphological symmetry groups and equivariant policies (Ordoñez-Apraez et al.), and the symmetry classification of
  gaits (Golubitsky, Stewart, Buono, Collins).
- Monotone co-design with guaranteed fixed points (Censi), grammar-based robot search, and trajectory optimization
  with design variables.
- Anytime-valid sequential inference, already implemented in FrankenSim (`fs-race`, `fs-eproc`), and published for
  robot policy comparison.
- Sampling-based predictive control of legged robots without offline training.
- One policy across a class of bodies, and policy sharing across design candidates.
- Certified collision-free regions of configuration space; support-region and wrench-cone feasibility as linear
  programs (Bretl and Lall; Orsolino et al.).
- Exact family answers on small plants by standard means. In the pilots behind this version, a lifted robust linear
  program, a projection, an SMT solver and quantifier elimination each returned the same complete family answer as a
  specialized method on every fixture tried (FACT, Appendix K).
- Adaptive stress testing and importance sampling for rare failures; delta debugging; conformal prediction; topology
  optimization.

What was not found is their composition: one design identity and one evidence ledger carried across static analysis,
simulation tiers, statistics, family queries, adversarial search, calibration and solid mechanics, in one typed
algebra, so that a statement proved or measured at one layer is usable at the next and is withdrawn when an edit
invalidates it. FrankenSim's thesis is that such a typed algebra collapses an archipelago of tools into a continuum
(FACT: FrankenSim plan §1). FrankenRobotics applies that thesis to robots and takes it one step further: the algebra
is not only the type system, it is the source code of the kernels.

That the composition is worth more than its parts is a HYPOTHESIS, and it is the central one. Partial precedents exist
(a co-design framework with a structural filter, a static sizing toolkit for arms, anytime-valid policy comparison).
Almost every mechanism in this plan can in principle be hosted by an incumbent engine with a layer on top (H-19,
ACTIVE). The only test of the composition is the end-to-end comparison against a composed incumbent baseline in §39,
and §4 (BET-14) says what the program does if that baseline ties.

### 1.5 What FrankenRobotics is

Six products that share one model, one evidence ledger and one verb registry.

1. **A proving ground (Arena, Cortex).** A vectorized, device-resident environment API over batched physics. It runs
   legged, wheeled, tracked and hybrid robots across generated terrain and generated or ingested interiors: homes,
   apartments, offices, warehouses, manufacturing plants, retail stores, commercial kitchens. Many different robots
   share one batch (Phylum). Missions are stated as requirements, and a result is qualified in a lane that the
   discovery process cannot read.
2. **A design studio for agents (Atelier, Tether).** A CLI and an MCP server with verbs to create and edit a robot
   design, analyze it without simulation, simulate it, compare it against another design with statistical honesty,
   read structured telemetry about why it behaved as it did, optimize it, and ask which earlier verdicts survive an
   edit.
3. **A mission-query engine (Augur).** Given a mission, a catalogue of parts, a controller class and a description of
   what the robot can observe and when, it returns the set of designs that can do the job: an inner set with
   witnesses, an outer set with exclusions, the unresolved cells between them, and the cheapest experiment that would
   shrink the gap. The body, a sensor and the building are all admissible answers.
4. **An adversary and a counterfactual debugger (Nemesis, Autopsy).** A search for the worlds that break a design,
   bounded by physical legality and by a witness that the design's own body could have coped; a reduction of each
   failure to a minimal counterexample world; valid bounds on rare failure rates; and an explanation of a failure
   obtained by intervening on forked replays, reported with the stability of the attribution.
5. **A path to reality and to the workshop (Ground, Foundry).** Calibration of the model against imported measurements
   with predictions frozen in advance, reality bands issued only inside a calibrated family, and build packets (parts,
   geometry, tolerances, fatigue margins) that carry machine-readable flags saying they authorize nothing.
6. **A mathematical instrument (Marrow, Lemma, Spark).** A Lie-algebraic formulation of design, simulation and control
   in which the mathematics is load-bearing: it generates kernels, supplies test oracles, prunes designs before
   simulation, and, where a checker can accept it, carries proofs and portable certificates that an offline auditor
   re-checks.

Five nouns recur and are defined in Appendix A. A **design** is a robot's intrinsic properties and connections. A
**world** is geometry, material fields, lighting, moving objects and their behaviour. A **task** is initial states,
observations, actions, goals, terminal events and metrics. A **mission** is a task family with requirements and the
quantifiers that relate designs, controllers and worlds. A **study** binds versions of these to controllers, random
streams, numerical settings, hardware profiles and one declared analysis rule.
