### 1.7 Why the suite, and why now

FACT, from inspection of the sibling repositories on 2026-11-21 (FrankenSim at commit `483d09c682f2`):

- **FrankenSim already contains the hard referee-grade pieces.** SE(3) and SO(3) with exponential, logarithm, adjoint,
  coadjoint and Jacobians (`frankensim/crates/fs-ga/src/lie.rs`); Featherstone forward and inverse dynamics for
  floating-base trees (`fs-mbd/src/articulated.rs`); a 29-degree-of-freedom Unitree G1 model with provenance
  (`fs-mbd/src/robot_models.rs`); a semismooth-Newton Signorini–Coulomb contact solve and certified continuous
  collision detection (`fs-contact`); a discrete Euler–Poincaré step on SE(3) with its adjoint (`fs-time`); CMA-ES,
  Bayesian optimization and MAP-Elites (`fs-dfo`, `fs-bo`, `fs-archive`); max-plus algebra (`fs-tropical`);
  anytime-valid racing and e-processes (`fs-race`, `fs-eproc`); units, intervals, evidence and a ledger.
- **It also contains pieces version 0.2 did not use.** Multilevel Monte Carlo, control variates, Gaussian importance
  sampling and Shapley effects (`fs-uq`); value-of-information ranking (`fs-voi`); sum-of-squares programs and
  interval verification (`fs-sos`); dimensional-analysis regimes (`fs-regime`); an out-of-process package checker
  (`fs-checker`); Floquet analysis of a supplied monodromy (`fs-spectral/src/floquet.rs`); topology optimization and
  tolerance allocation (`fs-topopt`, `fs-toleralloc`); rods and fatigue (`fs-solid`, with the rainflow counter in
  `fs-material`); port-Hamiltonian interconnection (`fs-phs`); film and tribology models (`fs-tribo`, `fs-lbm`). No
  splitting or subset-simulation code exists there.
- **FrankenSim does not contain what a gym needs.** No batched environments, no GPU path in its workspace, no terrain
  or interior scene representation for robots, no robot sensors, no MCP server. Its articulated contact step refuses
  more than 21 contacts (`fs-contact/src/sustained/solve.rs`: `MAX_CONTACTS = 21`) and it has no complete persistent
  contact time stepper (`fs-contact/CONTRACT.md`). Its accelerator doctrine says "FrankenSim does not ship an
  accelerator backend" and "The CPU reference is permanent" (`frankensim/docs/ACCELERATOR_DOCTRINE.md`).
- **The suite has proven the GPU pattern outside FrankenSim's workspace.** One kernel source compiled for CUDA through
  `cudarc` and NVRTC and for Metal through a prelude of macros, checked against a CPU emulation
  (`frankensim/apps/instrument-lab/render-gpu-piano/src/{kernel.h,cuda.rs,metal.rs,emulate.rs}`), and a generic Metal
  compute gateway whose documentation names "a physics integrator" as an intended consumer
  (`frankentorch/crates/ft-kernel-metal/src/compute.rs`). The gateway accepts at most 31 buffer arguments
  (`MAX_ARGUMENTS = 31`).
- **The MCP substrate exists.** `fastmcp_rust` is a cancel-aware MCP framework built on asupersync contexts and
  checkpoints, with tool, resource and prompt surfaces (`fastmcp_rust/crates/fastmcp/src/lib.rs`). Its own
  documentation says support for the 2026-07-28 protocol revision is under implementation and not yet claimed, so
  `frob-mcp` is admitted through INT-FMCP-01, and KILL-MCP names its fallbacks, the last of which is the CLI alone
  (§32, §33).
- **The limits of the siblings are known and shape the design.** FrankenTorch tensors are host memory and its device
  tags are metadata, so the learner runs in this project's own device kernels (§23). `fs-qty` needs the nightly
  feature `generic_const_exprs` (`frankensim/crates/fs-qty/src/lib.rs`), and most FrankenSim physics crates depend on
  it, which ties the toolchain to nightlies on which that feature compiles: a named risk tested at
  INT-TOOLCHAIN-01, with a small stable `frob-units` crate as the documented escape hatch. The siblings are on four
  different pinned nightlies today (`2026-07-06`, `2026-08-20`, `2026-08-25`, `2026-08-31`). That is the starting
  state. The whole build graph uses one toolchain T, chosen at INT-TOOLCHAIN-01, and the siblings that are not on T
  are moved to it in their own repositories by a toolchain train (§33.13). FrankenLean's tactic crate
  (`franken_lean/crates/fln-anvil`, 1,423 lines) implements a discrimination tree and the `omega` procedure, and its
  other tactics are stubs; FrankenSymPy's real-root machinery is capped (8 variables, degree 256, 4,096 bits,
  zero-dimensional ideals), and it has no homotopy solver. Proof routes (§12) and synthesis lanes (§25) are sized to
  those caps.

FACT (to recheck), reported by review and not yet reproduced by this program at a pinned commit. Each becomes an
admission test and an upstream work item (§33, Appendix F) before anything depends on the component:

- Three errors in `fs_g1_train::ppo_update` (`frankensim/crates/fs-g1-train/src/ppo.rs`): for a negative advantage the
  clipped surrogate is applied on the wrong side of the ratio; the critic gradient into the shared bias is zero where
  the squared-error objective gives a non-zero value; and concatenating two independently reset one-step episodes
  moves a frozen policy's second ratio from 1 to 1.582459.
- A wrong joint law in the action sampler of the same file (`fs_g1_train::gaussian_action`): each marginal is
  correct, and adjacent channels agree in sign with probability 0.6655 where independence gives one half (§23.25,
  §33.17).
- A near-straight integration defect in `fs-mbd`'s planar drive (`frankensim/crates/fs-mbd/src/planar_drive.rs`): at a
  heading of 32 rad with wheel speeds that differ by 6 × 10⁻¹³ m/s the routine returns zero translation where the true
  one-second displacement is about (0.834, 0.551) m. It must be qualified against an independent SE(2) exponential
  before it is used as an oracle.
- A stride-convention trap between `franken_numpy` and `frankentorch`: an unconverted stride reads 12 where 3 is
  correct.
- A fixed-witness assumption in the sustained articulated contact path of FrankenSim: it assumes fixed material
  witnesses and a fixed frame, and rolling around a sharp lip changes both. The referee's transactional step therefore
  migrates witnesses (§16).

These are five defects or limits (§33.11, §33.17). Beside them stands one convention hazard, confirmed by reading:
`fs-mbd::Wrench` holds a world-frame force and a body-frame torque in one value, unlike §11.1, and it crosses the
airlock only through a typed conversion (§33.17). Six further facts found later are counted separately and recorded with their admission tests in the last subsection of §33: two cases in which the bound verifier of `fs-sos` returns a value that is not a bound; welded masses omitted by the suite's G1 catalog builder; a series limit that refuses the differential of the SE(3) exponential beyond 32 m of translation; a swept-sphere helper that covers straight motion only; and two more convention hazards, the sign of the legacy transformer in `fs-phs` and a ray direction renormalized under a scaled instance in `f3d-math`.

FrankenRobotics is therefore the missing product on top of a mostly present foundation. FrankenSim is the referee and
the bedrock, consumed by path behind one airlock crate and never forked (§33). FrankenRobotics owns the batched
Lie-algebraic rollout engine, the scenes, the sensors, the learning loop, the mission layer, the adversary, the record
and the agent-facing studio.

### 1.8 The two machines

The program has two machines and uses each for what it is good at (DESIGN; orchestration across them is [F], §21 and
§36).

| | Linux host `trj` | This Mac Studio |
|---|---|---|
| Hardware (FACT) | Two RTX 4090, 24 GB each, no link between the cards; often heavily loaded | M5 Ultra: 36 CPU cores, an 80-core GPU, 256 GB of unified memory; a measured Metal working-set limit of about 222 GiB and a largest single buffer of about 167 GiB; memory bandwidth 1.2 TB/s by the vendor's figure |
| Role | Training and high-throughput rollouts on CUDA; the two cards run independent shards | The world bank and large scenes; proof and symbolic work; the sampled referee; replay; the viewer; large-memory jobs; a Metal rollout tier whose throughput is a measured number (BET-09) |
| Crosses the boundary | Seeds, policy weights and receipts only | Seeds, policy weights and receipts only |

Scale facts that follow from byte models and one incumbent measurement (FACT and derivation, Appendix H): per-world
state is about 20–53 kB for a quadruped and 56–180 kB for a humanoid, so 8,192 quadruped worlds or 4,096 humanoid
worlds use about 1 to 3% of a 24 GB card and memory does not bind at the planned batch sizes; a 2 cm home scene is
tens of megabytes and a 2 cm warehouse several gigabytes, which is why the Mac holds the world bank; a CPU referee at
0.2–1.0× real time per core on 24 cores can shadow about 0.1–2.4% of GPU world-seconds, which is why referee work is
sampled; the figure scales with referee speed and is measured at M2. Whether the step on an RTX 4090 is bound by
memory bandwidth at these state sizes is a HYPOTHESIS for the M2 profile: bandwidth arithmetic suggests it, and an
incumbent step trace with 47% of its time in the solver does not show it. On the Mac, the BET-09 threshold needs
about a tenth of the available memory bandwidth, so command-buffer overhead and the GPU's arithmetic rate are what
must be measured.

## 2. The ten-fold thesis

The owner's ambition for this project is comparative: an order of magnitude better than every existing system at
getting from a robot-design question to an answer that can be trusted. This chapter states what that means as a
measurement, where the time in today's loops goes, which ceilings follow from that, which mechanisms the program bets
on, what will not deliver the result, and what range the evidence supports. The protocol is in §39. Nothing here is a
result.

### 2.1 The metric

**Time to an independently accepted answer.** DESIGN: the unit of success is an answer, not a step and not a score.
The reason is that every published bound on step speed, and every pilot behind this version, says the same thing: the
time between a question and a trusted answer is dominated by what happens around the step (§2.2).

- An **answer** is what the mission asks for. It is one of: a design and controller that pass a frozen acceptance
  battery; a family answer with inner and outer design sets and witnesses (§25); a correct withdrawal or confirmation
  of earlier verdicts after an amendment (§28); or a truthful `unknown` with the required witness, where the question
  is whether the evidence identifies the choice at all.
- **Independently accepted** means that a checker which is not the proposing system accepted it: an acceptance battery
  on worlds and in an evaluator that neither arm trained in, the offline auditor `frob-verify` for every submitted
  certificate, and a neutral adjudicator who releases receipts only after both arms close (§39).
- The **clock** T starts when the agent or engineer receives the mission and the permitted inputs. It stops when the
  checker accepts the first correct answer with all requested scope and precision. Unsuccessful runs, training,
  tuning, compilation, device transfer, waiting, investigation of unknowns, certificate checking, repair and review
  are all inside it.
- The **restricted mean time** at a common deadline H is RMT = E[min(T, H)], taken over the sealed missions of a
  stratum. A mission that is unresolved at H costs H.
- The **ratio** for a stratum is R = E[min(T_rival, H)] ÷ E[min(T_frob, H)], where the rival is the **strongest
  composed rival**: leading simulators, an optimizer, analytic bounds, a verifier and the same AI agent, assembled and
  tuned by a competent baseline engineer on development fixtures and then frozen (§39).

Four properties of the metric are fixed here because they shape the plan.

1. **Missed deadlines cap the ratio.** If the candidate misses a fraction q of deadlines, then R ≤ 1/q. With 12%
   unfinished the ratio cannot exceed 25/3 ≈ 8.33. Coverage is therefore a first-order design goal, and a refusal that
   arrives late is as costly as a failure.
2. **Correctness is a gate, not a term.** One false certificate disqualifies an arm from the scoped claim. A
   dangerously wrong accepted answer fails the mission. The time score is never improved by lowering the bar for what
   counts as accepted.
3. **Cold and warm runs are separate results.** A cold run includes authoring the environment and the design domain,
   for both arms. A warm campaign runs a declared sequence of amendments with identical reusable inputs and cache
   budgets, keeps failed amendments in the sequence, and reports the **crossover reuse count**: the number of
   amendments after which the candidate's one-time authoring has paid for itself. A fair rival also caches graphs,
   factors and compiled kernels.
4. **The clock is not the only column.** GPU-hours, CPU-hours, energy, agent tokens, human minutes and money are
   reported beside wall time under identical resource caps. Two derived units are reported for the design loop:
   designs decided per hour, and compute per established decision at a matched error rate.

The decision rule that turns measured ratios into the word "ten-fold", with its power analysis, its censoring rule and
its multiplicity control, is in §39. One finding binds it from here: a draft rule that required a point estimate of at
least 10 on every brief confirmed a true ratio of 10 in at most 18% of simulated campaigns (FACT, Appendix K). The
rule of §39 is therefore specified on a pooled ratio, and its power against a true ratio of 10 is computed before the
sealed suite is opened. The sealed-suite result is a finite-suite result: it describes the missions of that suite. A
claim about the population of missions needs at least 32 independent mission families, and the suite size, the unit
of independence and the estimator are fixed in §39 (§39.7, §39.20). A measured ratio is always reported with its
interval, whatever it is.

### 2.2 The Amdahl ledger: where the time goes today

The table composes published figures for the phases of an agent-driven design loop on incumbent stacks. Every row is a
FACT about its source (Appendix H) unless marked. It is not a measurement of a loop: no end-to-end phase ledger of a
design loop on the late-2026 software stack was found, so the denominator of any ratio must be measured by this
program at M0 and M1 before a mechanism is funded against it (§39).

| Phase | Published figure | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Propose and diagnose (the agent's turn) | One published agent co-design loop reports about 1 h per round of 16 candidates on eight GPUs, "dominated by RL evaluation". Its estimate of 4 minutes of language-model time per round appears in one version of the paper only and is modelled, not measured. | Agent latency per serial turn is taken as 60–120 s in the bounds below (HYPOTHESIS; the M0 ledger measures it). It is common to both arms. |
| Realize the design | Text to mesh in 1–2 minutes and mesh to robot description in about 30 s in one published pipeline. | A parametric edit is assumed to take 0.5 minute in an incumbent (HYPOTHESIS). |
| Compile and first step | One stack reports that just-in-time compilation "can be slow (1-3 minutes)"; a second compiles kernels at first launch, "can take a minute", and caches them on disk; a third starts in 4.4–6.3 s with cached shaders and 263 s without, and loads a warehouse scene in 27 s. | No latency from a topology edit to the first GPU step is published. The compile region of the quadruped run below is about 45 s and is inside its 410 s. |
| Train, quadruped | About 410 s on one RTX 4090 and about 325 s on two for a flat-ground joystick policy; under 4 minutes on flat ground and 20 minutes on rough terrain on one GPU in an earlier result. | The dominant phase for quadruped briefs: about 85% of a composite iteration of 5.9 minutes. Deleting training and compilation outright would give 6.6×. The composite joins figures from different stacks and is not a measurement. |
| Train, humanoid | Under 15 minutes for one humanoid and under 30 minutes for two others on two RTX 4090 (first-stage flat-ground training); about 1 h for a default rough-terrain run on one RTX 4090 (derived). | The dominant phase for humanoid briefs: over 90% of a composite iteration of about 31 minutes. |
| Environment step as a share of training | 87% for a rough-terrain humanoid, 85% for a dexterous hand and 46% for a cart-pole on one stack; on another, physics is about 29% of the full environment step. | Sets the bound on what a faster step can do (§2.3). |
| Evaluate | 128 rollouts of 1,000 steps per design in one campaign: seconds at 10⁵ steps/s (derived). | Not a bottleneck in incumbents. |
| Confirm | Five retrainings of the winner in two published campaigns. | Multiplies the training phase for finalists. |
| Trainings per campaign | 80, 80, 125 and 1,600 trained candidates in four published campaigns; 100 new robots per generation for 20 to 50 generations in a fifth. | 7.5 to 30 GPU-minutes per trained candidate. |
| Compute per campaign | About 40 GPU-hours per five-round run on eight GPUs; about 200 GPU-hours per seed on eight A100. | — |
| Candidates that fail trivially | Under 2% of morphology proposals fail validation before training in one loop; 15.8% of trained candidates are degenerate after a full training run with a strong language model, and 35–49% with smaller ones. | If 16% is the ceiling, pruning trivial failures alone cuts trainings by at most 1.19×. |
| Human or agent diagnosis | Not published. | Measured in the phase ledger. |

### 2.3 The ceilings

Each ceiling is arithmetic on the FACT rows above. Each is the reason one tempting strategy is not the plan.

1. **Engine speed alone.** At a fixed sample count, an infinitely fast environment step speeds training by at most
   1/(1 − s), where s is the step's share: about 7.7× (1/(1 − 0.87)) for the rough-terrain humanoid, 6.7× for the
   hand and 1.9× for the cart-pole on one incumbent stack, and about 1.4× from physics alone on another. An incumbent
   already measures about 2.55 M humanoid world-steps/s. There is no order of magnitude left in the step, and a
   faster simulator alone cannot deliver ten-fold end to end.
2. **The design cycle alone.** A design-check-simulate-explain-edit cycle of 120 s with no training in it (NS-06) is
   3.0–3.5× faster than an incumbent quadruped cycle of 360–420 s (300 s of training plus an agent turn of 60–120 s),
   and about 15× faster than a 30-minute humanoid run. The comparison is valid only if a controller that needs no
   per-design training can stand in for a trained policy when designs are ranked. That is untested (BET-17).
3. **One design per agent turn.** With the same agent latency t in both arms and about 300 s of incumbent training
   (a round planning value just under the published 325 s on two RTX 4090), deciding one design per turn gives at
   most (300 + t)/t, which is 3.5–6× for t between 60 and 120 s, even if FrankenRobotics spent no compute at all.
   Against the one-card figure of 410 s the same cap is 4.4–7.8×. It is below ten either way.
4. **Compute per decision.** Let C be the incumbent's cost per trained candidate, c the cost of the cheap rung per
   design, c_T the cost of the training rung, and f the fraction of simulated designs that are trained. The compute
   ratio is C ÷ (c + c_T·f). With C = 410 GPU-s (one RTX 4090), an illustrative c of 38 GPU-s and c_T = 410 GPU-s
   (training at parity), the ceiling at f = 0 is about 10.8×, a ratio of ten needs f ≤ 0.7%, and no f reaches ten if
   the cheap rung costs more than 41 GPU-s. A cheaper cheap rung, many designs per rung, or a cheaper training rung is
   required; pruning alone is not enough.
5. **The general bound.** If a fraction f of the strong baseline's matched wall time is improved by a factor r and the
   method adds overhead h, the speedup is at most 1/(1 − f + f/r + h). Infinite acceleration of 85% of the time cannot
   reach ten. With f = 0.97, r = 40 and h = 0.02 the ceiling is about 13.5×. The three terms are measured on the
   rival's critical path, and a pruning ratio is never multiplied by a GPU speedup measured on work the pruning
   already removed.
6. **Unremovable cost.** If the cost that no mechanism removes (authoring the mission, checking certificates,
   serializing, reviewing) already exceeds one tenth of the strongest baseline's time, ten-fold requires changing
   another stage or changing the claim. In one pilot a residual of 575.7 µs that the solver does not touch (parsing,
   assembly, checking, serialization and harness, not separately timed) capped the measurable ratio at about 1.46
   (842.8 ÷ 575.7; FACT, Appendix K).
7. **Completion.** R ≤ 1/q (§2.1). An arm that leaves one mission in eight unresolved cannot show ten-fold however
   fast it is on the rest.

Three smaller ceilings close other doors: per-design specialization of the recursions is capped near 1.2× on an
incumbent's step trace (H-04); whether structure-exploiting constraint assembly and solve give more than parity is
open and is measured at M2 (H-04b, §16); exact reuse of rollouts after a mass or geometry edit is at most about 10%
of compute (H-09); and stopping rules give 2–5× when candidates are well separated and about 1× when they are not
(H-10).

### 2.4 The levers

No single mechanism delivers ten-fold, and no conjunction has been shown to (§0.8). The candidate thesis is a
conjunction of eight levers, each of which attacks a different row of the ledger. Seven of the eight are methods a
composed rival can also host; §2.6 says what that implies. The "surviving number" column gives the range the evidence
supports; every entry is a HYPOTHESIS about this system, and published figures behind it are FACTs in Appendix H.
Gates are named by the section that owns them; their identifiers and thresholds are in §40.

| # | Lever | Mechanism and section | Surviving number | Tier | Gate |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Decide many designs per turn** | A design family per dispatch: per-world model variants inside padded capacities and size buckets, many different robots in one batch (Phylum, §17); population verbs and slot-level dispatch so one agent turn returns a ranked family and not one score (§28, §32). | One incumbent solver's mixed batch runs at 0.86 of the harmonic mean of its homogeneous rates; that solver is not deterministic and is slower than its framework's reduced-coordinate solvers. Published population methods report compute gains of about 3–4× (H-03, H-23). Removes the (300 + t)/t cap of §2.3. | [S] for parameter variants within a topology; [F] for mixed topologies | The head-to-head of §17 with a per-family-template control arm; two numbers against the incumbent mixed batch (BET-18) |
| 2 | **Train few** | Family policies per morphology class, conditioned on the design; inheritance along lineage edges; both admitted only where measured rank agreement with per-design specialists is high enough (Cortex, §23). | Zero-shot at 70–85% of specialist return within a class on flat or mildly varied ground; fine-tuning from a class prior at about 2–25% of a from-scratch run stopped at matched return; the one published parent-to-child figure is about 50%; single-limb topology edits 33–100% (H-02, H-21). Rank agreement is unmeasured; the nearest published figure, 0.40, is for an easier comparison (H-22a). | [F] | The rank-agreement gate of §23 and §28 (BET-17), then BET-15 and BET-16. A paired correction gains 1/(1 − ρ²) in the limit of free GPU samples: 2× at a tier correlation of 0.7, 3× at 0.82 and 10× at 0.95; the correlation is unmeasured and may be near zero for fall events. | [S] for stopping; [F] for ladder allocation | The cascade gates of §28; the fidelity gates of §16 |
| 4 | **Find failures instead of waiting for them** | Adversarial search inside legality bounds with a solvability witness; reduction to minimal counterexample worlds; bounded-weight rare-event estimation, with exploration kept apart from certification (Nemesis, §26). | Published measured gains in finding failures are 2–20×; 10–100× at failure probabilities of 10⁻⁴–10⁻⁵ is a TARGET. The gain is in finding failures and in refuting a failure-rate target; certifying absence is never cheaper than crude sampling (H-07). | [S] for bounded-weight estimation; [F] for minimal counterexample worlds | The planted-trap gates of §26 (BET-22, BET-32) |

The levers multiply only where they act on different time. Lever 1 and lever 2 act on the two largest rows of the
ledger and carry most of the thesis. Levers 3, 4 and 7 reduce the number of episodes and of agent turns. Lever 5
changes what an answer is. Levers 6 and 8 are hygiene that keeps the others from being eaten by overhead.

### 2.5 What will not deliver ten-fold

Stated plainly, so that no work package is funded on a hope the evidence has already closed.

- **A faster step.** Engine throughput is a parity requirement (§36). The plan must match incumbents closely enough
  that the levers above are not cancelled; it does not look for the result there. One engine-internal throughput
  question is open: structure-exploiting constraint assembly and solve (§16). Its ceiling on an incumbent's trace is
  2.6×. It is measured at M2 and is not counted in the thesis until then.
- **Per-design kernel specialization.** Specialization of the recursions is capped near 1.2×. It is an optimization
  for survivors, and only if our own profile shows the recursion share justifies it.
- **Half precision or tensor cores for contact.** Refuted (H-15). Not built.
- **Sampling control as a stand-in evaluator.** Even the most sample-efficient published controller costs about
  4 × 10³ times a policy rollout per simulated second, so a battery of 256 twenty-second episodes takes about 86
  minutes of a device against about 1.3 s for a policy. It is a screening rung, a fallback and a source of
  demonstrations. Its episodes are acceptance evidence only for itself, where it is the delivered controller (§22.8,
  H-01).
- **One universal policy.** Out of reach at an affordable pretraining budget (H-02).
- **Static checks alone.** Pruning trivial failures caps near 1.19× on trainings. Their value is feedback in seconds
  and typed repairs, which is lever 1 and lever 7, not pruning.
- **Reusing rollouts across edits.** Exact reuse is at most about 10% (H-09).
- **A faster solver for family queries.** In the pilot, a specialized solver measured 1.345× warm and 1.088× cold
  against a composed one, with a ceiling of about 1.46× set by a residual the solver does not touch (FACT, Appendix
  K).
- **Certificates, full-room multiphysics and generative structure.** Certificates change what can be trusted, coupled
  multiphysics changes which failures are visible, and structure optimization improves the built object. None shortens
  the time to a decision (H-12, H-16), and none is counted in the thesis.
- **Any published ten-fold.** None was found for time to a qualified legged-robot design.

### 2.6 The expected range, by mission class

HYPOTHESIS, to be replaced by the partial gate at M3 and the tournament at M7. The ranges are what the ceilings of
§2.3 and the surviving numbers of §2.4 allow. They are stated against the incumbent as it is commonly run, with
per-design training and a standard outer loop. The metric of §2.1 is against the strongest composed rival, which may
host every portable lever; against that rival the expected ratio on fixed-topology CUDA missions is near one unless
an engine-internal property binds, and no range is offered. §39 reports both, with the recovery ratio between them.
They are not forecasts with probabilities.

| Mission class | Incumbent denominator (FACT) | Binding ceiling | Expected ratio against per-design training | What must be true |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Quadruped locomotion briefs with parametric and single-limb edits | Training in about 410 s on one RTX 4090; a cycle of about 360–420 s | One design per turn caps at 3.5–7.8×; compute per decision caps near 10.8× at f = 0 | 3 to 10 | Many designs per turn; under about 1% of simulated designs trained; rank agreement above threshold for the class |
| Humanoid locomotion briefs | Training in under 30 minutes on two RTX 4090; about 1 h for a default rough-terrain run | Phase arithmetic does not bind, since training is over 90% of the iteration; the cycle arithmetic of §2.3 gives 15–30×, and the completion ceiling 1/q applies | 5 to 20 | A baseline or family policy stands in for training when designs are ranked (BET-06, BET-15, BET-17). Otherwise near parity |
| Wheeled, tracked and hybrid briefs in interiors | No published loop; scene build time at thousands of worlds not published | Unmeasured | 3 to 10, with low confidence | Clearance and static analysis remove candidates before any training |
| Family queries with amendments, warm | An expert with a linear-programming, SMT or reachability tool over an incumbent | The residual a faster solver does not touch (parsing, assembly, checking, serialization and harness); the crossover reuse count | 1 to 3 per query, more only through reuse across amendments; cold may be below 1 | Deriving the abstraction from a rich plant is cheaper than an expert doing it by hand |
| Failure discovery and repair | Uniform randomization and logs | The proposal must cover the failure mode; certifying absence gains nothing | 2 to 20 in episodes to a planted failure (published range), up to 100 as a TARGET; about 3 in repair turns | A good distress score; the solvability witness |
| Facility and multi-robot missions | No composed incumbent workflow was found | Unmeasured | Not estimated | [M] scope; a ratio is claimed only for strata that were run |

On quadruped missions the range against per-design training tops out at ten, and reaching the top needs every lever
to work at once, including the two that are least measured (family policies and rank agreement). The denominator is
an accepted decision and not a training run: a 1% failure bound at 95% confidence costs 299 failure-free episodes per
accepted design in every arm. On humanoid missions the range is wider because the incumbent's training phase is
longer. If, on any stratum, a short
robust program over an incumbent engine reaches the same accepted answers in comparable time, the report says so, the
mechanisms ship as a layer over that engine for that stratum, and engine work continues only for the gaps that are
internal to an engine (BET-14).

### 2.7 What the program does first because of this

1. **Measure the rival before building against it.** At M0 and M1 the incumbent loop is timed by phase on `trj`,
   starting with what needs no agent: cold start, a topology edit to the first step, and training to threshold on one
   and two cards. Versions and warm configurations are pinned and frozen first (§39).
2. **Run the rank-agreement experiment early.** Whether cheap rungs order designs as the trained, referee-promoted
   rung does decides lever 2 and half of lever 3. About forty per-design trainings (about 5 GPU-hours where the
   specialists of §23 are reused, about 45 otherwise; §28.10) need the owner's approval because they exceed the
   default compute envelope (§23, §42).
3. **Put the first mission slice on the CPU at M1.** The docking fixture of NS-22 exercises the mission query, the
   clock contract, the certificate bundle and the auditor before any GPU work exists.
4. **Hold a partial gate at M3** on legged and wheeled briefs, with a written rule for each outcome (BET-13), and the
   tournament at M7.

## 3. Twelve principles

Each principle is the short form of a section. The plan stands or falls with them.

1. **Algebra first, numbers last, and no ornamental mathematics.** State is stored as elements of Lie groups and
   advanced by maps that stay on the group. Every hot kernel is the image of an algebraic object under a derivation we
   can replay, with a content hash. A construction stays in the plan only if it owns a type, a verb an agent can call,
   a test that fails when the mathematics is wrong, and a measured payoff or a kill date (§9, §10, §13, §21).
2. **One model, three tiers, one ledger of disagreement; the CPU reference is permanent.** The referee tier, the CPU
   batch tier and the GPU tier run the same model, and their differences are measured and stored, never assumed away.
   GPUs propose and the referee disposes: a fast-tier result is provisional until it is promoted, and any world can be
   re-run alone on the CPU from its address (§16, §21, §29).
3. **Compose, don't enumerate; a body is data.** A robot is a composition of modules over typed ports, which is also
   FrankenSim's governing rule. Because a design lowers to tables and not to code, many different robots run in one
   batch, a new design recompiles nothing, and the unit of dispatch is a family (§14, §17).
4. **Consume the suite, never fork it, behind one airlock.** FrankenSim is taken by path dependency and pinned by
   commit; one crate names its volatile types. Every sibling is the owner's, so what is missing or wrong in one is
   changed there, in its own repository and under its own rules, as an upstream work item with a failing fixture,
   an interim posture and a switch-over rule. Fallbacks are named in order before they are needed (§33).
5. **Check before you simulate, simulate before you train, train before you claim; every design stands on day one.**
   Static analyses return in seconds with typed repairs. A baseline estimator and controller are synthesized from the
   model, so no design waits for a learned policy before it gets feedback. Each rung of the ladder is trusted only as
   far as its measured rank agreement with the rung above (§22, §23, §28).
6. **The unit of work is a decision over a family of designs, not a score for one design.** A mission names the design
   family, the worlds, what the controller may observe and when, and the quantifiers that relate them. The answer is
   an inner set, an outer set, witnesses, and the next experiment. The body, a sensor, the timing of a packet and the
   building are all design variables (§19, §20, §25).
7. **Counterexamples are an output.** The system searches for the world that breaks a design, shrinks it to the fewest
   edits that still break it, and ships it as a regression. Every rule in this plan travels with the smallest
   hand-checkable case that defeats a plausible shortcut, and every gate has a negative control it must catch (§26,
   §38, Appendix N).
8. **An edit invalidates evidence.** A hash identifies an artifact; only an implication licenses skipping a recheck.
   After any edit the system says which verdicts survive, which are withdrawn and what it would cost to restore them.
   One false reused verdict kills the reuse rule that produced it (§28, §29).
9. **Discovery cannot read confirmation worlds.** Search, tuning and training run in an open lane. Qualification runs
   on fresh sealed world clusters with pre-committed requests and an error budget that shrinks with each submission,
   so the error rate holds across an agent's adaptive retries. Anytime-valid studies and fixed-n studies are both
   offered and never mixed inside one study (§24).
10. **A proof is what a checker accepted; the weakest input wins and nothing is laundered into a proof.** Every result
    carries a claim product whose class is set by its weakest input, by construction of the type. A certificate about
    a family travels in a bundle that an offline auditor re-checks. The word "verified" is not used, and every
    exported artifact says in machine-readable form that it authorizes nothing (§8, §12).
11. **Refuse by name, never approximate in silence; `unknown` is an answer.** A request outside a validity domain gets
    a typed refusal with ranked repairs or a separating witness. A solver that fails leaves the verdict unknown; it
    does not become a failure of the design. Under load the system sheds presentation or refuses; it never lowers the
    physics tier of a running world (§35, §25).
12. **Engine speed is parity, not the thesis; a number is a target until a gate records it.** Throughput must match
    the incumbents and is not where the gain is sought. A recorded number names its world count, time step, substeps,
    solver iterations and contact count; a ratio against a rival names the rival's frozen configuration and every cost
    in the denominator; and a speed test is run only after its ceiling has been computed (§2, §36, §39).

## 4. Bets, each with its falsifier

A bet is a claim the project depends on and could lose. Each names what would falsify it, the competing arm it must
beat or the potency control that shows the test is able to fail, the fallback named in advance, and where it is
measured. Thresholds are TARGETs. Gates carried from version 0.2 are cited by identifier; for new bets the "tested at"
column names the owning section, and the gate identifier and threshold are in §40.

Two terms are used throughout. A **competing arm** is a rival method given the same information, the same budget and a
competent implementation; a bet that never meets one has not been tested. A **potency control** is a planted effect
that the test must detect, or a null on which it must stay silent; a test that passes without one may simply have no
power (§0.7). A falsified bet is reported as falsified, and its fallback ships under the fallback's own name.

BET-01 to BET-12 are carried from version 0.2 with their wording corrected by the incumbent audit. BET-13 onward are
new. BET-13, BET-14 and BET-17 are the three on which the thesis of §2 turns.
