[F] | Zero-shot return on held-out in-class designs is below 70% of the per-design specialist's; or rank agreement with specialists is below the BET-17 threshold; or pretraining, counted in compute, is not repaid within the break-even count N = P/(s·(1 − f)) of §23.11 at the measured P, s and f (illustrative: 60 GPU-hours at f = 0.1 repay after about 590 quadruped designs at s = 410 s, or 70 to 130 humanoid designs). | Arm: per-design PPO from the baseline warm start. Control: designs outside the class must be flagged out-of-distribution, not walked badly in silence. | The per-design behaviour-cloning warm start of version 0.2; the sampling fallback for out-of-distribution designs. No universal policy is attempted. | §23; pilot before funding; M4. Needs an owner-approved compute envelope |
| BET-16 | **Inheritance.** A child design's policy, fine-tuned from its parent along a lineage edge, reaches its return target in a small fraction of from-scratch steps. [F] | A parameter edit needs more than 20% of the steps of a from-scratch control stopped at 95% of its final return; or inheritance does not beat a raw-checkpoint warm start for the edit class; or after a chain of ten inherited generations the final return is more than 5% below a from-scratch control (loss of plasticity). | Arm: from-scratch training with the baseline warm start. Control: an arm that resets on a measured regression of its audit twin, and an arm with a depth schedule. | Inheritance for parameter edits only, with resets on a measured regression and a depth schedule where no audit twin exists; topology edits start from the family policy or from scratch. The gain is bounded by the share of designs that are trained at all. | §23, M4 |
| BET-17 | **Rank agreement between rungs.** Cheap rungs (static check, baseline controller, family policy, short horizon) order designs as the trained, referee-promoted rung does, well enough to eliminate. [F] | Kendall τ between the baseline-controller rung and the trained-policy rung on the held-out corpus is below 0.7 for a morphology class and task family, with thresholds fixed before data are collected. Below 0.5 the cheap rung's verdicts are advisory for that class and the class leaves the speed claim. Or top-k recall, measured by the audit lane, is below its declared floor; or a cut sized from τ alone discards the higher rung's best design in the calibration set (the winner check of §23). | Arm: successive halving on a fixed schedule. Controls: a planted winner; sampled discarded strata; classes expected to be hard (stairs, rubble, bipeds). | The rung is demoted to advisory for that class, the elimination margin widens, and more designs are trained. | §23, §28; M3 (legged, wheeled), M4 (tracked, hybrid). The decisive early experiment (§2.7) |
| BET-18 | **Mixed-topology batches.** Many different robots in one batch beat per-family templates and are competitive with the published incumbent mixed batch on the two numbers that matter. [F] | Against Newton with Kamino or Steel on `trj` we lose on both numbers (distinct designs times steps per second; time from an edit to the first GPU step); or nine per-family templates cover at least 95% of the mutation corpus at higher throughput; or the mixed batch runs below 0.5 of the harmonic mean of its homogeneous rates (the tolerance is 0.70, §36.3 row 10); or any of the 512 designs of a mixed cohort fails to reproduce the digests of its single-design run. | Arms: per-family templates; padding every world to the largest robot; the incumbent heterogeneous solver. | Per-family templates with per-world parameter variants, which are [S]; then sequential environments. | §17, §21; M2 |
| BET-19 | **Mission queries.** A query over a design family, answered with inner and outer sets, witnesses and a next experiment, reaches an accepted answer sooner than point-by-point evaluation and survives amendment. [F] | On the family strata of the sealed suite, a matched reducer (a lifted linear program, an SMT or interval tool, an expert's program) with the same grammar and information reaches the same witnessed answer at comparable cost; or an answer accepted by `frob-verify` is wrong on any locked case. | Arm: an expert with standard solvers. Controls: the quantifier-order fixture, in which every design has a command that works and no single command works for all, must give different answers to the two queries; registered certificate mutations must be rejected. | A tie retires any claim of exclusive expressivity on that fixture, and the query interface ships as a front end that compiles to standard solvers. A false answer withdraws the proof rule that produced it. | §25: a CPU slice at M1, scale at M4; §39 |
| BET-20 | **Region certificates.** Per-constraint certificates with a split set of about six parameters, composed by monotonicity, symmetry and witnesses, resolve a useful share of a family. [F] | On the reference families the unresolved band O ∖ I exceeds the mission's declared maximum after the budget; or a certificate check exceeds its budget; or a registered mutation (swapped contact ordering, an unreported force floor, a passive-authority tag) is accepted. | Arm: dense sampling with statistical labels. Control: the midpoint counterexample (two feasible designs whose midpoint is infeasible) must be excluded from every inner set. | Family answers are reported as tested sample sets with witnesses and make no inner-set claim. Isotropic paving of a high-dimensional box is not attempted in any case (H-06). | §12, §25; M4, M5 |
| BET-21 | **Blinded qualification.** Error control holds across an agent's adaptive retries. [S] | The false-promotion rate exceeds α under 500 adaptive retries on no-signal worlds; or power on planted gains falls below 0.8. | Control: the unblinded procedure, repeated comparison on the same held-out worlds, must show an inflated error rate on the same no-signal worlds. That shows the test can fail. | Fixed-n exact confirmation with a hard cap on submissions per campaign. | §24, M3 |
| BET-22 | **Minimal counterexample worlds.** Adversarial search inside legality bounds finds failures faster than randomization, and each failure shrinks to a world of at most three edits that reproduces bit for bit and that the design's own body could have coped with. [F] | Planted traps of probability at most 3 × 10⁻⁵ are found less than 3× faster than by uniform randomization; or fewer than 70% of reported counterexamples carry a solvability witness; or a shrunk world fails to reproduce bit for bit. | Arms: uniform randomization at equal compute; a scenario-language generator given the same monitors. Controls: planted traps; an unsolvable world, which must be rejected. | Importance-weighted tail sampling, with failing worlds reported unshrunk. | §26, M3 |
| BET-23 | **Interventional autopsy is stable enough to act on.** Attribution by intervention on forked replays names the cause and says how stable the attribution is. [S] | Top-1 accuracy on planted causes is below 90%; or the placebo flip rate exceeds 0.2 on more than half of the reference failures, so that most are unattributable; or an agent with autopsy needs more than one third of the repair turns of an agent with logs. | Arms: first-anomaly ordering; an agent with logs only. Controls: the placebo fork, which must replay bit for bit; planted causes. | Single-factor paired rewind; then first-anomaly ordering, labelled Estimated. | §27, M3 |
| BET-24 | **A requirement language.** Bounded-time requirements serve as the acceptance metric and as a falsification score. They do not replace shaped rewards (H-13). [S] | Requirement robustness disagrees with the reference monitor on any trace of the conformance corpus; or designs accepted by requirement verdicts fail the sealed variants at a rate no lower than designs accepted by a reward threshold. | Arm: acceptance by reward threshold. Control: a policy known to exploit a shaped reward must pass the reward threshold and fail the requirement. | Metric thresholds with declared comparators. Training keeps shaped reward terms in either case. | §24, M3 |
| BET-25 | **An energy-budget safety tier.** A safety claim stated as an energy budget needs no contact model and survives contact uncertainty; reduced-order shields add a statistically measured margin. Classed Tested, never Proved (H-20). [F] | Any false admission on the `.fenergy` mutation corpus; or a shielded policy keeps less than 85% of unshielded return; or the shield costs more than 5% of step time; or the measured margin is violated on shifted worlds beyond its stated rate. | Arm: an unshielded policy trained with a penalty. Control: two friction regimes with identical histories before first slip (the pre-slip aliasing fixture of §22.21), where a monitor alone cannot see the breach in time. | Monitors and reports only, with no shield claim. No full-order certificate is attempted in any case. | §22, §12; M4 |
| BET-26 | **Gait orbits as screening.** Periodic orbits of a design under its baseline controller, continued in design parameters, give a screening signal for periodic gaits on regular ground. Never a referee-ready controller (H-05). [F] | The median orbit solve takes more than 10 minutes of CPU (published solves span 4 to 260 s, which is about 1% to 63% of a 410 s training run); or continuation fails on half the catalogue; or a grazing or unstable control case is not refused; or the orbit rung fails BET-17 for the class. | Arm: baseline-controller rollouts without orbit analysis. Control: grazing and unstable orbits planted in the catalogue. | The gait table and max-plus timing analysis of version 0.2. | §22, M4 |
| BET-27 | **A sampling controller as fallback.** With class-default costs it controls designs the synthesized baseline cannot, and supplies demonstrations for distillation (H-01). [F] | On designs marked `not-synthesizable`, fewer than half traverse the reference task under it; or a 20 s episode costs more than 1 GPU-minute for a quadruped or 6 for a humanoid at the median (the thresholds of GATE-REFLEX-06); or distillation from its demonstrations does not reduce training steps. | Arm: training from scratch. | Those designs route to training. A sampling controller never stands in for a trained policy as acceptance evidence; its own episodes are accepted only under the delivered-controller lane of §22.8. | §22; M3, M4 |
| BET-28 | **Calibration bands.** Within one calibrated robot and task family, conformal bands on the gap between simulation and measurement reach their stated coverage (H-14). [F] | On held-out real episodes in the family, empirical coverage misses nominal by more than the finite-sample allowance (about six points at n = 20); or the exchangeability alarm fires and a band is issued anyway; or a band is issued for a design that was never built. | Arms: uncalibrated simulation with randomization ranges; measuring the target directly. Control: a fixture with an omitted law that passes every in-family residual check and reverses the decision (one pilot: 675 of 675 correct in class, 0 of 225 on the omitted law; FACT, Appendix K) must trigger the alarm or a refusal. | `reality: no-claim`. | §30, M5. An import lane: without data the gate records no-claim |
| BET-29 | **Generative structure.** Links optimized under simulated load histories are lighter than engineered parts at equal margin. It improves the output and is not counted in the thesis (H-12). [F] | On the reference links the optimized part is less than 7% lighter than the engineered part at equal stiffness and fatigue margin; or the build packet fails its geometry round trip or its tolerance closure. | Arm: the engineered reference part. | The structural margin analysis alone (A-15). | §31, M5 |
| BET-30 | **Equivariance under the observation-preserving subgroup.** The right group is Γ_obs ≤ Γ_mech, the subgroup that also preserves sensors, payload and task. [F] | On a robot with asymmetric sensing, a policy constrained to Γ_mech does not lose return against one constrained to Γ_obs (then the distinction is unnecessary); or the Γ_obs policy fails the BET-07 threshold. The geometric-algebra tree policy [M] is falsified if it does not reach threshold in 1/1.3 of the steps of a plain morphology transformer (H-24). | Arms: Γ_mech-equivariant; augmentation only; a plain morphology transformer. | Augmentation and metamorphic tests under Γ_obs. | §23, M4 |
| BET-31 | **Campaign quotienting.** Exact deduplication of designs under symmetry and mission-observable equivalence removes a measurable share of campaign work without removing a winner. [F] | One false equivalence (two designs in one class whose mission outcomes differ beyond the determinism class); or the planted winner loses rank 1; or fewer than six of the top eight agree with the unquotiented arm; or digest classes save less than 5% of dispatches on the campaign corpus. | Arm: the same campaign with quotienting off. Controls: a planted winner; the coupled-bus fixture, in which two modules with identical local summaries share one current-limited bus and must not be merged. | Deduplication by canonical form and content hash only. | §14, §28; M3, M4 |
| BET-32 | **Rare-failure bounds.** Bounded-weight importance sampling gives valid bounds on failure rates. Once failures are found it refutes a failure-rate target, and tightens an estimate, with fewer episodes than crude sampling; it does not certify absence more cheaply (H-07). [S] | On fixtures with a planted failure rate, the bound's coverage is below nominal; or the effective sample size falls below 30% on the reference family; or, on a fixture whose planted rate of 10⁻⁴ is above the target, the episodes needed for a lower confidence bound to exceed the target are not at least 3× fewer than crude sampling needs (published range 2–20×); or a planted second failure mode outside the proposal is reported as absent. | Arm: crude Monte Carlo with an exact binomial bound. Control: a planted rate. | Crude sampling alone. Splitting remains exploration and yields Estimated rates only. | §26, M3 |
| BET-33 | **Revalidation.** "Which verdicts survive this edit" is answered without ever returning a stale verdict (H-09). [S] | One false reused verdict on the sealed amendment suite, which kills the reuse rule that produced it; or unnecessary invalidations above the declared share. | Arm: a hermetic dependency graph with full recomputation of dependents, which tied a more elaborate rule exactly in one pilot. Control: omitting one declared dependency must produce a stale verdict that the shadow recompute catches. | Full recomputation per verb, with compile-only memoization. | §28, M3 |
| BET-34 | **Referee coverage.** The referee, with its transactional event-located step, completes the scenes where decisions are made, and the sampled referee covers enough of the fast tiers. [S] | At M2 exit the referee completes fewer than 90% of standard-battery scenarios (the upstream contact step refuses more than 21 contacts; FACT, §1.7); or a promotion exceeds its time budget; or sampled coverage is below 0.1% of GPU world-seconds, with coverage computed from the referee's measured world-seconds per second and no band assumed. | Control: a thin-barrier fixture and a witness-migration fixture that a fixed-step tier gets wrong. | Upstream work items FD-FSIM-12 and FD-FSIM-13. Until they land, the strict `batch-cpu` profile stands as the highest tier for scenes the referee cannot complete, and results there stay provisional and say so. | §16, M2 |
| BET-35 | **Two machines.** The division of labour of §1.8 pays. [F] | A campaign on both machines is less than 1.3× faster than on the two RTX 4090 alone; or a larger world bank does not reduce the held-out gap; or more than 1 GB per campaign-hour crosses between the machines. | Arm: the two cards alone. | The machines run as independent shards, and the Mac keeps proof, replay and viewer work. | §21, §36; M4 |
| BET-36 | **Living worlds change decisions.** A contact-level film-friction law and rigid proxies stand in for coupled matter [S]; whether they reproduce the failures of coupled models is the pilot of §19.10.7; films advected by the robot change design rankings [F] (H-16). | The film law misses its known answers, changes fewer than 10% of episode outcomes on the wet-floor battery or adds more than 5% to step time (KILL-FILM, §18.8); or, in the pilot of §19.10.7, the proxies reproduce fewer than 90% of the coupled model's failures in the same class (the proxy claim is then withdrawn for that class and the island stays as an escalation); or advected films leave design rankings on the spill battery at a rank correlation of 0.95 or above with static patches, or cost more than 15% of the step (KILL-ADVECT, §19.10.7). | Arm: static friction maps. | Static friction maps with wet patches, as in version 0.2. Coupled multiphysics islands stay [M]. | §19; M3, M6 |
| BET-37 | **The building is a design variable.** A priced retrofit catalogue finds a cheaper fix in the world than in the robot for a meaningful share of failures, with the policy frozen. [F] | Kits of at most three items fix fewer than 30% of minimized failures on the retrofit corpus; or an accepted kit violates a dimensional norm from its cited source. | Arm: robot-only repair. Control: a failure that no listed retrofit can fix must return the bottleneck and no kit. | The clearance complex reports the bottleneck only. | §19, M4 |

Moonshot items (continuation-based synthesis, coupled multiphysics islands, rods, cloth and slosh,
the rotor port, tactile hands, firmware export, lifecycle compression, facility co-design and multi-robot handoff,
skill transport with learned residuals) are not bets. The plan does not depend on any of them. Each has a pilot, known
answers and a kill gate in its own chapter.

Bets are tested in an order that puts the cheapest decisive evidence first: BET-04 and BET-12 at M0 and M1; BET-17 as
soon as two rungs exist; BET-02, BET-08, BET-09, BET-18 and BET-34 at M2; BET-13 and BET-14 in part at M3 and in full
at M7.

## 5. Readers

| Reader | Their question | What they take away | Where answered |
|---|---|---|---|
| A design agent (primary user) | What can I call, what does it cost, what will it refuse, and how do I know a result is real? | Parent and candidate designs, paired trials, a qualified result with its claim product | §28, §32, App. J |
| A mission author (agent or engineer) | Which designs can do this job, which cannot and why, and what should I measure next? | Inner and outer design sets, witnesses, exclusions, a next experiment, a certificate bundle | §24, §25, §12 |
| A training agent | How do I get device-resident observations for thousands of worlds, and how do I reproduce one of them? | Weights, a training budget, a frozen evaluation, failure episodes by address | §23, §21, §29 |
| A controls engineer | Where does the controller lose stability or authority, and what did each clock see? | The first diverging event, estimator traces, commanded against delivered effort | §20, §22, §27 |
| An environment author | Which physics and sensor workloads can this scene support, and what is unsupported? | A scene pack, a registration report, a list of unsupported properties | §19, §20 |
| An implementing agent | What exactly do I build, against which oracle, and when is it done? | A bead with its test, its gate and its contract | §0.2, Parts II to V, §38, §45 |
| The owner | What am I betting on, what could kill it, and what do I have to decide? | The bets, the kill rules, the open questions with defaults | §2, §4, §39, §40, §42 |
| An agent working in a sibling project | What does this program change in this repository, and what holds until the change lands? | An upstream work item with a failing fixture, its interim posture and its switch-over rule | §33, App. F |
| An adjudicator of the ten-fold test | What is the protocol, what is frozen, and what do I check? | The sealed suite, both arms' receipts, the phase ledgers | §2, §39 |
| An engineer of a rival stack | What must my stack be given so the comparison is fair, and how do I drive this environment from my learner? | The frozen rival configuration and the Gymnasium-compatible adapter | §39, §23 |
| An auditor holding a certificate bundle | Does this claim follow from what is in the bundle, on my machine, without the agent or a GPU? | A verdict from `frob-verify` and the reason for any rejection | §8, §12 |
| A bench or manufacturing engineer | What does the simulation predict before I measure, and what would I build? | Frozen predictions, a reality band or a refusal, a build packet that authorizes nothing | §30, §31 |
| A sceptical reviewer | Where is the mathematics decoration, where is a number unearned, and which ideas were killed? | The killed-idea register, the counterexample catalogue, the verdict register | §0.8, §9, App. C, App. N, §36 |

## 6. Goals, non-goals, anti-goals

### 6.1 Goals

GOAL-01 to GOAL-20 are carried from version 0.2, with wording corrected where the incumbent audit showed the old
wording claimed too much. GOAL-21 onward are new. A tier tag on a goal is the tier of its least certain mechanism; a
goal with no tag is [S].

| ID | Goal | Primary section |
|---|---|---|
| GOAL-01 | Simulate articulated robots with contact at referee quality on the CPU, built on FrankenSim, with a transactional, event-located step. | §16 |
| GOAL-02 | Simulate thousands of worlds per device on CUDA and on Metal from one kernel source, at parity with published incumbent throughput on the same hardware. | §16, §21, §36 |
| GOAL-03 | Support legged robots: quadrupeds, hexapods and other multi-legged layouts, bipeds and humanoids. | §14 |
| GOAL-04 | Support wheeled robots (differential, Ackermann, omnidirectional), tracked robots, and hybrids such as wheel-legs and stair-climbing wheel clusters. | §18 |
| GOAL-05 | Provide terrain: slopes, stairs, gaps, stepping stones, rubble, and soft ground. | §19 |
| GOAL-06 | Provide interiors as seven archetypes from one grammar system: homes, apartments, offices, warehouses, manufacturing plants, retail stores, commercial kitchens, generated from grammars and ingested from scans. Generators for homes, kitchens, retail stores and warehouses exist elsewhere; none was found for manufacturing plants or commercial kitchens. | §19 |
| GOAL-07 | Formulate design, simulation and control in Lie theory and abstract algebra, with every construction load-bearing. | Part II |
| GOAL-08 | Use FrankenSim, FrankenTorch, FrankenNumpy, FrankenSymPy, FrankenLean and fastmcp_rust for what each can really do today, and do the rest as upstream work items in their repositories. | §33, App. F |
| GOAL-09 | Give agents a design studio: typed designs, typed edits, static analysis, simulation, comparison, telemetry, optimization. | §28, §32 |
| GOAL-10 | Make any world reproducible: re-run any world alone on the CPU from its address, bit for bit where the device reaches class D1, and independent of the batch it ran in. A hypothesis until GATE-SPARK-01, GATE-SPARK-02 and the batch-composition invariance test pass. | §29, §35 |
| GOAL-11 | Account for energy: a per-actuator and per-contact balance in which every joule that enters a rollout is attributed to where it went, closing to a stated residual. | §29 |
| GOAL-12 | Model actuators honestly: torque-speed and voltage limits, reflected inertia, friction, joint stiction and backlash, delay, heating, battery sag. This is parity with the best incumbent actuator models and is not claimed as new. | §15 |
| GOAL-13 | Synthesize a baseline estimator and controller for any well-formed design, per morphology class, in seconds, with no per-robot cost tuning. | §22 |
| GOAL-14 | Train policies on device with PPO first, with correct gym semantics (explicit reset with the final observation preserved; termination distinguished from truncation; the likelihood of the applied action), and with equivariance available where robot, sensors and task share a symmetry. | §23 |
| GOAL-15 | Compare designs on common world addresses under one of two declared study types, anytime-valid e-processes or fixed-n exact tests, never mixed inside one study. | §24, §28 |
| GOAL-16 | Detect results that depend on simulator artifacts or on model form before they are reported: promotion between tiers, exploit detectors, a model-form rank check, a work–energy audit of the simulator. | §16, §23, §28 |
| GOAL-17 | Attach offline-checkable certificates of algebraic identities to derived kernels and to selected safety claims. | §12 |
| GOAL-18 | Expose everything through one verb registry that generates the CLI, the MCP tools (built on fastmcp_rust), the schemas and the documentation. Every verb carries a compute budget, provenance and a typed refusal. | §32 |
| GOAL-19 | Simulate the sensors a robot would carry, with the ways real ones fail: encoders, IMU, force and contact, depth, lidar, height scans, and cameras with exposure and rolling-shutter timing. | §20 |
| GOAL-20 | State determinism as a class on every result, and test it. | §35 |
| GOAL-21 | Answer mission queries over design families: inner and outer design sets with witnesses, exclusions with impossibility witnesses, unresolved cells, and the next experiment. [F] | §25 |
| GOAL-22 | Run many different robots in one batch: per-world model variants inside padded capacities and size buckets, with no recompilation per design. [S] within one topology, [F] across topologies. | §17 |
| GOAL-23 | Decide most designs without per-design training: family policies per morphology class and inheritance along lineage edges, each admitted by measured rank agreement. [F] | §23 |
| GOAL-24 | Qualify a result so that the error rate holds across an agent's adaptive retries: a blinded lane on fresh sealed world clusters. | §24 |
| GOAL-25 | State missions as requirements: a bounded-time requirement language as the acceptance metric and as a falsification score, beside the reward terms that training keeps. | §24 |
| GOAL-26 | Search for the worlds that break a design, inside legality bounds and with a solvability witness, and reduce each failure to a minimal counterexample world. [F] | §26 |
| GOAL-27 | Bound rare failure rates with valid estimators, keeping exploration apart from certification. | §26 |
| GOAL-28 | Explain a failure by intervention on forked replays, with a stability figure on every attribution. | §27 |
| GOAL-29 | Say which verdicts survive an edit, memoize everything downstream of identity, and never return a stale verdict. | §28, §29 |
| GOAL-30 | Treat time as part of the model: rational periods with phase accumulators, seven distinct instants per sample, and packet queues in every checkpoint. | §20 |
| GOAL-31 | Treat sensing as part of feasibility and of symmetry: observation-alias witnesses that show when no policy on the present sensors can succeed, observability analysis, and the observation-preserving subgroup. [F] | §20, §28 |
| GOAL-32 | Make the world a design variable: clearance complexes that return a route witness or an impossibility cut, and a priced retrofit catalogue that shares one budget with robot edits. [F] | §19 |
| GOAL-33 | Model worlds that the robot changes: a film-friction law and rigid proxies in the core; advected films, slosh, cables and cloth behind flags. [S] core, [F] and [M] behind flags | §18, §19 |
| GOAL-34 | Offer a safety tier that survives contact uncertainty: energy budgets and runtime shields, classed Tested. [F] | §22, §12 |
| GOAL-35 | Treat gaits as orbits and skills as artifacts: orbit analysis with continuation in design parameters as a screening rung, and skill artifacts that carry an infeasibility witness when a body cannot produce a task wrench. [F] | §22 |
| GOAL-36 | Synthesize, not only analyze: bounded exact linkage synthesis and trajectory optimization with design variables. [F] | §25 |
| GOAL-37 | Calibrate against reality: predictions frozen before comparison, identification from imported measurements, reality bands inside a calibrated family and a refusal outside it. [F] | §30 |
| GOAL-38 | Produce manufacturable output: structure, tolerance and fatigue analysis and a build packet, every artifact flagged as authorizing nothing. [F] | §31 |
| GOAL-39 | Carry every result as a claim product, and every family claim in a portable bundle that an independent offline auditor re-checks. | §8, §12 |
| GOAL-40 | Measure the product against the strongest composed rival, with a phase ledger for both arms, and let rival learning stacks drive this environment through a Gymnasium-compatible adapter. | §39, §23 |
| GOAL-41 | Use the two machines for what each is good at, with only seeds, weights and receipts crossing between them. [F] | §21, §36 |
| GOAL-42 | Give people a view of what agents see: a terminal dashboard, a viewer with physical overlays, and self-contained replay pages. | §32 |
| GOAL-43 | Keep frontier physics and frontier outputs available without putting them on the critical path: Cosserat rods and cables, cloth, slosh, coupled multiphysics islands, a rotor port, tactile hands, firmware export, lifecycle compression, facility co-design and multi-robot handoff. [F] and [M] | §16, §18, §19, §31; M6, M8 |

### 6.2 Non-goals

Version 0.2 excluded several areas outright. Under this version's brief, five of them are admitted in a bounded form,
at [F] or [M], behind flags and off the critical path, each with known answers and a kill gate. The identifier is kept
and the row states what moved in and what stays out.

| ID | Not in scope | What changed, and the reason |
|---|---|---|
| NONGOAL-01 | A photorealistic renderer. | Unchanged. Sensors need geometry-correct depth, timing and labels first. Hero images come from FrankenSim's path tracer offline (§20). |
| NONGOAL-02 | Full-room fluid, granular or cloth simulation inside every training world, and soft robots as primary bodies. | Narrowed. Cosserat rods and cables, cloth, films advected by the robot, slosh and coupled multiphysics islands are admitted at [F] or [M] behind flags (M6). Their [S] counterparts, a film-friction law and rigid proxies, are in the core. Full-room fluid is out of memory by orders of magnitude (H-16). |
| NONGOAL-03 | Full aerodynamics, and swimming robots. | Narrowed. A compact rotor port for flight is admitted at [M] (M6). The aerodynamic crates in FrankenSim remain a separate program. |
| NONGOAL-04 | Motor actuation, safety-rated board support, hardware sign-off, ROS integration, and any real-time or hardware-in-the-loop claim. | Narrowed. Firmware export is admitted at [M] as an exported artifact behind a caller-owned hardware interface, carrying the no-authorization flags, in the frontier-delivery milestone (§43). Bench measurements enter only as imported data (§30). |
| NONGOAL-05 | A general Python API for authoring designs or driving the studio. | Narrowed. The Rust `VecEnv` is primary. An optional Gymnasium-compatible adapter lives under `bindings/`, because the ten-fold test needs rival learning stacks to drive this environment (§23, §39). |
| NONGOAL-06 | Windows. | Unchanged. Targets are Linux x86-64 and macOS on Apple silicon. |
| NONGOAL-07 | Dexterous in-hand manipulation benchmarks. | Narrowed. Mobile-manipulation reach and carry tasks are in scope at M4, and tactile hands are admitted at [M] (M6). In-hand manipulation benchmarks stay out. |
| NONGOAL-08 | General-purpose formal verification of robot controllers; full-order barrier certificates; unbounded proofs about contact chaos or learning convergence. | Unchanged in substance. Lemma covers kernels, a short list of theorem cards, family certificates on small sub-boxes and reduced-order shields classed Tested (§12). |
| NONGOAL-09 | Hardware certification or authorization of any kind. | New. Every exported artifact says in machine-readable form that it authorizes nothing (§8). |
| NONGOAL-10 | One universal policy across all morphologies. | New. Out of reach at an affordable pretraining budget (H-02). Family policies per class only. |
| NONGOAL-11 | Certified isotropic paving of a high-dimensional design box. | New. Out of reach beyond a split set of about six parameters (H-06). Family answers are built per constraint. |
| NONGOAL-12 | Half-precision or tensor-core arithmetic for contact. | New. Refuted (H-15). |
| NONGOAL-13 | Per-design kernel specialization as the default path. | New. Recursion-only specialization is capped near 1.2× (H-04). Survivors only, and only if our own profile justifies it. |
| NONGOAL-14 | Sampling-based control as a stand-in evaluator for a trained policy. The delivered-controller lane of §22.8 is the one exception. | New. It costs thousands of policy rollouts per simulated second (H-01). |
| NONGOAL-15 | Gradients through contact in the rigid core before M6. | Carried from the parked list of version 0.2. Revisited if a rigid legged co-design result shows contact gradients beating population methods. The mechanism and its kill gate are specified in §16.21 [M]. |
| NONGOAL-16 | Simulated humans as validated agents; browser-based CAD sculpting. | New. Scripted humans appear as scenario dressing only. |

### 6.3 Anti-goals

Things that would make the product worse even if someone asked for them.

- Lowering physics fidelity silently to keep a frame rate or a throughput figure. Under load the system sheds
  presentation or refuses; it never changes the physics tier of a running world (FACT: the same rule in the Wright
  Flyer plan §4.3).
- Wrapping MuJoCo, PhysX or any foreign engine as the production engine. Foreign engines are development-time
  comparison oracles and the rival arm of the ten-fold test, run out of process (§38, §39). If the composed-incumbent
  arm ties, the layer ships over that engine openly, under BET-14, and not as a hidden dependency.
- Publishing a throughput number without the disclosure block (§36), or a ratio against an incumbent without the
  rival's frozen configuration and every cost in the denominator (§39).
- Accepting inertial parameters on faith. An imported model that is not physically consistent is refused or repaired
  with a recorded repair (§14).
- Putting a language model inside the physics or control loop.
- Hiding nondeterminism. A result whose determinism class is `Unspecified` is never cited as evidence, and paired
  statistics are refused under an uncontrolled class.
- Mathematical decoration, and ornamental labels on ordinary mechanisms. See D-2.
- Tuning against the confirmation benchmark, or letting discovery read confirmation worlds.
- Improving a time score by lowering the bar for what counts as accepted.
- Converting a tested or estimated result into a proof, by wording or by type. Using the word "verified" for a result.
- Silent clamping of a parameter, a command or a contact count. A clamp is a refusal or a recorded event.
- Multiplying a pruning ratio by a speedup measured on work the pruning already removed, or reporting an operation
  count as a speedup.
- Running a speed test whose ceiling is below the claim it is meant to test.
- Fast-math switches, fused multiply-add, built-in transcendentals or floating-point atomics in batched kernels.
- Forking a sibling, or patching it locally, where the change belongs in its own repository as an upstream work item;
  and a milestone that waits on an upstream change with no interim posture.
- A gate that needs hardware, a bench or a review panel the program does not have. Such a gate is an import lane with
  a recorded no-claim.
- Composing two individually successful episodes and calling the result a composed guarantee.
- A learned correction between tiers, or a learned surrogate of the physics step, which would hide exactly the
  artifacts the trust ladder exists to expose.
- An exported artifact that could be mistaken for permission to run hardware.

## 7. North-Star scenarios

Each is a before-and-after acceptance story, tagged with the first milestone that can demonstrate it. In the "after"
parts, numbers are TARGETs or illustrative values unless the story says they are a known answer. Incumbent figures in
the "before" parts are FACTs from Appendix H. Verb spellings follow the registry (Appendix J); where a story names a
capability without a spelling, the registry is the authority. NS-01 to NS-12 are carried from version 0.2 with their
incumbent denominators corrected; NS-13 to NS-24 are new.

- **NS-01 Check before you simulate [M1].** *Before:* an agent edits XML, launches training, and learns minutes to
  about an hour later that the knees saturate (training takes about seven minutes for a flat-ground quadruped task and
  about an hour for a default rough-terrain humanoid run). *After:* `frob design check` returns in under two seconds:
  the mass spiral closes at 14.2 kg, peak knee torque demand exceeds the selected actuator's continuous rating by 31%,
  the design has mechanical symmetry group C₂ × C₂ of which its front-only depth camera preserves C₂, and three ranked
  repairs are offered as typed edits.
- **NS-02 Teleport a world [M2].** *Before:* world 1,337 of 4,096 produces NaNs on the GPU. Where an incumbent's
  deterministic mode is on, the same batch can be re-run on the same GPU; none documents a bitwise re-run of that one
  world on a CPU. *After:* `frob sim replay --world 1337 --tier batch-cpu` reproduces that world alone on the CPU from
  its address (seed, world, episode), stops at the first step whose digest differs from the GPU's or at the first
  refusal, and reports the contact that started it. Where the device reaches class D1 the digests agree to the end,
  and the report says which class applied.
- **NS-03 An honest A/B [M3].** *Before:* two designs are compared on mean reward over an arbitrary number of
  episodes. *After:* `frob eval compare A B --task warehouse-tote` runs both on common world addresses under a
  declared anytime-valid study, stops when the e-process crosses its threshold, and reports "B beats A on energy per
  metre, evidence 240 to 1, valid at any stopping time". It reports separately whether each design meets the mission's
  hard limits, because a paired win establishes neither.
- **NS-04 A kitchen with a wet floor [M3].** A humanoid crosses a generated commercial kitchen whose floor friction
  map includes a wet patch governed by the film-friction law. Telemetry reports slip distance per stance, the friction
  utilization margin, and the stills at the moment of the slip. The agent can ask which link a pixel belongs to.
- **NS-05 Symmetry for free [M4].** The studio reports the symmetry group of a hexapod and the subgroup that its
  sensors, payload and task preserve, lists the gaits that subgroup permits, and trains a policy equivariant under it
  that reaches the target return in at most 0.7× the steps of an unconstrained one.
- **NS-06 Thirty iterations in an hour, three hundred designs decided [M4].** An agent runs thirty
  design-check-simulate-explain-edit cycles on a wheel-leg hybrid in one hour on `trj`. Each cycle dispatches a family
  of at least ten variants in one batch, so at least three hundred designs are decided in the hour. Every design
  version is content-addressed, every comparison is a declared study, and `frob design bisect` finds the edit that
  broke stair climbing. The unit of the story is designs decided per hour: the cycle count alone is worth only
  3.0–3.5× against an incumbent quadruped loop (§2.3).
- **NS-07 An import that tells the truth [M1].** Importing a public humanoid description yields a loss report: which
  fields were dropped, which inertias fail the physical-consistency test, and which actuator limits were absent and
  filled from a card marked `assumed`.
- **NS-08 Tracks on rubble [M4].** A tracked robot climbs stairs and crosses rubble; on soft soil the sinkage model is
  active and labelled Frontier in the evidence.
- **NS-09 The exploit is caught [M3].** A policy that scores well by exploiting contact compliance is re-evaluated on
  the referee tier; the score falls outside the promotion envelope and the result is labelled `provisional:
  tier-sensitive`. A design whose rank among finalists changes under another admissible contact law is labelled
  model-conditional and may not spend prototype budget.
- **NS-10 The same task on a Mac [M2].** The quadruped task trains on this Mac through Metal. Results agree with the
  CUDA run inside the declared determinism class, and the report says which class. The throughput is reported beside
  the one Metal-capable incumbent's on the same machine and beside one RTX 4090's.
- **NS-11 A kernel with a certificate [M5].** `frob prove kernel K-cay-step` returns a certificate that the update
  stays on the group and conserves spatial momentum in free flight, checked by FrankenSymPy's proof kernel, with a
  Lean capsule re-checked by FrankenLean where the theorem's dependencies allow. The certificate says nothing about
  floating-point results, and its text says so.
- **NS-12 Your own kitchen [M5].** A walkthrough video becomes a private scene pack through the owner's existing
  reconstruction pipeline, and a candidate home robot is evaluated in it. Scale is labelled `Estimated` unless
  anchored, surfaces the scan never saw are treated conservatively and listed as a re-scan request, and the scan never
  leaves the machine.
- **NS-13 A mission answered over a family [M1 on the CPU, M4 at scale].** *Before:* an agent evaluates candidate
  bodies one at a time and reports the best score. Nothing says whether an untried body would also work, or why a
  failed one cannot. *After:* the mission is a query with a free parameter. A robot carries 400 N on four point feet
  at (±a, ±b) with a = 1/3 m; its centre of mass may lie anywhere in a rectangle of half-dimensions 150 mm by 75 mm;
  each foot delivers a commanded normal force in [0, 160] N; the half-width b is free. `frob mission synthesize`
  returns I ⊆ F ⊆ O. Every b ≥ 3/14 m is in the inner set, with the corner allocation (160, 130, 110, 0) N as its
  witness. Every b < 3/14 m is excluded, with a dual vector as the impossibility witness: at b = 0.20 m one foot would
  have to carry 165 N. The answer says that the boundary has zero reserve on two constraints. `frob-verify` re-checks
  the bundle offline in exact rational arithmetic. When the mission is amended to a passive equal-spring suspension,
  `result.revalidate` withdraws the earlier inner set and says what must be re-solved: at b = ¼ m, which had been
  admitted with the allocation (155, 135, 105, 5) N, the springs deliver (175, 115, 85, 25) N against the 160 N
  rating. These numbers are a known answer (Appendix M), not targets.
- **NS-14 256 different robots in one batch [M2].** *Before:* a population of designs with different topologies is a
  sequence of rebuilds. On GPU engines a structural edit needs a host compile and a new graph capture, and one stack
  reports just-in-time compilation of one to three minutes. *After:* one dispatch steps 256 distinct designs (three
  leg counts, mixed link lengths and actuator cards, in size buckets) with 32 worlds each on one RTX 4090. No kernel
  is compiled. Each world reproduces the digest of its single-design run. The report carries the two numbers of N11
  against the incumbent's mixed batch and against the per-family-template control arm, and says which arm won.
- **NS-15 A minimal counterexample world of three edits [M3].** *Before:* domain randomization reports a failure tail
  of 0.4% and the agent reads logs to guess why. *After:* the Nemesis search (§26) finds a failing world inside the
  legality bounds, confirms with a witness that the candidate's own body and actuators could have completed the
  mission in it, and shrinks it to a `.fmcw` file of three edits against the nominal scene: a door sill raised by 9
  mm, a friction coefficient of 0.31 on one floor tile, and a depth packet delayed by 40 ms. Removing any one edit
  removes the failure. The world reproduces bit for bit and joins the regression battery.
- **NS-16 An autopsy that names the cause [M3].** *Before:* an agent given a failed episode orders the anomalies by
  time and guesses. *After:* Autopsy (§27) forks the snapshot taken before the fall under twelve typed interventions,
  singly and in pairs, on identical random streams. The placebo fork replays the failure bit for bit. The report says
  that lifting the knee torque limit prevents the fall in 94% of perturbed forks against a placebo flip rate of 3%, so
  it is a but-for cause, and that restoring nominal friction does so in 8%, so it is not. The gear-ratio intervention
  is re-run from the episode start, because winding temperature depends on the whole history. Attribution runs in
  double precision, and the first-ranked repair comes back as a typed edit. An episode whose placebo flip rate is high
  is labelled `chaotic: unattributable` and is given no cause.
- **NS-17 Qualification that survives 500 adaptive retries [M3].** *Before:* an agent submits fifty candidates against
  the same held-out scenes until one passes. Each comparison is valid alone and the campaign is not. *After:* `frob
  eval qualify` pre-commits the candidate, the baseline, the mission and the metrics. Submission i runs on fresh
  sealed world clusters at level α_i = α / [i·(i + 1)], a series that sums to α. The discovery lane cannot read those
  worlds, and only the decision and an aggregate receipt come back until the campaign closes. The gate behind the
  story drives the lane with 500 adaptive retries on worlds that carry no signal and requires a false-promotion rate
  of at most α, with power preserved on planted gains.
- **NS-18 A twelve-dollar ramp against a chassis redesign [M4].** *Before:* every repair an agent considers lives in
  the robot. *After:* a wheeled carrier fails kitchen doorway D. The clearance complex returns an impossibility cut
  that names the bottleneck, a 19 mm threshold. The retrofit catalogue (§19) reports that one 1:12 rubber threshold
  ramp, priced at USD 12, makes the mission solvable with the policy frozen, and that the alternative in the robot is
  a larger drive wheel that changes the gearbox and adds USD 140 in parts. Both enter the same budget, and the mission
  answer lists them as competing, testable decisions. Prices and dimensional norms come from a cited catalogue; where
  none is cited they are labelled `assumed`.
- **NS-19 A family policy walks an unseen design [M4].** *Before:* every new design waits for its own training run,
  about seven minutes for a quadruped and up to an hour for a humanoid. *After:* an agent lengthens the femur by 8%
  and widens the stance. The family policy of the quadruped class, conditioned on the design, walks it with no
  training. The report gives its return as 0.78 of the specialist reference for the class, the in-distribution check,
  and the rank-agreement status that says whether this rung may eliminate designs. When the design is shortlisted,
  inheritance from its parent reaches the target return in 12% of the steps of an early-stopped from-scratch control.
  A six-legged variant falls outside the class, is flagged out-of-distribution, and is routed to the baseline
  controller.
- **NS-20 A build packet [M5].** *Before:* the loop ends with a scored design. *After:* from a qualified design and
  task, Foundry (§31) emits a `.fbuild` packet: a bill of materials against a pinned catalogue, faceted solid
  geometry, a tolerance stack that closes, fatigue margins computed from the simulated load histories, and one link
  re-optimized to be 18% lighter at equal margin. The packet's claim product is Estimated, because its material cards
  are, and every file in it carries the three no-authorization flags of §8 and the packet flag
  `fabrication_released`, all false.
- **NS-21 A calibrated reality band [M5].** *Before:* every report says `reality: no-claim`. *After:* bench
  measurements of one quadruped on one floor are imported with their provenance. Predictions for the held-out episodes
  are frozen before the comparison. For that robot and task family, Ground reports a cost of transport of 0.62 with a
  band of [0.55, 0.71] at 90% nominal coverage from 20 calibration episodes, and states that coverage at this sample
  size varies by about six points. The same question about a design that was never built returns a refusal that names
  the missing calibrated family.
- **NS-22 The docking fixture [M1].** The first mission slice, on the CPU. A cart must reach position 1 at rest in
  three one-second ticks. Its acceleration is g·u with an unknown gain g ∈ {1, 2} and commands bounded by U. The only
  informative packet is the first velocity reading. *Before:* a simulator scores a given controller on sampled worlds
  and cannot say whether any controller exists. *After:* the mission query returns four facts, each with a
  certificate. With the packet on time and U = ¾, a first command of ¼ identifies the gain and both worlds dock
  exactly. Docking tolerates a sensor error ε exactly when ε < (U + ½)/4, so choosing the probe and the feedback
  together raises the tolerable error from 1/8 to 5/16 on the same actuator. With the packet late, no causal
  controller docks in both worlds. When a third gain 33/32 is admitted it aliases with gain 1 at an error radius of
  1/64, exact docking becomes impossible, and every label that was feasible reverses. These are known answers
  (Appendix M).
- **NS-23 An energy-budget safety claim [M4].** *Before:* a safety statement about a humanoid stepping off a kerb
  depends on a contact model that nobody trusts at impact. *After:* the claim is stated as an `.fenergy` budget: the
  kinetic and potential energy that can arrive at the ankle on a 12 cm step-down is below what the joint and its bump
  stop are rated to absorb, with every term taken from the energy ledger. No contact law enters the claim. A runtime
  shield enforces the budget as a filter on commands, at a measured cost and with a statistically measured margin. The
  claim product is Tested, and the type offers no conversion to Proved.
- **NS-24 The sealed ten-fold tournament [M7].** Missions in named strata are sealed, and some worlds come from an
  evaluator independent of both arms. The rival is the strongest composed incumbent workflow, improved by a competent
  baseline engineer on development fixtures and then frozen. Both arms get the same agent model, token budget,
  hardware envelope and prior information, in fresh contexts. A neutral adjudicator releases paired receipts after
  both arms close. The report gives, per stratum, the ratio of restricted mean times with its interval, cold and warm
  separately, the crossover reuse count, and a phase ledger for each arm that sums to wall-clock. Every submitted
  certificate is replayed by `frob-verify`, and one false certificate disqualifies that arm from the scoped claim.
  Where the composed-incumbent arm ties, the report says so and the layer ships for that stratum.

## 8. The seven claims and the claim product

Every result this system produces makes exactly one kind of claim, and each kind is established by a different kind of
evidence. Gates, reports and documentation keep them apart. Version 0.2 had six claims; this version adds **Design
comparison**, because "this design is better" and "this design meets the mission" are what the studio most often says,
and neither is a fidelity statement or a known answer.

### 8.1 The seven claims

| Claim | Meaning | Evidence that establishes it | What it does not establish |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Proof** | A stated proposition holds in the declared model. | A checker accepted it: a Lean kernel for a general theorem (class Proved); or, for an instance-level statement, FrankenSymPy's proof kernel, an interval or exact-rational certificate, or the offline auditor `frob-verify` on a family certificate bundle (class Certified) (§12). | Anything about floating-point results; the model's agreement with the world; any quantifier order other than the one stated. |
| **Known answer** | The implementation recovers an analytic or synthetic truth. | A known-answer test with a derivation on file (§38, Appendix M). | Correctness away from the tested cases. |
| **Parity** | The implementation reproduces a reference tool or a published number. | A fixture captured from a pinned oracle that was never regenerated from the candidate, or a comparison with a published figure under stated conditions (§38). | That either side is right. Two programs that share a solver have correlated error. Agreement with a published real-robot figure is still Parity. |
| **Fidelity** | A faster tier agrees with a slower, more trusted tier. | The fidelity ledger: per-quantity disagreement distributions on the standard battery, and agreement of the task decisions the two tiers lead to (§16, §35). | That the trusted tier is right. Anything outside the battery. |
| **Design comparison** | One design is better than another, or a design meets a mission, on a stated family of worlds. | A declared study, anytime-valid or fixed-n exact, on common world addresses; for a qualified result, the blinded qualification lane (§24, §28). | That either design meets a hard limit when the verdict is a paired one; anything outside the stated world family; anything about reality. |
| **Reality** | The simulation agrees with physical measurement. | Imported real-robot measurements with their own provenance, predictions frozen before comparison, and a reality band for a calibrated family (§30). Everywhere else this claim is `no-claim`, and reports say so. | Anything about a design that was never built or a family that was never calibrated. |
| **Performance** | A speed or scale figure on named hardware. | A recorded run with the disclosure block (§36); for a ratio against a rival, the protocol of §39. | Anything about another workload, world count or machine. |

Three clarifications fix the edges (DESIGN).

- **A claim has a kind and a class.** The kind is one of the seven. The class is one of the four evidence classes of
  §12, ordered Proved, Certified, Tested, Estimated from strongest to weakest. Only a Proof claim can be Proved or
  Certified. The other six are Tested or Estimated however much evidence they rest on: no amount of testing becomes a
  proof.
- **A family certificate is a Proof claim of class Certified.** It says that, in the declared model and under the
  declared assumptions, every design in an inner cell satisfies the mission, or none in an excluded cell does. The
  assumptions are inputs (rule 6 below).
- **A comparison of methods is a Design comparison.** The "method" gates of version 0.2, which test whether a method
  of this plan beats a competing arm on a corpus of designs, name this claim. The unit compared changes; the evidence
  required does not.

Each claim has a permitted wording, and reports use no other.

| Claim | Permitted wording in a report |
|---|---|
| Proof | "proved: ⟨statement⟩; checker ⟨name and build⟩; certificate ⟨hash⟩" or "certified: ⟨statement⟩; auditor `frob-verify` ⟨build⟩; bundle ⟨hash⟩" |
| Known answer | "recovers ⟨KA identifier⟩ within ⟨tolerance⟩" |
| Parity | "matches ⟨oracle⟩ at ⟨pin⟩ within ⟨tolerance⟩ on ⟨fixture⟩" |
| Fidelity | "tracks ⟨higher tier⟩ within ⟨envelope⟩ on ⟨battery⟩; decisions agree on ⟨share⟩" |
| Design comparison | "⟨B⟩ beats ⟨A⟩ on ⟨metric⟩, evidence ⟨e-value or exact interval⟩, study ⟨identifier⟩" or "qualified at level α_i on sealed clusters ⟨identifier⟩" |
| Reality | "inside the calibrated band for ⟨family⟩, nominal coverage ⟨level⟩ at n = ⟨count⟩" or "reality: no-claim" |
| Performance | "measured ⟨figure⟩ on ⟨hardware⟩; disclosure block ⟨identifier⟩" |

### 8.2 The claim product

In version 0.2 the rule "a result inherits the weakest claim among its inputs" was prose. Here it is a type (DESIGN).
The reason is that an optimizing agent will find any path by which a statistical result can be reported as a proof,
and a rule that lives in a style guide is such a path. `frob-core` owns the type; every verb's output envelope carries
one (§32); `frob-verify` reads one from every bundle (§12).

```rust
// DESIGN sketch: fixes intent, not signatures. Owned by frob-core.

/// The four evidence classes of §12. Combination takes the minimum.
pub enum EvidenceClass { Estimated, Tested, Certified, Proved }   // Ord: Estimated < Tested < Certified < Proved

/// Exactly one of the seven claims.
pub enum ClaimKind { Proof, KnownAnswer, Parity, Fidelity, DesignComparison, Reality, Performance }

/// What a result asserts, how strongly, about what, and that it authorizes nothing.
pub struct ClaimProduct {
    kind: ClaimKind,
    class: EvidenceClass,           // minimum over inputs; no setter
    weakest: InputRef,              // the input that set the class: content hash and field path
    scope: Scope,                   // design family, world family, quantifier order, horizon, validity region
    tier: Tier,                     // lowest physics tier among the inputs
    determinism: DetClass,          // weakest of D0..D4 among the inputs
    reality: RealityScope,          // NoClaim, or the calibrated family a band was issued for
    conditions: FlagSet,            // union over inputs: tier-sensitive, controller-sensitive, model-conditional
    inputs: Vec<InputRef>,          // every consumed artifact, each with its own claim product
    authorization: NoAuthorization, // three constants, all false
}

impl ClaimProduct {
    /// The only way to build a product from parts. Class, tier and determinism take the weakest; scope takes
    /// the intersection; conditions take the union; a mismatch of quantifier order is a refusal.
    pub fn combine(kind: ClaimKind, parts: &[ClaimProduct]) -> Result<ClaimProduct, Refusal>;
}

/// `False` is a unit type that serializes as the JSON literal false. No constructor produces `true`.
pub struct NoAuthorization {
    pub execution_authorized: False,
    pub hardware_safety_signoff: False,
    pub sim_to_real_certified: False,
}
// A build packet adds a fourth constant, `fabrication_released: False`, in the packet's own sealed type (§31.12).

// Three things do not exist, and a compile-fail test pins each: a conversion from ClaimProduct into a
// Proved value; a setter for `class`; a public constructor that takes a class as an argument.
```

A leaf product is created only by the component that produced the evidence: a checker creates Proved or Certified, the
Gauntlet harness and the study runner create Tested, and everything else creates Estimated. An actuator, interface or
material card creates one product per field from that field's provenance, so that a single assumed number is visible
as the weakest input of everything built on it.

A worked case. A comparison of two designs consumes: a kernel whose group-membership identity is Certified; a friction
coefficient from an interface card field marked `assumed`, which is Estimated; and a paired anytime-valid study on the
GPU tier under determinism class D2, which is Tested. The product is a Design comparison of class Estimated, its
weakest input is the friction field of the card, its tier is the GPU tier and so it is provisional until promoted
(§16), and its reality scope is `no-claim`. The report prints all of that in one line and offers, as its first next
action, the measurement that would raise the weakest input.

### 8.3 Rules

1. **A gate names exactly one claim.**
2. **A failure is a failed cell, never an excluded cell.** Partial coverage never rounds up, and every failed episode
   occupies a row.
3. **Parity is not Reality.** Agreeing with another simulator establishes that two programs agree. A comparison with a
   published real-robot figure, made before any calibration data is imported, is labelled Parity.
4. **Fidelity is directional.** It says the fast tier tracks the referee on a battery, not that either is right.
5. **The weakest input wins, by construction.** A proved kernel fed an assumed friction coefficient produces an
   estimate, and the type leaves no other outcome.
6. **Assumptions are inputs.** A certificate over a model with an assumed friction interval is Certified as a
   statement about that model. Any statement about the robot inherits the class of the assumption. A bundle lists its
   assumptions as inputs with their own claim products, and `frob-verify` refuses a bundle whose assumptions are
   missing.
7. **A comparison is relative.** A paired verdict that B beats A is emitted together with each design's own verdict on
   the mission's hard limits. A relative win with no regression does not establish that either design meets the
   mission.
8. **Quantifiers are part of the claim.** "For every world, some controller works" and "one controller works for every
   world" are different claims with different evidence. Evidence for the easier order is rejected, and the auditor
   rejects an unknown proof kind or a changed quantifier even when every hash is consistent. The smallest case that
   separates the two orders is in Appendix N: a plant in which every build has a command that works and no single
   command works for all builds.
9. **`unknown` is a verdict.** A solver failure, a timeout or a refusal leaves a verdict unknown. It is never recorded
   as a failure of the design and never as a success. Where contact is set-valued, a fork with any failing admissible
   branch invalidates a universal success claim.
10. **A claim does not outlive its inputs.** After an edit, a claim is carried forward only if revalidation shows that
    each input is unchanged or is implied by what changed (§28). A hash identifies an artifact; only an implication
    licenses reuse.
11. **Conditions travel.** Flags such as `tier-sensitive`, `controller-sensitive` and `model-conditional` are joined
    by union and cannot be dropped by a consumer. A model-conditional result may not spend prototype budget.
12. **Composition needs inclusion.** Two claims compose into a claim about a sequence only when the guaranteed end set
    of the first lies inside the entry set of the second, with matching clocks, uncertainty dependencies and state
    memory. Two individually successful episodes prove no such inclusion.
13. **Nothing authorizes.** Every exported artifact carries `execution_authorized: false`, `hardware_safety_signoff:
    false` and `sim_to_real_certified: false`. No verb, flag or configuration produces any other value.
14. **The word "verified" is not used.** Reports, documentation and tool output use the permitted wordings of §8.1.

---

# PART II. THE MATHEMATICAL SPINE

## 9. Doctrine

The owner's brief is that the whole robot design, simulation and control problem be formulated in the language of
abstract algebra and Lie theory, and that this machinery guide the system instead of decorating it. The rules
below are how that brief is kept honest. D-1 to D-8 govern how mathematics enters the system. D-9 to D-19 govern
how a mathematical claim is allowed to leave it.

- **D-1 Algebra first, numbers last.** The primary description of every object is algebraic: a group, an algebra,
  a cone, a representation, a poset. Floating-point arrays are a lowering of that description, produced as late as
  possible and by a replayable derivation.
- **D-2 No ornamental mathematics.** A construction earns its place with four things: a Rust type, a verb an
  agent can call, a test that fails when the mathematics is wrong, and a measured payoff or a date by which the
  payoff is measured. A construction missing any of the four is moved to Appendix C as parked or rejected. The
  rule also binds vocabulary: a mechanism is named by what it computes, and a term from a richer theory is used
  only where a theorem of that theory is used.
- **D-3 Group elements, not coordinates.** State is stored as group elements. Coordinates (angles, Euler triples)
  appear only at import, export and display, each at one boundary.
- **D-4 Structure is a test oracle.** Every conserved quantity, every symmetry and every algebraic identity is a
  metamorphic test that costs nothing to state. The Gauntlet's property tier is generated from Part II (§38).
- **D-5 Proof classes are typed, and the weakest link wins.** `Proved`, `Certified`, `Tested`, `Estimated` are
  distinct evidence classes (§12.2). A result is no stronger than its weakest input, and the type that carries a
  combined result has no conversion to a stronger class.
- **D-6 The moonshot budget is capped.** At most four [M] items are active at once. An item is active from the
  funding of its pilot until its expiry gate; the others wait in the register of Appendix C. Each has a falsifier
  and an expiry gate. Nothing tagged [M] is on the critical path of §43.
- **D-7 Derive, don't hand-write.** The arithmetic of a kernel comes from a symbolic derivation with a content
  hash (C-14). Hand-written arithmetic is allowed in the referee tier and in kernel skeletons (loops, gathers,
  sorts), not in the mathematical core of a batched kernel.
- **D-8 Every domain ships its adjoint or its excuse.** A kernel either has a derivative program or a recorded
  reason it does not, with the estimator that replaces it (inherited from FrankenSim's expansion charter, D8).
- **D-9 A plausible shortcut ships with its counterexample.** Where an obvious simplification is wrong, the plan
  states the smallest case a reader can check by hand that breaks it, and that case becomes a permanent negative
  control (Appendix N; the negative-control registry of §38). Examples in this Part: taking the lower three rows
  of a space Jacobian (C-04), projecting an action and then clipping it (C-31), intersecting per-world answers
  (C-18), and accepting pairwise compatibility as joint compatibility (C-19).
- **D-10 Every Frontier or Moonshot construction has a pilot and a ceiling.** Before its work package is funded,
  an [F] or [M] construction runs a paper-scale pilot with a written falsifier. Before any speed test, it states
  the most the mechanism could gain. If a fraction f of the matched wall time is improved by a factor r and the
  method adds overhead h, the gain is at most 1/(1 − f + f/r + h); a pruning ratio is never multiplied by a
  speedup measured on work already removed.
- **D-11 A hash identifies; only an implication licenses skipping a recheck.** A content hash says that two
  artifacts are the same bytes. It never says that a verdict about one transfers to a different one. A verdict is
  reused after a change only under a recorded implication: polarity in the assumption lattice (C-18), a
  monotonicity argument, a symmetry together with its stabilizer check (C-09), or equality of every dependency.
  A checker rejects an unknown proof kind or a changed quantifier even when every hash is consistent.
- **D-12 Quantifiers are part of the claim.** A claim names the order of its quantifiers, the population it
  ranges over, and the information available to the policy when it acts. Evidence for an easier quantifier
  order, such as a separate policy per world where one policy for all worlds was asked, is rejected by type
  (C-17).
- **D-13 Answers are two-sided, and unknown is a verdict.** A set-valued answer is an inner set, an outer set and
  the unresolved remainder between them. A point answer carries a witness or a refutation of matching scope. A
  solver failure, a timeout or an unenclosed branch yields `unknown`; it never yields failure and never success.
- **D-14 Symmetry is used only where it holds.** A symmetry of the mechanism is intersected with the stabilizers
  of payload, gravity, task, observation and contact mode before it reduces any calculation. Augmenting data
  with a transformation that preserves a distribution and reducing one world by a transformation that preserves
  that world are different operations with different preconditions (C-09).
- **D-15 A derivative carries its validity label.** Extending D-8: every derivative that leaves a kernel or an
  analysis says whether it is smooth, a saltation composite, a fixed-mode conditional, one-sided, generalized,
  smoothed or a finite difference, and a query near grazing or an ambiguous event order is refused by name
  (C-16).
- **D-16 Exploration and certification are separate lanes.** A method that finds failures quickly (splitting,
  adaptive search, a discovery run) issues no bound. A bound comes from a lane whose validity does not depend on
  where the search looked: crude sampling, bounded-weight importance sampling, or a sealed confirmation run that
  discovery could not read (C-27, §24).
- **D-17 A specialized method names the generic method it must beat.** Each construction that claims an
  advantage names the off-the-shelf method that answers the same question: a lifted linear program, a
  satisfiability solver, a reachability tool, successive halving, a plain transformer. If the generic method
  ties, the plan says so and ships the generic method. FACT (planning pilot, to be re-run in this repository
  before a gate cites it): on the static-stance family of C-32 a lifted robust linear program and the
  specialized projection each reached the optimum in one solve.
- **D-18 A strict decision is computed exactly.** Predicates with strict comparators, digests and certificate
  arithmetic run in an exact-integer kernel class, in exact rationals, or in guarded single precision with an
  exact fallback (§35). FACT (same pilot archive, same caveat): an unguarded `f32` screen of 65,536 boundary
  cases produced 452 false admissions and 23,438 false exclusions, and a guarded or integer kernel produced none.
- **D-19 A model assumption is an input with a name.** Actuator authority, load-sharing law, hidden-parameter
  support, delivery deadline and controller information are fields of the claim, not prose around it. FACT
  (same archive): changing one winding feed-forward term in a sampled wheel controller moved a one-tick spectral
  radius from 1.48 to 0.92 and changed 24 of 156 task labels; admitting one extra hidden gain reversed every
  feasible label on the pilot's grid of the docking fixture of C-19.

## 10. The constructions (C-01 onward)

Each construction is stated with one schema: the **object**, what it **replaces**, the **payoff**, the **honest
limits** where the evidence narrows the claim, the **foundations** as they exist today, the **test**, and the
**tier**. A construction tagged [F] or [M] adds a **pilot and ceiling** line (D-10), and where it helps a
**retired when** line names the observation that withdraws the optimization. Symbols are defined in §11 and
Appendix D.

Four reading rules apply to the whole chapter.

1. Foundations are FACT, observed on 2026-11-21 at FrankenSim `483d09c682f2`, FrankenSymPy `29f847c1` and
   FrankenLean `4426f8ea7`. A foundation that exists is not a foundation that is admitted: admission is §33.
2. Numbers inside a test are exact arithmetic on the stated fixture, written so that a reader can check them by
   hand. They are known answers, not measurements.
3. Thresholds are TARGET. A figure quoted from a publication, or from a planning pilot that ran outside this
   repository, is FACT with an entry in the source register (Appendix H), to be re-read from the primary source
   or re-run here before a gate cites it.
4. A construction fixes mathematics and its test. Types, kernels, verbs and gates are owned by the chapter and
   the crates named in the table below, and each gate lives in that chapter.

### C-01 Configuration is a Lie group, and joints are subgroups

- **Object.** A floating-base robot's configuration space is Q = SE(3) × G₁ × … × Gₙ. Joint j contributes the map
  θ ↦ ∏ₖ exp(θₖ Sₖ) for screws Sₖ ∈ 𝔰𝔢(3). When span{Sₖ} is closed under the bracket, the joint is a connected
  subgroup of SE(3). Those subgroups fall into twelve conjugacy classes (Hervé): the identity; line translation;
  rotation about an axis; helical motion of pitch p; planar translation; cylindrical; spatial translation; planar
  gliding SE(2); spherical SO(3); translating screw; Schönflies; and SE(3) itself. The six lower pairs are the
  revolute, prismatic, helical, cylindrical, planar and spherical classes. A joint that is not a subgroup (a
  universal joint) is a product of one-parameter subgroups. Joint limits cut a feasible subset out of Q and loop
  closures cut level sets; the regular part is a manifold where the constraint Jacobian has constant rank, and
  singular poses, unilateral contacts and mode changes need the stratified description of C-16. State also
  includes motor, battery, thermal, contact-memory, estimator and controller coordinates.
- **Replaces.** `enum JointKind` with one hand-written code path per case.
- **Payoff.** One kernel generator parameterized by a screw basis covers every joint. Mobility analysis (A-01) can use
  intersections and products in the subgroup lattice, which gives the right answer for the exceptional
  over-constrained linkages whose mobility follows from subgroup structure (Sarrus) and returns no verdict for
  paradoxical ones (Bennett, Bricard), whose mobility rests on metric conditions and is decided by the rank test
  alone; both kinds are linkages where the Grübler–Kutzbach count is wrong.
- **Foundations.** `fs-mbd` has `JointKind = Fixed | Revolute | Prismatic | Helical` only, with no spherical,
  universal or planar joints; `fs-ga` has `Twist::bracket` and `Twist::ad`. The joint catalog crate
  `fs-kinematics` proposed by FrankenSim's charter does not exist.
- **Test.** Bracket-closure classification of a screw basis in exact rational arithmetic (T-11). Known answers:
  the Sarrus linkage has mobility 1 where the count gives 0, and the Bennett linkage has mobility 1 where the count
  gives −2.
- **Pilot and ceiling.** For lattice mobility: the Sarrus and Bennett linkages and one over-constrained leg linkage,
  against the rank of the constraint Jacobian at exact rational sample points. The lattice must return 1 for Sarrus
  and `undecided` for Bennett, where the rank test returns 1. Falsifier: one wrong mobility. Ceiling: a correct
  analysis where the count is wrong; no speed is claimed. Fallback: the numerical rank test alone.
- **Tier.** [S] for the generator and classification; [F] for lattice-based mobility.

### C-02 The frame groupoid and typed spatial algebra

- **Object.** Frames are objects and a rigid transform `a_from_b` is a morphism from b to a, so transforms form a
  groupoid. The adjoint Ad is a functor from that groupoid to invertible maps on 𝔰𝔢(3); the group coadjoint is
  its contragredient on 𝔰𝔢(3)*, the inverse transpose. A twist is a vector typed by a frame, a wrench is a
  covector typed by a frame, and their pairing is power, which does not depend on the frame. Three maps move
  quantities between frames and each is its own type (§11.3): the twist map Ad_g, the wrench pushforward
  Ad_g⁻ᵀ, and the wrench pullback Ad_gᵀ. A reflection is not a morphism of this groupoid, because improper
  isometries are not in SE(3); it acts through the parity rule of §11.4 as a separately typed map. Coordinate
  charts (logarithms, joint charts) are partial maps with stated overlap domains.
- **Replaces.** 4×4 matrices and 6-vectors whose frames live in comments.
- **Payoff.** `a_from_b · b_from_c` has type `a_from_c`, and nothing else composes. A twist in frame b cannot be
  added to a twist in frame c, and a wrench cannot be moved by the twist map. Static frames are phantom types;
  model-indexed frames are checked at model compile time, so batched kernels pay nothing. A derivative query at
  a chart cut requests another chart or receives a typed refusal.
- **Foundations.** `fs-ga` provides `Se3::{compose, inverse, adjoint, coadjoint}`, `Twist::transform_by`,
  `Wrench::{pairing, transform_by}`; `Se3::coadjoint` is documented as Ad⁻ᵀ, which fixes the convention of
  §11.2. `fs-mbd` already names transforms `world_from_base`.
- **Test.** Ad(gh) = Ad(g)·Ad(h); invariance of the pairing under a change of frame (T-04, T-05). The sample set
  includes tiny angles, translations near the origin, rotations approaching π from both sides and
  sign-equivalent quaternions. A single reversed adjoint must fail at least three independent fixtures: the
  composition law, the pairing, and the planar fixture of C-04. A loop of chart changes returns to the identity
  inside its stated error budget.
- **Retired when.** A loop of chart changes exceeds its error budget: that chart pair is withdrawn from the
  derivative path and the query is refused.
- **Tier.** [S].

### C-03 Inertia lives on a cone

- **Object.** A rigid body's ten inertial parameters are equivalent to the 4×4 pseudo-inertia matrix
  P = [[Σ, h], [hᵀ, m]], with Σ the second moment of mass and h the first. The parameters are physically
  consistent exactly when P is positive definite (Wensing, Kim, Slotine). The cone of such matrices with its
  affine-invariant metric is a Riemannian symmetric space; the log-Euclidean parametrization S = log P is an
  equivalent chart for optimizers and either may be used. Positivity is necessary and not sufficient for a
  declared envelope: a body whose mass lies inside a ball of centre o and radius ρ also satisfies the
  mass-support bound ‖c − o‖² + tr(I_C)/(2m) ≤ ρ², whose left side is the mass-weighted mean squared distance
  from o.
- **Replaces.** Ten free floats.
- **Payoff.** Import validation is an eigenvalue test with a certificate (T-19). Optimization and identification
  steps follow geodesics and cannot leave the feasible set. By default inertias are not parameters at all: they
  are computed from geometry and material density, so an agent designs shapes and materials. A body with a
  declared wall thickness is a shell, computed by the difference rule of §11.5, and a solid fill of a large
  enclosure raises a density warning instead of passing silently.
- **Foundations.** `fs-mbd::SpatialInertia`; `fs-mbd-material` (material-derived inertia, about 60k lines);
  `fs-opt` manifold variables with retractions.
- **Test.** Round trip between P and spatial inertia; detection of triangle-inequality violations; an audit of
  every reference robot in Appendix G. Mass-support fixture: a centred 1 kg part with three principal moments of
  0.008 kg·m² passes the positivity and triangle tests yet needs 0.012 m² where a ball of radius 0.10 m allows
  0.010 m²; an isotropic thin shell of that radius, with moments 1/150 kg·m², reaches equality. Shell fixture: an
  aluminium box of 0.4 × 0.3 × 0.2 m at 2,700 kg/m³ has mass 64.8 kg as a solid and 3.45 kg with a 2.5 mm wall,
  a ratio of 18.8.
- **Pilot and ceiling.** For Riemannian identification: recovery of planted inertial parameters of one link
  from simulated excitation, against a projected Euclidean fit. Falsifier: no fewer infeasible iterates and no
  better recovery at equal data. Ceiling: identification quality for the calibration lane of §30. Fallback:
  a Euclidean fit projected onto the cone.
- **Tier.** [S] for validation and geometry-derived inertia; [F] for Riemannian identification.

### C-04 Dynamics is the Euler–Poincaré equation on a tree

- **Object.** With body velocity ξ = g⁻¹ġ of the base and shape s (the joints), the body momentum is
  μ = 𝕀(s)·(ξ + 𝔸(s)·ṡ). Here 𝕀(s) is the locked inertia, which is the composite rigid-body inertia at the base,
  and 𝔸 is the mechanical connection. The base obeys μ̇ = ad*_ξ μ plus applied wrenches, with ad*_ξ = ad_ξᵀ as
  fixed in §11.2. Featherstone's recursions (RNEA, CRBA, ABA) evaluate these equations on the kinematic tree
  using Ad, ad and ad*. In generalized coordinates the smooth equations read
