| ID | Invariant |
|---|---|
| INV-CORTEX-01 | The final observation of every ended world is retrievable in every reset mode. |
| INV-CORTEX-02 | Behaviour weights and the observation normalizer are frozen during collection. |
| INV-CORTEX-03 | A likelihood ratio is computed for the random variable that was sampled. |
| INV-CORTEX-04 | A checkpoint is inseparable from its manifest and mapping table, and a policy reaches a design only through that table. |
| INV-CORTEX-05 | Every training gate record contains its negative controls. |
| INV-CORTEX-06 | No rung selects or discards designs without its rank-agreement record. |
| INV-CORTEX-07 | Invalid and padded samples have weight zero in every loss and statistic, and are counted in every failure report. |

| ID | Obligation | Verification |
|---|---|---|
| PO-CORTEX-01 | The value bootstrap is cut by termination only and the trace by any reset. | All eight flag combinations on a three-step fixture against a hand table |
| PO-CORTEX-02 | A frozen policy's likelihood ratio is exactly 1 on any replay of its own collection, under any packing or minibatch order. | Property test over 10⁴ random packings |
| PO-CORTEX-03 | The update is invariant to the partition into shards inside the D3 envelope, empty shards included. | 10³ random partitions |
| PO-CORTEX-04 | The actor's output does not depend on any channel outside its schema, nor on anything not yet delivered. | The causal test; inference with the other channels absent |
| PO-CORTEX-05 | Conversion between stride conventions round-trips or refuses. | Exhaustive over two- and three-dimensional views with element strides in −2 to 2 |

| Fixture | Expected answer | Negative control |
|---|---|---|
| Bootstrap | 0 for a true deadline; 9.9 for a cut with V = 10 and γ = 0.99; termination wins when both are set | A single `done` flag gives 0 for both |
| Final observation | The same values in explicit mode and in `final_obs` under masked autoreset | A mode that returns only post-reset observations fails the truncation fixture |
| Reward rate | A rate term totals the same at 50 Hz and 100 Hz | A per-step penalty totals 500 and 1,000 |
| Physical discount | 2.000·r and 1.995·r | A per-step γ gives 2.0·r and 1.0·r |
| Action law | 3.15149 for the clipped law; 1.64872 for the latent law | A mixture is refused |
| Clipped surrogate | Finite differences 0, −0.5, −1 at ratios 0.5, 1, 2 for a negative advantage | The reversed branch gives −0.25, −0.5, 0 |
| Critic gradient | 4·c_V at output 2 and target 0 | The stored-value form gives 0 |
| Packed episodes | Ratios 1 and 1 | Reading across the reset gives 1.582459 |
| Shard gradient | 0.25 | The mean of shard means gives 0.5 |
| Shard statistics | Mean 4/3, variance 32/9 | Per-shard variance 0 |
| Stride conversion | Element 3; the order (1, 0, 3, 2) | A verbatim copy reads element 12 |
| Mixed-unit requirement | The clearance binds, with margins 0.5 and 1.2 | The unscaled minimum changes with the unit |
| Training gate controls | Zero-weight, random and shuffled-label policies fail | An exported all-zero policy head passes a plumbing test and fails this one |
| Box-cone exploit | Flagged `law-sensitive`; the ranking is typed `model-conditional` | An honest policy on the circular cone is not flagged |
| Family break-even | About 590 quadruped designs at P = 60 GPU-hours and f = 0.1 | — |

### 23.23 Gates and kill gates

**The behaviour-not-plumbing rule.** A training gate is a claim about learned behaviour. Its record must hold a
zero-weight policy and a random policy that both fail the same threshold, a shuffled-label student where
distillation is involved, and a replay of the exported checkpoint that reproduces the behaviour. A record without
them is refused (FROB-REF-544, INV-CORTEX-05). A test that a training loop runs, exports and reloads is a
plumbing test and satisfies no gate below.

| Gate | Claim | Threshold (TARGET) | At |
|---|---|---|---|
| GATE-CORTEX-01 | Known answer | PPO on the reference quadruped's flat velocity task reaches the return threshold on `batch-cpu` and on each GPU backend; a zero-weight policy and a random policy both fail the same threshold. The exported checkpoint, reloaded on `batch-cpu`, reproduces the return inside the D3 envelope, and its policy head is not zero. | M2 |
| GATE-CORTEX-02 | Parity | On-device backward kernels match FrankenTorch autograd within 10⁻⁵ relative on 10³ random batches. | M2 |
| GATE-CORTEX-03 | Design comparison | BET-07 as the three-arm experiment of §23.13, ten paired seeds with intervals: the equivariant arm reaches the return in at most 0.7 times the steps of the unaugmented arm with no loss of final return; the one-sided patch is passed; the comparison with the augmented arm is reported, whichever wins. | M4 |
| GATE-CORTEX-04 | Known answer | Each detector of §23.16 flags its planted exploit and passes an honest policy. | M3 |
| GATE-CORTEX-05 | Performance | Wall-clock to the return threshold of GATE-CORTEX-01 on one RTX 4090 is at most 1.25 times an incumbent's wall-clock for the comparable task, re-measured on the same card under the disclosure block of §36. Published context: about 410 s. This is parity, not advantage. | M2 |
| GATE-CORTEX-06 | Known answer | Rules E-1 to E-9 each pass their fixture; the final observation is retrievable in both reset modes; the 0 and 9.9 bootstrap fixture; the 500 against 1,000 reward fixture is invariant under rate terms. | M2 |
| GATE-CORTEX-07 | Known answer | The PPO battery P-1 to P-11 passes for our implementation, and three planted defects that reproduce the sibling's errors each fail it. | M2 |
| GATE-CORTEX-08 | Parity and Performance | Two-shard and one-device updates agree inside the D3 envelope on 10³ random batches, an empty shard included; the 0.25 and 32/9 fixtures; strong scaling of at least 1.25 times at constant global workload and equal task quality (§36.3 row 5; 1.6 is the ambition and the funding threshold of KILL-SHARD). | M2 |
| GATE-CORTEX-09 | Known answer | The stride fixture reads element 3; the negative-stride view is materialized or refused; a stale-epoch read is refused. | M2 |
| GATE-CORTEX-10 | Known answer | Streaming past-time robustness equals offline evaluation on 10⁴ random traces; the mixed-unit fixture binds on the clearance in both unit systems; a future-time online reward is refused. | M3 |
| GATE-CORTEX-11 | Design comparison | Family policy in one class, on held-out parametric designs: median return with no adaptation at least 70% of a specialist's; fine-tuning reaches specialist return in at most 20% of the steps of a from-scratch run stopped at 95% of its final return, on the task family's terrain set including stairs, slopes and wet patches; out-of-class designs are declined; re-described robots keep at least 80% of return. | M4 |
| GATE-CORTEX-12 | Design comparison | The rank-agreement experiment of §23.11 is run and its consequence applied: τ, top-10 recall and intervals are recorded per class and task family, and a rung without a record is refused. The gate passes when the record exists and the rule is enforced, whatever τ is. | M3 as a pilot on incumbent tools; M4 on ours |
| GATE-CORTEX-13 | Design comparison | Inheritance on 12 parent-child edit pairs, 4 of them blind: median adaptation samples for parameter edits at most 20% of a from-scratch run stopped at 95% of its final return, and fewer than a raw-checkpoint warm start needs; the inherited child more than 5% worse in at most 20% of edits; a chain of 10 edits shows no decline under scheduled resets, with the audit twin within 5%. Topology edits are reported, not required. | M4 |

### 23.25 The joint law of sampled actions

**What it is.** [S] A rule for the action sampler, added to the PPO battery of §23.6 as P-12: the joint law of the
sampled action equals the law that the likelihood computation assumes, across the channels of one decision, across
consecutive decisions of one world, and across neighbouring worlds. Marginal checks do not establish it.

**Why it is a rule.** FACT (`frankensim/crates/fs-g1-train/src/ppo.rs:172–189` at `483d09c682f2`; to be re-run at
admission, §33.11): `gaussian_action` draws each channel from `gaussian_sample`, a Box–Muller cosine over a counter
advanced by the constant 0x9E3779B97F4A7C15, with the phase uniform taken from the top 53 bits of the counter times
0x94D049BB133111EB. The phase is therefore a linear function of the counter modulo 1, and consecutive draws differ in
phase by the fixed fraction 0.167245 of a turn, an angle of 0.334490·π. For a uniform angle θ, cos θ and cos(θ + φ)
have the same sign with probability 1 − φ/π, so two adjacent channels agree in sign with probability 0.665510 where
independence gives 0.5. Reported counts in 100,000 two-channel calls per seed are 66,552, 66,552 and 66,551, while
each channel alone is positive half the time. The trainer scores these samples with a product of marginal densities,
so its likelihood ratio is computed for a random variable that was not the one sampled, which is the failure rule
P-3 exists to prevent.

**Mechanism.** DESIGN:
- Every noise draw is a Philox output keyed by `(WorldAddr, decision index, stream id, channel)` (§35.9). A
  Box–Muller pair consumes two uniforms from distinct counters, and its second output is used or discarded by a
  declared rule. No draw is a function of a neighbouring draw's counter.
- The sampler has a manifest: the declared joint law (a product Gaussian, or a full covariance when the policy has
  one), the transform and bounds of P-3, and the stream layout.
- `frob-conformance` qualifies a sampler against its manifest with four statistics over N decisions: the
  sign-agreement frequency of every pair of channels; the same for one channel at consecutive decisions; the same
  for one channel in adjacent worlds; and the empirical covariance of the standardized noise. Under a product law
  every agreement frequency has mean ½ and standard deviation ½/√N.
- `train.start` refuses a sampler that has no qualification receipt for the pinned kernel (refusal: action sampler
  not qualified against its likelihood).

Owner: `frob-learn`; kernels in `frob-kernels`; fixtures in `frob-conformance`.

**Known answer and negative control.** The recurrence above, re-implemented as a planted sampler, must be rejected:
its adjacent-channel agreement is 0.6655, more than 100 standard deviations from ½ at N = 10⁵. The qualified sampler
must show every agreement inside ½ ± 0.005 at N = 10⁵ (TARGET: 3.2 standard deviations; the number of pairs tested
is recorded, so the family-wise rate is stated).

| | |
|---|---|
| GATE-CORTEX-18 | Known answer. For action dimensions 2, 12 and 29, N = 10⁵ decisions and 64 worlds: every channel-pair, consecutive-decision and adjacent-world sign agreement lies in ½ ± 0.005; every off-diagonal entry of the standardized covariance is below 4/√N in magnitude; the planted linear-phase sampler is rejected with an agreement of 0.6655 ± 0.005. M2. |

### 23.26 The actor's information contract covers every field it can read

**What it is.** [S] Rule E-10, extending E-8 and E-9 of §23.3. The actor's information contract lists every value an
online actor can read at a decision instant, with its delivery instant under the clock contract of §20: observation
channels, earlier rewards, termination and truncation flags, action masks, and each field of `info`. Outputs of the
trainer and of the scorer are outside the actor's view unless the mission declares them delivered.

**Why.** A reward is a function of state, and delivered to the actor it is a sensor. Smallest case, on the docking
model of §20.16 (three one-second ticks, hidden gain g ∈ {1, 2}, acceleration g·u): with first command u₀ = ¼ the
position after one tick is x₁ = g/8, so a shaped reward −|1 − x₁| is −7/8 under g = 1 and −3/4 under g = 2. When the
velocity packet arrives late, no causal policy docks in both worlds (§25.15). If the wrapper hands that reward to
the actor before the second command, the two worlds are distinguished and the commands (¼, ½, −¾) and (¼, 0, −¼)
dock both. An exclusion computed without reward visibility in its contract is then false for the environment that
was run.

**Mechanism.** DESIGN:
- `ActorView` is a typed projection of `StepView` that contains only fields of access class `actor`. `reward`,
  `terminated`, `truncated`, masks and every `info` field carry an access class and a delivery instant. The default
  class of `reward` and of every `info` field is `trainer-only`. A recurrent policy that takes the previous reward
  as an input requires the task to declare reward as an `actor` channel.
- The digest of the contract (channels, classes, instants) is part of the `TaskId`, of every memo key and of every
  certificate's assumption set (C-18), so a cached answer is not reused under a different contract.
- `sense.causal-test` (§20.15) gains four planted leaks that must each fail: the previous reward wired into the
  actor; an `info` field that carries a hidden parameter; an action mask computed from hidden state; a termination
  flag delivered before its instant.
- The Gymnasium-compatible adapter (§23.18) returns rewards to the learner, as that interface requires, and records
  whether the driven policy consumed them. A run whose policy read an undeclared field is labeled and cannot be
  cited for a mission answer (refusal: actor read a field outside its information contract).

Owner: `frob-learn` (types), `frob-sense` (test), `frob-spec` (declaration).

**Known answer.** The late-packet docking exclusion, run through `VecEnv` and through the adapter. With the reward
hidden the verdict is excluded. With the reward declared and delivered before the second command the verdict
changes to feasible, with the witness above. Both runs are required: a harness that reports the same verdict in
both is defective.

| | |
|---|---|
| GATE-CORTEX-19 | Known answer. Each of the four planted leaks fails `sense.causal-test` in 100 of 100 seeds; the docking exclusion holds with reward hidden and flips with reward delivered, on `VecEnv` and on the adapter; a contract change alters the `TaskId` and invalidates the cached exclusion. M2; adapter rows at its release. |

### 23.27 A threshold crossing is not attainment

**What it is.** [S] A rule for every figure of the form "time to a target", which includes the training-time parity
rows of §36.3 and GATE-CORTEX-05. A recorded score crossing is a descriptive event. Attainment is a claim about the
policy's population performance, and it needs error control over every evaluation look that could have produced the
crossing.

**Counterexample.** A policy with true success rate 0.89 is evaluated against a target of 0.90 with 30 episodes per
look. A look with 30 successes of 30 has an exact one-sided 95% lower bound of 0.05^(1/30) = 0.90497, above the
target. One look does this with probability 0.89³⁰ = 0.0303. Across 50 independent looks at the unchanged policy the
probability of at least one such crossing is 1 − (1 − 0.0303)⁵⁰ = 0.78548. A rule that stops the clock at the first
crossing reports attainment, about four times in five, for a policy that never attains.

**Mechanism.** DESIGN:
- Evaluation during training runs on a fixed development stream, disjoint from training worlds, at a cadence
  registered before the run. The run record holds every look, not only the best.
- `train.status` reports two fields. `crossing` is the first look whose point score met the target, and is
  descriptive. `attained` is the first look at which a procedure valid for the registered cadence rejects "at or
  below target". The default procedure allocates error across looks as αₖ = α/[k·(k + 1)], the series of §24.13,
  and applies an exact one-sided binomial bound at level αₖ for success targets, or a confidence sequence on bounded
  returns (C-15) for return targets. With all-success looks against a 0.90 target at α = 0.05, look k needs at
  least ln(1/αₖ)/ln(1/0.9) episodes: 36 at k = 1, 46 at k = 2, 74 at k = 10, 103 at k = 50.
- Alternatively the checkpoint chosen on the development stream is evaluated once on a final holdout. That
  qualifies the chosen checkpoint and leaves its first attainment time unknown; the reported time is then an upper
  bound and is labeled as one.
- Non-attainment within the training budget is right-censored at the budget and summarized by a restricted mean.
- In a parity comparison both arms are scored by the same rule on the same stream sizes. An incumbent's published
  time to threshold is context; the figure re-measured under this rule is the comparator.

`eval.preanalyze` prints, for a registered cadence, episode count and target, the probability that an unchanged
policy at stated true rates produces a crossing. Owner: `frob-learn`, with the study machinery of `frob-arena`.

| | |
|---|---|
| GATE-CORTEX-20 | Known answer. In 2,000 simulated trainings of an unchanged policy at true success 0.89, with 50 looks of 30 episodes, the first-crossing rule reports attainment in 78.5% ± 3 points and the spending rule in at most 5% (exact one-sided test at the 1% level); the four episode counts above are reproduced exactly. M2. |

### 23.28 The winner check for a selecting rung

**A selecting rung must pass a winner check [S].** This extends the consequences fixed in §23.11 and the
rank-agreement row of §28.10. A lower bound of 0.7 on the top-band Kendall τ admits a rung to selection. But τ
counts inverted pairs and weighs every pair equally; it does not say that the best design survives a cut.

*Counterexample.* Forty designs. The cheap rung reproduces the true order exactly, except that the true best is
ranked third. Among the true top ten, 2 of 45 pairs are inverted, so τ = (43 − 2)/45 = 41/45 ≈ 0.911, far above
0.7. A cut that keeps the top 5%, two designs, discards the winner.

*Rule.* For a rung admitted to selection with m finalists wanted, the number of designs advanced is the largest of
three numbers: m; the survivor count of the conformal margin rule (§28.9, layer 2); and the **containment rank**
k_c(m), the smallest k such that, in the calibration experiment and in every audit-lane draw to date for the class
and task family, the higher rung's top m all lie inside the lower rung's top k. The ledger row of §28.10 gains two
fields: `containment_rank(m)`, and the **regret** of a cut, which is the higher-rung score of the best design the
cut discards minus that of the best design it keeps. Positive regret means the winner was lost. A selection whose
retention is below k_c(m) is refused, with k_c(m) as the repair. Where a class has no calibration, the rung
discards by the fixed table and does not select.

*Owner and verbs.* `frob-opt`. `eval.rank-agreement` reports τ, top-k recall, the containment rank and the regret
of the requested cut; `opt.cascade` reads k_c(m) when it sizes a rung transition.

| Gate | Claim | Threshold (TARGET) | First milestone |
|---|---|---|---|
| GATE-CORTEX-21 | Known answer | On the forty-design fixture `eval.rank-agreement` returns τ = 41/45 on the true top ten, top-1 recall 0 at k = 2, containment rank 3 for m = 1 and positive regret at k = 2. A request to select with k = 2 is refused and the same request with k = 3 is accepted | M3 |

### 23.29 Short-horizon gradient training with design parameters

**Short-horizon gradient training with design parameters [M].** This is the learning arm that would consume the
step adjoints of §16; the gradient mechanism, its step labels and its kill gate are specified there. It is off the
critical path and is not funded before the step-adjoint gate has passed.

*What it is.* Policy parameters θ and a continuous design vector φ (up to about 20 entries of the parameter row of
§16.6) are updated together from analytic gradients of a short rollout. For a window of K control steps, K ∈ {16,
32}, the loss is the negated sum of rewards in the window plus a learned value V_ψ at its end. Its gradient in θ
and φ is one reverse sweep through the window: policy network, step adjoints, reward terms. The critic V_ψ is
fitted to temporal-difference targets as in on-policy actor-critic training. Three guards make it usable where
contact changes.

1. *A cosine monitor.* On a fixed share of windows (DESIGN default 1 in 16) the analytic design gradient is
   compared with the paired central difference of §17.13 on the same world addresses. The running median cosine is
   logged. Below 0.5 the window halves; at K = 8 and still below 0.5 the design update switches to the paired
   stencil and the run is labelled `gradient: stencil`.
2. *Step labels.* A window that contains a step the adjoint labels anything other than `smooth` contributes to the
   policy update and not to the design update, because its design gradient is one-sided or fixed-mode.
3. *Design updates are proposals.* φ moves inside the family's box. Every design the run reports is a typed edit
   sequence, recompiled and scored by the ordinary ladder (§28.9). No verdict cites a gradient.

Training with analytic gradients is a labelled D4 training profile (§35); every score that enters the ladder is an
evaluation on a D2 profile.

*Why the window is short.* At the closed-loop exponent quoted in §27.9, 0.16 per control step, a perturbation
grows by e^(0.16·K): 13 at K = 16, 167 at K = 32 and 7.8 × 10⁸ at K = 128. A gradient through 128 steps is
dominated by its variance, and its mean tells the optimizer nothing. The exponent is a published figure for other
systems; the monitor measures ours.

*Rival check.* FACT (Appendix H): several incumbents differentiate their step, and short-horizon actor-critic
training on a differentiable simulator is published. This is not a differentiator, and a composed incumbent can
host it. It is here because joint refinement of a selected design and its controller is the one stage where
population methods are known to be slow.

*Ceiling, before any speed test.* The finalist refinement stage only. Its share of the phase ledger (§39) bounds
the end-to-end gain, and nothing here helps screening.

*Pilot before funding.* One quadruped on rough ground and stairs with 20 design parameters, three seeds. Arms at
equal GPU-hours: this method; PPO with a derivative-free outer loop on φ; PPO with the paired stencil. Falsifier:
the method does not reach the matched, referee-promoted return in at most 0.35 of the derivative-free arm's
GPU-hours, or the median cosine is below 0.5 on more than 40% of monitored windows.

*Owner and verb.* `frob-learn`; `train.start --algo short-horizon-ac --design-params <list>`.

| Gate | Claim | Threshold (TARGET) | First milestone |
|---|---|---|---|
| GATE-CORTEX-22 | Design comparison | The pilot's comparison on both tasks: matched referee-promoted return in at most 0.35 of the derivative-free arm's GPU-hours; cosine at least 0.5 on at least 60% of monitored windows; every reported design re-scored by the ladder, none promoted on a gradient | M6 |

| Kill gate | Trigger | Fallback |
|---|---|---|
| ✖ KILL-SHORTGRAD | The pilot's falsifier fires, or the gate fails after one repair cycle | PPO with the paired stencil of §17.13 where that passes its own gate; otherwise derivative-free search over φ |

## 24. Arena: tasks, requirements, fixtures, metrics, qualification

Crates `frob-spec` and `frob-arena`, both in layer 4.

### 24.1 What Arena owns

Arena defines what a robot is asked to do and how an answer is scored. It owns the task families, the task file
`.ftask`, the requirement language and its monitors, the mission-level verdict, the fixtures whose answers are known
before any run, the metrics and scorecards, the batteries and the design corpus, the two study types, and the blinded
qualification lane. `frob-spec` holds the language: parser, unit and clock checker, normalizer, monitor compiler and
the verdict type. `frob-arena` holds the registry of tasks and fixtures, the metric definitions, scorecards, study
plans and the qualification service.

Arena does not own the machinery it scores with. The boundaries are fixed here so that no other chapter has to guess.

A note on numbers. A value in this chapter that follows from a stated formula is a derived value: it is a known answer
of §24.16 and is recomputed by its test. Every other number carries its label where it appears.

| Concern | Owner | What Arena contributes |
|---|---|---|
| Observation, action and reward terms; reset and bootstrap semantics | Cortex (§23) | The task file carries the terms. Arena never reads a reward to decide a verdict |
| Mission queries with quantifiers over designs, policies and worlds | Augur (§25) | The acceptance predicate of a mission query is a requirement of this chapter |
| Search for worlds that break a design; rare-failure bounds | Nemesis (§26) | The falsification score is the requirement margin; infeasible worlds are counted here |
| Attribution of a failure | Autopsy (§27) | The outcome that an intervention flips is a verdict of this chapter |
| Paired comparison, racing, the ladder of rungs, promotion between tiers | Atelier (§28), Kinesis (§16) | The study types and the confirmation lane wrap those mechanisms |
| Telemetry channels, snapshots, the failure taxonomy | Chronicle (§29) | Requirements read channels by name, kind and clock |
| Scene splits and held-out scene families | Habitat (§19) | Arena enforces the split at scoring time (GATE-ARENA-02) |

### 24.2 Decisions

- **ADR-ARENA-01. Requirements decide acceptance; reward terms train.** [S] A mission is accepted or rejected by a
  requirement that returns a verdict and a margin. Reward terms remain the training signal. Reason: as an evaluation
  metric a requirement is close to definitional, a pass or a fail with a distance to the boundary. As the only
  training signal the margin is the weak baseline in the field's own results. FACT (Appendix H, temporal-logic
  reinforcement learning): decomposing a formula into timed subgoals and invariant constraints raised task success by
  an average of 31.6% over the best baseline, in a field where earlier methods used margins as sparse terminal
  rewards; and margin-only optimizers reached between 6.67% and 29.9% success in a study of robustness metrics for
  robot tasks.
- **ADR-ARENA-02. Bounded time only.** [S] Every temporal operator carries a finite window. Reason: a monitor needs
  fixed memory, a verdict needs a finite horizon, and formulas with unbounded time admit no learning guarantee except
  where they are decidable within a finite horizon (FACT, Appendix H).
- **ADR-ARENA-03. Every atom is normalized by a declared scale.** [S] An atom states an inequality and the physical
  scale that makes its margin dimensionless. Reason: the minimum of a clearance in metres and a thermal margin in
  kelvins has no meaning, and the composition rules of the language are minima and maxima.
- **ADR-ARENA-04. Past time online, future time offline.** [S] Operators that look backwards are computed inside the
  step and are available as signals. Operators that look forwards are evaluated on a completed trace and are the
  verdict. Reason: an online value of a future-time operator is a silently truncated window.
- **ADR-ARENA-05. The declared comparator decides at the boundary, in exact arithmetic.** [S] The sign of a
  floating-point margin does not decide a case that sits on the boundary. Reason: a strict and a non-strict inequality
  differ exactly there, and single precision misclassifies near-boundary cases in bulk (§24.5).
- **ADR-ARENA-06. Clocks are explicit and rational.** [S] Every signal and every requirement names its clock. Periods
  are rational numbers of seconds with a phase. Reason: sensor, policy and physics rates are not integer multiples of
  each other in real robots, and a requirement evaluated on an unstated clock is a different requirement on every
  backend.
- **ADR-ARENA-07. A study is anytime-valid or fixed-n, never both.** [S] Reason: each kind of inference is valid only
  under its own stopping rule (§24.12).
- **ADR-ARENA-08. Discovery and confirmation are separate lanes with separate data rights.** [S] Reason: an optimizing
  agent that may resubmit to the same held-out worlds will eventually pass by chance (§24.13).
- **ADR-ARENA-09. An infeasible scenario is kept and counted.** [S] Reason: a failure is a failed cell, never an
  excluded cell (§8), and a suite that sheds its impossible cases reports a success rate over a population nobody
  declared.
- **ADR-ARENA-10. A fixture is complete before its first run.** [S] Every mass, constant, seed and rule of a fixture
  is recorded and hashed before either design runs, with a derivation on file for each analytic answer. Reason: a
  fixture whose constants can move after the outcome is seen is a tuning harness.

| Timed docking | Reach a pose with zero velocity by a deadline under a hidden plant gain (the exact mission slice of §25; its boundary case is a known answer of §24.16) | M1, CPU |
| Velocity tracking | Commanded planar velocity and yaw rate on flat and rough ground | M2 |
| Terrain traversal | Stairs up and down, gaps, stepping stones, slopes, rubble | M2 |
| Split-grip landing | A quadruped climbs a ramp onto a landing with a low-grip strip (fixture 2, §24.11) | M2 |
| Interior navigation | Point goal through doors and thresholds in each archetype | M3 |
| Payload transport | Carry or tow a stated mass along a warehouse route, including a ramp | M3 |
| Low-friction crossing | Cross a kitchen galley with a wet or greasy patch | M3 |
| Tight-space maneuvering | Turn around, parallel shift and dock in an aisle of stated width | M3 |
| Moving surfaces | Board and leave a conveyor | M4 |
