| Gate | Claim | Threshold (TARGET) | Earliest |
|---|---|---|---|
| GATE-NEMESIS-01 | Known answer | Legality and oracle: 100 of 100 planted illegal edits refused; 0 of 100 planted impossible traps counted; at least 95 of 100 planted solvable traps receive a witness | M3 |
| GATE-NEMESIS-02 | Design comparison | On planted traps of nominal probability at most 3 × 10⁻⁵, in 30 paired repetitions, the search reaches a first promoted failure with at least 3 times fewer simulated steps than card-uniform randomization at a 95% lower bound, and at least 70% of reported counterexamples are `solvable-causal` or `plant-feasible` | M3 |
| GATE-NEMESIS-03 | Known answer | Shrinking: planted causes recovered exactly in at least 95 of 100 trials; every `.fmcw` replays with identical digests in 100 of 100; on unplanted failures the share of worlds with at most three edits is recorded | M3 |
| GATE-NEMESIS-04 | Known answer | Bounds: over 10⁴ synthetic studies with known p the 95% upper bound covers p in at least 95%; the defensive mixture covers under a mis-centred proposal; non-nominal episodes are refused | M3 |
| GATE-NEMESIS-05 | Design comparison | Exploration: on planted failures of probability 10⁻⁴ and 10⁻⁵, one with two separate modes, at equal episode budget and 30 repetitions, exploration reaches failures with at least 10 times fewer episodes than crude sampling at 10⁻⁵, and both modes are found in at least 80% of repetitions | M3 |
| GATE-NEMESIS-06 | Known answer | Guard: 100 of 100 planted artifact failures labelled and none in the hard-world set; at least 95 of 100 genuine planted failures survive promotion | M3 |
| GATE-NEMESIS-07 | Known answer | Screening audit: a planted winner removed by a biased screen is reported in 100 of 100 runs; the stratified bound covers the planted false-discard rate in at least 95% of 1,000 synthetic campaigns | M4 |
| GATE-NEMESIS-08 | Known answer | Coverage: lazy and plain greedy agree; on 1,000 random instances of at most 20 scenes the brute-force optimum is at or below the certificate and greedy is at or above (1 − 1/e) of it | M3 |
| ✖ KILL-NEMESIS | — | Trigger: GATE-NEMESIS-02 fails after one repair cycle. Fallback: the search methods are removed; Nemesis keeps the legality profile, the oracle, the guard and shrinking, applied to failures that card randomization finds | M3 |
| ✖ KILL-RARE | — | Trigger: in the exploration pilot the gain is below 10 times at 10⁻⁵, or the coverage of any interval offered as a bound is below 85%, or a planted mode is missed in more than 20% of repetitions. Fallback: crude nominal sampling with the binomial bound alone; splitting is removed and tilting is kept only inside `nemesis.search` | M3 |
| ✖ KILL-MCW | — | Trigger: on unplanted failures fewer than half of shrunk worlds have at most three edits, or fewer than 90% replay. Fallback: Nemesis ships full failing worlds with replay and the single-edit contrasts ranked by margin; the format stays | M3 |

**Pilots before funding.** Both Frontier claims have a paper-scale pilot that runs before their work packages are
funded. For exploration: planted failures of known probability 10⁻⁴ and 10⁻⁵ on one quadruped, one of them with two
separate failure modes; crude sampling, splitting, subset simulation and the defensive mixture at equal episode
budget, 30 repetitions; the falsifier is the trigger of KILL-RARE. It needs tens of CPU core-hours on the CPU referee,
or on a development oracle outside the product (§38) if it runs before M1. Its ceiling is stated in advance: a clean
bound at 10⁻⁵ costs about 3 × 10⁵ episodes whatever the explorer does, on the order of one or two training runs, so a
perfect explorer saves at most about a factor of three on a finalist and nothing on other candidates. For search and
shrinking: ten planted traps in two generated interiors on the CPU referee, the search against card randomization,
with the falsifier of GATE-NEMESIS-02.

### 26.16 Open questions

- **OPEN-NEMESIS-1.** Sources for the legality bounds of interiors. Owner: project lead, with OPEN-HAB-1. Blocks
  claims that a counterexample is realistic, not its validity. Default: bounds are `assumed` and counterexamples say
  so.
- **OPEN-NEMESIS-2.** The distress score when the requirement margin is flat until shortly before failure. Owner:
  Nemesis lead. Blocks GATE-NEMESIS-05. Default: no splitting for that requirement; crude sampling.
- **OPEN-NEMESIS-3.** The compute envelope for a 10⁻⁶ claim, which exceeds the one-hour job rule of §21 at the
  illustrated throughput. Owner: project lead. Default: certify to 10⁻⁵ and report 10⁻⁶ as `Estimated`.
- **OPEN-NEMESIS-4.** The sample caps of 10⁶ in `fs-eproc`'s Bernoulli sequence and in `fs-uq`'s importance execution,
  and the absence of splitting upstream. Owner: airlock maintainer. Default: our own exact binomial bound for larger
  counts; upstream work items FD-FSIM-18 and FD-FSIM-19 are open (Appendix F) and no milestone waits on them.
- **OPEN-NEMESIS-5.** How a hard-world set is carried across a change of robot class or task version. Owner: Arena
  lead. Default: a set belongs to one class and task version; worlds are re-promoted before they enter another.

## 27. Autopsy: counterfactual debugging

Crate `frob-autopsy`, layer 5.

### 27.1 What Autopsy owns

`frob explain` assembles what happened: the failure class, the energy ledger, saturation, slip, and the earliest
anomaly before the terminal event, which it labels `Estimated` because ordering anomalies in time is a heuristic.
Autopsy turns that heuristic into a measurement. It restores the world to a moment before the failure, changes one
thing, runs forward, and records whether the failure still happens. A proposed cause is tested by intervention; it is
never inferred from the order in which monitors or solver stages reported.

Autopsy owns the semantics of forks (their classification and the earliest tick at which a given change may be
applied), the intervention vocabulary `do(factor := value)`, placebo forks, interventional contrasts with their flip
rates, coalition experiments and budgeted Shapley summaries, minimal repair sets, paired re-runs from the episode
start for design parameters, the reading of first divergences on forks (§27.10; the algorithm and its verb belong to
§29.8), and the transcript of a debugging session. It consumes snapshots, ring buffers, replay and the fork mechanism
from Chronicle (§29), verdicts from Arena (§24), the typed world edits of §26.3 and
the typed design edits of §14, the shrinker of §26.7, and the tiers of §16.

A value in this chapter that follows from a stated formula is a derived value and a known answer of §27.16; every
other number carries its label.

Everything in this chapter is [S] except one claim. Forks, classification, contrasts with a stability report,
coalition tables and the divergence algorithm are established technique applied carefully. The claim that an agent
repairs designs in fewer turns with these tools than with logs is a HYPOTHESIS with its own gate (GATE-AUTOPSY-08).

Counterfactual replay from restorable simulator state is established practice, and incumbent simulators expose
restorable state and opt-in run-to-run determinism on one GPU (FACT, Appendix H). Nothing here is claimed as new. What
the engine must supply for it to work is listed as needs: an exact null replay, replay of one world outside the batch
it ran in, forks that mix interventions on different model variants in one batch, and a double-precision tier that
runs the same model.

### 27.2 Decisions

- **ADR-AUTOPSY-01. A cause is what an intervention removes, net of a placebo.** A factor is named only when removing
  it prevents the failure more often than an irrelevant perturbation does.
- **ADR-AUTOPSY-02. Classify a fork before restoring state.** Whether a change may be applied at a mid-episode state
  is decided from the model difference it makes, before any state is touched.
- **ADR-AUTOPSY-03. Design-parameter interventions re-run from the episode start.** History-dependent state would
  otherwise answer a different question (§27.8).
- **ADR-AUTOPSY-04. Attribution reports a flip rate at round-off scale; double precision is the default for one
  failure.** Closed-loop legged control amplifies round-off enough to flip marginal outcomes in single precision over
  long windows (§27.9). Single precision on the originating tier is admitted by a measured rule (the single-precision
  lane, §27.19).
- **ADR-AUTOPSY-05. Contrasts first; Shapley values are a summary on a budget.** The table of what each intervention
  and each pair did is the result. A Shapley summary is computed only when that table does not already answer the
  question.
- **ADR-AUTOPSY-06. Diagnostic interventions are not repairs.** Switching a torque limit off locates a cause; it is
  not an edit anyone can build. The two kinds are typed apart.
- **ADR-AUTOPSY-07. The cause is a cause in the model.** Every attribution is scoped to the model, the tier and the
  declared factor list.

### 27.3 Forks from snapshots [S]

A fork is a parent episode, a fork tick and a change set. DESIGN:

- **State.** A fork starts from a complete checkpoint in the sense of §29: physical state; contact feature memory and
  impulses; clock phases and packet queues; controller, filter and policy hidden states; actuator electrical and
  thermal states; terrain edits; the command cursor. Random streams are counter-based and keyed by address, so they
  have no state to save.
- **Where forks can start.** At any stored snapshot; at any tick held in the per-world ring buffer; and at any tick of
  any replayable episode, by replaying the world from its address up to that tick. The ring buffer is an optimization,
  not a requirement. At a per-world state of tens of kilobytes (§36), twenty snapshots covering two seconds for each
  of 8,192 worlds would take several gigabytes, so full-state rings are kept for a reservoir of worlds and every other
  failing world is reconstructed by replay, at the cost of one episode prefix on the CPU.
- **Identity.** A child world has the address of its parent extended by a fork path. It shares its prefix with the
  parent by reference. A fork never mutates its parent (INV-AUTOPSY-04).
- **Randomness.** By default a child reads the same streams as its parent, so the intervention is the only difference.
  A replicate changes one declared thing more: a state perturbation of stated size, or the key of one named stream.
- **Batching.** One failing world is forked K times into a batch of K children. This relies on the rule that a world's
  trajectory does not depend on the batch it ran in (§35). Children that carry different model variants use the mixed
  batches of §17.
- **Horizon.** A fork starts at a lead Δ before the failure, from the ladder 0.25, 0.5, 1 and 2 s, and by default runs
  to one second past the parent's failure time (TARGET), or to the episode horizon when asked.

### 27.4 Classifying a fork [S]

The service classifies every requested change before restoring anything, and returns the class, the earliest valid
fork tick, and the fields of the checkpoint that forced a later or earlier start. The five classes below are the
intervention semantics, and this section owns them. The fork mechanism of §29.8 (snapshots, restore, the shared
prefix, the verb `run.fork`) implements exactly these five and adds none.

| Class | What changes | Where it may start | State handling |
|---|---|---|---|
| Continuation | Nothing (the null fork), or a placebo | Any checkpoint whose physical, clock, sensor and policy contracts match the run | Restored bit for bit |
| Exogenous intervention | A future disturbance, a setpoint, a scene property the robot has not yet touched | The fork tick | Restored; nothing regenerated |
| Contact-affecting intervention | Friction or compliance of a surface in contact at the fork tick; the contact law | The fork tick | Positions and velocities restored; contact memory discarded and the first solve run cold with a raised iteration cap; the fork is labelled |
| Information intervention | Sensor noise or latency; an estimator replaced by privileged state | The fork tick | Packet queues and filter state re-initialized as the intervention states; labelled diagnostic where no hardware could realize it |
| Structural or design-parameter intervention | Mass, inertia, geometry, a gear ratio, an actuator card, a sensor mount, controller gains or memory, policy weights | The authored initial condition only | The edited design is settled from its own reset cache (§24.7); paired exogenous draws are reused; contact memory, proprioception, sensor histories and policy actions are regenerated |

A continuation whose contracts do not match is refused (FROB-REF-580). A structural change requested at a mid-episode
tick is refused with the earliest valid tick, which is zero, and the list of fields that forced the restart
(FROB-REF-581). Negative control: grafting the contact warm start of the 60 mm wheel of §24.10 onto the 75 mm design
at the lip must return a structured refusal (FROB-REF-582), not a run.

### 27.5 Interventions and the placebo [S]

An intervention is written `do(factor := value)`. A factor is a path into the world or the model whose mechanism is
declared: an edit class of §26.3 for worlds, a typed edit of §14 for designs, or one of a short list of diagnostic
factors such as `torque_limit := off`, `estimator := privileged` and `latency := 0`. Each intervention changes one
declared mechanism, and the model difference it makes is computed and stored with the fork (INV-AUTOPSY-02). A change
that would alter two mechanisms, such as a wet floor that changes both friction and depth returns, is split into two
interventions or refused (FROB-REF-586).

Three forks give every intervention its meaning.

- **The null fork** applies the empty intervention. It must reproduce the parent bit for bit on the originating
  profile (INV-AUTOPSY-01). If it does not, the record is unsound and nothing is attributed (FROB-REF-583).
- **A placebo fork** applies a change that no physical cause could depend on: one state coordinate perturbed by a
  relative 10⁻¹². The **placebo flip rate** ρ₀ is the fraction of placebo forks whose verdict differs from the
  parent's. It measures how much of an apparent rescue is mere sensitivity.
- **Replicates** of an intervention apply the same change with independent perturbations of the same size. A second
  series at a relative 10⁻⁷, the scale of single-precision round-off, is run for every intervention that changes the
  outcome.

### 27.6 Interventional contrasts and the flip rate [S]

For a failing world and an intervention c with R replicates, Autopsy reports three numbers.

| Quantity | Definition |
|---|---|
| Rescue rate | The fraction of replicates of do(c) in which the requirement is not violated |
| Contrast | The rescue rate minus the placebo flip rate ρ₀ |
| Flip rate under perturbation | The fraction of replicates whose verdict differs from the unperturbed fork of the same intervention, at 10⁻¹² and at 10⁻⁷ |

Over a set of failing worlds the rescue rate estimates the probability of necessity, P(no failure under do(¬c) |
failure). A factor is named only when its contrast is tested above zero against the placebo forks, by an exact
one-sided test at the fixed replicate count or by an e-process when forks are bought one at a time, with the level
divided by the number of factors (INV-AUTOPSY-05).

| Label | Condition (TARGET thresholds) |
|---|---|
| `but-for` | One factor with contrast at least 0.5, tested above the placebo, and a flip rate of at most 0.1 at 10⁻¹² |
| `contributing` | Tested above the placebo with a smaller contrast |
| `joint` | No single factor rescues and a coalition does |
| `alternative` | Several single factors each rescue |
| `precedes-snapshot` | No intervention at the fork tick rescues, and the same change applied from the episode start does |
| `precision-sensitive` | The failure is not reproduced in double precision and is not admitted to the single-precision lane (§27.9, §27.19) |
| `chaotic: unattributable` | ρ₀ above 0.2. No factor is named |

Illustrative numbers: of 200 failing worlds re-run from their forks, `do(torque_limit := off)` prevents the failure in
164, `do(friction := nominal)` in 38, and a placebo in 12. Net of the placebo the contrasts are 0.76 and 0.13. For a
marginal failure, or for causes that interact, the report names a set of factors and not a top factor.

### 27.7 Coalitions and budgeted Shapley summaries [S]

Causes interact, so single interventions are not enough. For a factor list N of size m, the value of a coalition S ⊆ N
is v(S), the rescue rate when all of S are applied together.

**Budget.** DESIGN: at most 12 factors, all singles and all pairs. That is 78 coalitions; with 8 replicates each, 64
placebo forks and the null fork it comes to 689 forks, and the 10⁻⁷ series adds 8 forks for each coalition that
rescues. With forks of two or three seconds this is a small batch on any tier. For each pair the interaction v({i, j})
− v({i}) − v({j}) + v(∅) is reported.

**Shapley summary.** The Shapley value of factor i is φᵢ = Σ over S ⊆ N∖{i} of |S|!·(m − |S| − 1)!/m! · [v(S ∪ {i}) −
v(S)]. It is computed exactly for m ≤ 5, which needs 32 coalitions, and by sampled permutations with an interval
otherwise. It is computed only when no single factor and no pair changes the outcome. Exact values over ten factors
would take 2¹⁰ = 1,024 coalitions and leave no budget for a single replicate, so the stability the method depends on
could not be measured.

**What the summary cannot say.** Two hand-checkable cases are in the counterexample catalogue (Appendix N).

- Two factors that rescue only together (v of the pair is 1, of each single 0) and two factors that each rescue alone
  (v is 1 for either single and for the pair) both have Shapley values (½, ½). The repair sets differ: both factors in
  the first case, either one in the second. The coalition table distinguishes them and the summary does not.
- With v(∅) = 0, v({1}) = 1, v({2}) = 0 and v({1, 2}) = 0 the values are (½, −½). They sum to v(N) − v(∅) = 0 as they
  must, a single-factor repair exists, and factor 2 has a negative value because applying it cancels the rescue. A
  Shapley value can be negative and never establishes that a factor is necessary.

FrankenSim's Shapley estimator is variance-based and says of itself that its effects "are not causal effects" (FACT:
`frankensim/crates/fs-uq/src/product_shapley.rs`). It is not used here; the interventional estimator is a few hundred
lines of our own.

**Minimal repair sets.** The shrinker of §26.7 runs over the intervention set with the test "the failure no longer
occurs", and returns repair sets that are 1-minimal. A rescue at a fork is not a minimal repair in any stronger sense,
and it is not evidence that an edited design passes the task; that takes §27.8 and then a study.

### 27.8 Design parameters re-run from the episode start [S]

An agent wants to know whether a different gear ratio would have prevented a thermal trip. Applying the new ratio one
second before the trip answers a different question: what happens to a motor that was heated by the old ratio's
currents and is then geared differently. Winding temperature, battery state of charge, wear, estimator bias, a
policy's hidden state and the contact memory all carry the history of the old design, and none has a canonical image
under the edit.

Counterexample, hand-checkable. One thermal node with time constant 60 s, ambient 25 °C and a trip at 115 °C. At a
gear ratio of 12 the steady-state rise for the task's torque is 192 K, so the motor trips at 60·ln(192/102) = 37.95 s
of a 45 s task. Heating scales with the inverse square of the ratio, so at 16 the rise is 108 K.

| Experiment | Result |
|---|---|
| Ratio 16 from the episode start | Peak temperature 25 + 108·(1 − e^(−0.75)) = 82.0 °C at 45 s. The task passes with 33 K in hand |
| Ratio 16 applied at 36.95 s, one second before the trip | The winding is already at 113.3 °C and still heading for 133 °C. It trips at 42.4 s. The fork says the edit does not prevent the failure |

The fork is not wrong about the experiment it ran. It ran the wrong experiment. DESIGN: an intervention classified as
structural or design-parameter is never applied to a mid-episode state (INV-AUTOPSY-03). `autopsy.rerun` does the
following instead.

1. Apply the typed edit, which gives a new `DesignId` and `ModelId` and a reset cache of its own.
2. Re-run the failing worlds from the start on the same world addresses, so scene, disturbances and noise are paired,
   while events that depend on the robot's actions keep their own logically keyed streams.
3. Re-run a sample of worlds that passed, because a repair can break what worked.
4. Report the paired outcomes, labelled `Estimated`, and hand the pair of designs to `eval.compare` for a verdict
   under §24.12.

The controller must be able to act on the edited body without retraining: the baseline controller re-synthesized from
the edited model (§22), a family policy (§23) or a sampling controller. A policy trained for the original body alone
is refused for design factors (FROB-REF-587), since its failure on the new body would be attributed to the edit. A
forced fork of a design parameter remains available in a diagnostic mode, labelled as such, because it is occasionally
the question someone means to ask.

### 27.9 Precision for attribution [S]

FACT (Appendix H): learned continuous-control policies in closed loop have measured maximal Lyapunov exponents of 0.03
to 0.16 per control step on walker and cheetah tasks, and a perturbation of 5 × 10⁻⁴ degrees in a torso angle produces
significant divergence after 50 steps. The uncontrolled systems are not chaotic; the sensitivity comes from the policy
with contact. At 0.16 per step over 80 steps, which is 2 s at that benchmark's 25 ms control period, a perturbation
grows by about 3.6 × 10⁵. Single-precision round-off of 6 × 10⁻⁸ then reaches about 2% of the state scale, enough to
flip a marginal failure; double-precision round-off of 10⁻¹⁶ stays near 4 × 10⁻¹¹.

DESIGN: by default attribution runs on `batch-cpu` in double precision, or on the referee. For a failure recorded on
a single-precision tier the procedure is:

1. Replay the null fork on the originating backend and require identical digests.
2. Replay the same checkpoint in double precision on `batch-cpu` and apply the decision-level equivalence test of §35:
   the same verdict, failure class and binding atom, with the failure time inside the recorded envelope.
3. If the two agree, attribute in double precision. If they do not, the failure goes to the single-precision lane
   (§27.19) with the numerical-variant interventions first; only if that lane does not admit it is the failure
   labeled `precision-sensitive`, attribution refused (FROB-REF-584) and the world passed to the artifact guard of
   §26.6.

Every attribution reports its flip rates at 10⁻¹² and at 10⁻⁷, and the growth of the separation between the placebo
forks and the parent over the fork horizon, so a reader sees how far the result is from the regime where nothing can
be attributed.

### 27.10 The first-divergence algorithm [S]

Comparing two runs, a fork with its parent, one tier with another, or one backend with another, starts with the first
place they differ. Chronicle's teleport does this for exact classes by stepping digests. The general algorithm covers
tolerance classes and avoids one trap. §29.8 owns it and `telemetry.divergence` runs it; it is restated here because
every attribution reads its output.

```text
first_divergence(A, B, mode):
  align the committed ticks and events of A and B by stable identifiers; a variable with no counterpart
    is listed as unpaired and is never matched by position
  if mode is exact:
      c_t = H(c_{t-1}, d_t) is the chained digest of the per-tick state digests d_t, stored at checkpoints
      bisect over checkpoints for the least k with c_k(A) ≠ c_k(B)
      replay both runs from checkpoint k − 1 and compare d_t tick by tick: the first unequal tick is t1
  if mode is tolerance, with a scale per class of variable:
      for each block of ticks, in chronological order:
          [lo, hi] = bounds on the block maximum of the scaled error
          hi ≤ 1 : the block agrees; go on
          lo > 1 : a mismatch lies inside; descend into the block
          otherwise : unresolved; refine this block before looking at any later block
      where samples are missing, report the earliest possible interval and the coverage gap
  at t1, re-run the tick with per-stage digests or residuals: the first stage over tolerance is s1
  report t1, s1, the variables that differ under their physical names and units, and the first tick at
    which a requirement atom or a task decision differs
```

**The trap.** Bisection is valid only on a predicate that is monotone and decided. "Some tick up to t differs" is
monotone. "The states differ at tick t" is not, because an error can vanish and return. Counterexample: two traces of
eight ticks that differ at ticks 1 and 5 and agree elsewhere. A midpoint search on the pointwise predicate probes tick
3 or 4, sees agreement, moves right and reports tick 5. The chained digest reports tick 1. The same trap applies to
`design bisect` over a lineage (§28), where the predicate must be "the outcome has changed by this edit" and each step
must be decided by a study.

**Rules for reading the result.** The first recorded discrepancy is labelled with its temporal resolution. The order
in which solver stages report residuals inside a tick is not evidence of a physical cause. For a fork against its
parent the first divergent tick is the intervention tick or later, and the useful output is the order in which classes
of variable leave tolerance and the first decision-level divergence. When topology differs between the runs, only
shared interfaces and task observables are compared: a leg that exists in one run has no counterpart in the other.

### 27.11 The decision model for attribution

States: the failure has a single removable cause, a joint cause, or none that can be attributed. Actions: buy a fork,
name a factor or a set, or decline. Loss: naming a wrong cause sends an agent to edit the wrong thing, which costs a
design iteration and its compute; declining costs one fallback to the heuristic ordering.

```text
Decision:          Which repair edit should the agent try first for this failure?
Artifacts:         Typed interventions; a fork ledger; the placebo flip rate; a rescue rate per factor and
                   per pair; minimal repair sets; one label from §27.6.
Obligations:       The empty intervention replays the failure bit for bit, so the starting point is exact.
                   Each intervention changes one declared mechanism (model difference on file).
                   A cause is named only when its contrast beats the placebo under a test at a stated level.
Failure modes:     Chaos makes every nudge look like a cause. The cause precedes the snapshot.
                   The failure does not survive double precision.
Fallback:          The first-anomaly ordering of §29, labelled Estimated.
Fallback trigger:  Null-replay mismatch; placebo flip rate above 0.2; failed equivalence in double precision.
Budgeted mode:     12 factors, singles and pairs, 8 replicates, 64 placebo forks: 689 forks. A Shapley
                   summary only if no single and no pair changes the outcome.
Baseline:          The heuristic ordering; and one-at-a-time contrasts without coalitions, to measure
                   whether ten forks answer as well as seven hundred.
Rollback:          A configuration flag to the heuristic; recorded forks remain valid experiments.
Verification:      Planted single and joint causes; a planted chaotic failure; the thermal counterexample.
```

### 27.12 Time-travel debugging as an agent workflow

The workflow is five moves: read the heuristic, fork, intervene, attribute, re-run. Each move is one verb with a
bounded output, and the session is recorded as a transcript, schema `frob.autopsy.transcript/1`, that replays every
fork from its address. A session on a quadruped in the wet-floor kitchen of NS-04:

```text
frob explain run r:19e2 --budget 600
    # first anomaly (Estimated): slip at the left front foot at 11.1 s, 0.2 s before the fall
frob run fork r:19e2 --world 311 --before failure --dt 1.0s --json
    # fork f:a41c at 10.30 s; class continuation; null replay bitwise on gpu-cuda;
    # double precision on batch-cpu is decision-equivalent (fall at 11.31 s against 11.30 s)
frob autopsy intervene f:a41c --placebo 64 --replicates 8 --coalitions pairs --json
        --do 'scene./floor/patch[galley-2]/film := dry'
        --do 'model.joint[*.knee].torque_limit := off'
        --do 'sense.imu.latency := 0 s'
        --do 'model.joint[*.knee].gear_ratio := 16'
    # exit 2: three interventions ran from the fork; gear_ratio is a design parameter and was
    # refused with FROB-REF-581 (earliest valid fork tick 0; forced by actuator thermal state,
    # policy history and contact memory)
frob autopsy attribute f:a41c --json
```

```json
{ "schema": "frob.autopsy.attribution/1", "fork": "f:a41c…", "tier": "batch-cpu", "precision": "f64",
  "horizon_s": "2", "forks_run": 137, "null_replay": "bitwise",
  "placebo": {"n": 64, "flips": 2, "rate": 0.031, "separation_growth": "2.1e4"},
  "contrasts": [
    {"do": "scene./floor/patch[galley-2]/film := dry", "class": "contact-affecting", "rescued": "8/8",
     "contrast": 0.97, "flip_rate": {"1e-12": 0.0, "1e-7": 0.0}, "label": "but-for"},
    {"do": "model.joint[*.knee].torque_limit := off", "class": "diagnostic", "rescued": "3/8",
     "contrast": 0.34, "flip_rate": {"1e-12": 0.125, "1e-7": 0.375}, "label": "contributing"},
    {"do": "sense.imu.latency := 0 s", "class": "information", "rescued": "0/8",
     "contrast": -0.03, "flip_rate": {"1e-12": 0.0, "1e-7": 0.0}, "label": "none"} ],
  "pairs": [ {"do": ["film := dry", "torque_limit := off"], "rescued": "8/8", "interaction": -0.34} ],
  "refused": [ {"do": "model.joint[*.knee].gear_ratio := 16", "code": "FROB-REF-581",
                "earliest_valid_fork_tick": 0} ],
  "evidence": {"class": "Estimated", "scope": "cause in the model at this tier, among the listed factors"},
  "next_actions": [
    {"command": "frob autopsy rerun r:19e2 --edit 'regear *.knee 16' --worlds failing,sample:64",
     "why": "A design parameter is tested from the episode start on the same world addresses."},
    {"command": "frob nemesis shrink r:19e2 --world 311",
     "why": "The film is a but-for cause; find the smallest world that still fails."} ] }
```

```text
frob autopsy rerun r:19e2 --edit 'regear *.knee 16' --worlds failing,sample:64 --json
    # new design d:8e77 with its own reset cache; baseline controller re-synthesized;
    # 23 failing worlds and 64 sampled passing worlds on the same addresses:
    # 17 of 23 now pass; 63 of 64 still pass, 1 new timeout; label contributing, Estimated
frob eval compare quad-a quad-a@regear --task kitchen-tray
    # the verdict comes from a study (§24.12), not from the autopsy
```

The numbers in the transcript are illustrative. What the transcript fixes is the shape: the heuristic proposes, forks
test, design parameters go back to the start, and a study decides. The viewer of §32 can overlay a fork on its parent
as a ghost, synchronized on the fork tick.

### 27.13 What Autopsy does not claim

- **Not a cause in the world.** The result is a cause in the model at a tier. FACT (Appendix H): causal models of
  robot failures learned from simulation reached a sim-to-real accuracy of 70% and 72% in one study, with variables
  chosen by the experimenter.
- **Not beyond the factor list.** A failure whose cause is not among the declared factors yields no named factor. The
  planted no-cause control tests this.
- **Not a minimal repair.** Repair sets are 1-minimal under the tested interventions.
- **Not necessity from a Shapley value.** §27.7.
- **Not a passing design.** A rescue at a fork, or a re-run on the failing worlds, is not a verdict on the task. A
  study is.
- **Not an answer in chaotic regimes.** Above the placebo threshold nothing is attributed.
- **Not a proof.** A contrast is a replayable experiment and has class `Tested` on its tier; an attribution drawn from
  contrasts has class `Estimated`.
- **Not a differentiator of the engine.** An incumbent with restorable state and a thin layer can host the same method
  (§39 includes that arm).

### 27.14 Verbs and refusals

| Verb | Kind | First milestone | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `autopsy.intervene` | run | M3 | Runs interventions, placebo forks, replicates and coalitions from a fork handle made by `run.fork` (§29.8) |
| `autopsy.attribute` | read | M3 | Contrasts, flip rates, pairs, labels, an optional Shapley summary |
| `autopsy.repair` | run | M3 | Minimal repair sets by shrinking the intervention set |
| `autopsy.rerun` | run | M3 | Paired re-run from the episode start for design-parameter and structural edits |
| `autopsy.show` | read | M3 | The transcript of a session, token-budgeted |

Autopsy registers no fork verb and no divergence verb. A fork point is made with `run.fork` (§29.8, M2), which
returns the class of a proposed change set under §27.4, the earliest valid tick and the null-replay result;
`--classify-only` restores nothing. The first divergence between two runs, in exact or tolerance mode (§27.10), is
read with `telemetry.divergence` (§29.8, M2).

| Code | Refusal |
|---|---|
| FROB-REF-580 | A continuation whose physical, clock, sensor or policy contract does not match the checkpoint |
| FROB-REF-581 | A structural or design-parameter intervention requested at a mid-episode tick; the earliest valid tick and the forcing fields are returned |
| FROB-REF-582 | State from one model grafted onto another |
| FROB-REF-583 | The null fork does not reproduce its parent |
| FROB-REF-584 | Attribution requested for a failure that neither lane admits, or under an uncontrolled determinism class |
| FROB-REF-586 | An intervention changes more than one declared mechanism |
| FROB-REF-587 | A design-parameter re-run with a policy that cannot act on the edited body without retraining |
| FROB-REF-880 | An attribution cited as an established cause, or as a cause in the physical robot |

### 27.15 Invariants and proof obligations

- **INV-AUTOPSY-01.** The empty intervention replays its parent bit for bit on the originating profile; otherwise
  nothing is attributed.
- **INV-AUTOPSY-02.** Every intervention changes one declared mechanism, and its model difference is stored with the
  fork.
- **INV-AUTOPSY-03.** No structural or design-parameter intervention starts from a mid-episode state, except in the
  labelled diagnostic mode.
- **INV-AUTOPSY-04.** A fork never mutates its parent; a child has its own address and shares the prefix by reference.
- **INV-AUTOPSY-05.** A factor is named only when its contrast is tested above the placebo at a stated level and the
  placebo flip rate is at most 0.2.
- **INV-AUTOPSY-06.** Every attribution carries its scope: the model, the tier, the precision and the factor list.

| Obligation | Statement | Class sought |
|---|---|---|
| PO-AUTOPSY-01 | The Shapley summary satisfies efficiency, the dummy property and symmetry on the computed coalition table | Tested in exact rational arithmetic on integer counts |
| PO-AUTOPSY-02 | `first_divergence` in exact mode returns the least tick at which the prefixes differ | Tested with planted divergences; the monotonicity argument is on file in `docs/derivations/` |
| PO-AUTOPSY-03 | In tolerance mode, an interval reported as agreeing has a true maximum scaled error of at most 1 | Tested with outward-rounded block bounds |

### 27.16 Known answers

| Known answer | Expected | Negative control |
|---|---|---|
| Planted single causes: 200 failures in five classes (friction drop, torque cap, payload shift, latency, terrain step), ten candidate factors each | The planted factor ranks first with label `but-for` | A failure planted through a factor outside the list names no factor |
| Null fork | Identical digests | A checkpoint with its packet queue stripped does not replay and is refused |
| Chaotic placebo: a doubling map with failure defined on its fortieth iterate | A 10⁻¹² placebo is amplified by 2⁴⁰ ≈ 1.1 × 10¹², about half of placebo forks flip, and the label is `chaotic: unattributable` | The same map over five iterates attributes normally |
| Joint and alternative pairs | Labels `joint` and `alternative`; Shapley values (½, ½) in both; repair sets {1, 2} and {1} or {2} | A summary that reports only Shapley values cannot tell them apart |
| Negative Shapley value | (½, −½) for the table of §27.7; the values sum to 0 exactly | — |
| Thermal re-run | 37.95 s; 113.3 °C at the fork; a trip at 42.4 s in the forced fork; 82.0 °C peak from the start | A tool that reports the forced fork's result as the answer to the design question |
| Warm-start graft | Refused with FROB-REF-582 | — |
| First divergence | Tick 1 for traces that differ at ticks 1 and 5 | The pointwise midpoint search reports tick 5 |
| Tolerance mode with a gap | The earliest possible interval and the coverage gap | A tool that skips the gap reports a later tick |
| Precision | A marginal failure built to flip under 10⁻⁷ and not under 10⁻¹² is labelled `precision-sensitive` when it came from a single-precision run | The same failure with a wide margin attributes normally |

### 27.17 Gates, kill gate and pilot

| Gate | Claim | Threshold (TARGET) | Earliest |
|---|---|---|---|
| GATE-AUTOPSY-01 | Known answer | Null forks of 1,000 failing worlds replay with identical digests on the originating backend; a world forked alone and in a batch of 512 children gives identical digests | M2 |
| GATE-AUTOPSY-02 | Known answer | Classification: 40 catalogued pairs of intervention and state are classified correctly; the warm-start graft and a mid-episode gear change are refused with the right fields | M2 |
| GATE-AUTOPSY-03 | Known answer | Planted single causes: the planted factor ranks first in at least 90% of 200 failures in double precision, and in the single-precision lane for windows of at most 1 s, and the top factor changes in at most 30% of cases under 10⁻⁷ perturbation; the agreement between ten one-at-a-time forks and the full coalition table is recorded | M3 |
| GATE-AUTOPSY-04 | Known answer | Coalitions: planted joint and alternative causes are labelled correctly in at least 95 of 100; the Shapley identities hold exactly; the negative-value case is reproduced | M3 |
| GATE-AUTOPSY-05 | Known answer | Abstention: a planted chaotic failure and a planted no-cause failure name no factor in 100 of 100 | M3 |
| GATE-AUTOPSY-06 | Known answer | The thermal counterexample: all four numbers within 0.1 s and 0.1 K; the mid-episode request is refused and the re-run passes | M3 |
| GATE-AUTOPSY-07 | Known answer | First divergence: planted divergences found at the right tick and stage in 100 of 100 in exact mode; the pointwise mutant is caught; tolerance mode reports gaps | M2 |
| GATE-AUTOPSY-08 | Design comparison | On the planted-defect designs of the corpus (§24.9), agents given Autopsy reach an accepted repair in at most one third of the serial turns of agents given logs and `explain` alone, pre-registered, with an anytime-valid verdict | M4 |
| ✖ KILL-AUTOPSY | — | Trigger: GATE-AUTOPSY-03 fails after one repair cycle: planted-cause accuracy below 90%, or the top factor changes in more than 30% of cases at 10⁻⁷. Fallback: single-factor paired re-runs from the episode start, with the first-anomaly ordering labelled `Estimated`; coalitions and Shapley summaries are removed | M3 |

**Pilot.** The planted-cause test runs at paper scale before the coalition machinery is funded: one trained quadruped
policy on a development oracle outside the product (§38) or on the CPU referee, 200 planted failures in five cause
classes with ten candidate factors, one-at-a-time contrasts against exact Shapley over 1,024 coalitions, each repeated
under 20 snapshot perturbations at 10⁻⁷ and at 10⁻¹². It takes about a day on a 32-core machine. Its falsifier is the
trigger of KILL-AUTOPSY, and it also answers whether ten forks suffice. The ceiling of the benefit is stated in
advance: the output is an accuracy, not a time. It can shorten a design decision only by removing agent turns spent on
wrong repairs, so its ceiling is the share of turns that diagnosis takes in the phase ledger of §39. If
GATE-AUTOPSY-08 fails, the tools stay, because they are cheap and exact, and the claim about turns is withdrawn.

### 27.18 Open questions

- **OPEN-AUTOPSY-1.** Default replicate count and perturbation sizes. Owner: Autopsy lead. Decided by the pilot.
  Default: 8 replicates at 10⁻¹², and 8 at 10⁻⁷ for interventions that change the outcome.
- **OPEN-AUTOPSY-2.** Whether one-at-a-time contrasts suffice, which would make pairs optional. Owner: Autopsy lead.
  Decided by GATE-AUTOPSY-03. Default: singles and pairs.
- **OPEN-AUTOPSY-3.** Lyapunov exponents of our own controllers and policies on our tiers, which set the usable fork
  horizon. No measurement exists for trained quadruped policies in any engine we could find. Owner: Cortex lead.
  Default: leads of at most 2 s, with the growth of placebo separation reported in every attribution.
- **OPEN-AUTOPSY-4.** The size of the snapshot reservoir on each device. Owner: Chronicle lead. Default: a reservoir
  sized by the budget estimator; every other fork point is reconstructed by replay.

### 27.19 Attribution in single precision on the originating tier

**The single-precision lane [F].** This amends ADR-AUTOPSY-04 and §27.9. Double precision on the CPU remains the
default for one failure, where it costs little. It is not a requirement of the evidence. What the evidence
supports is a flip rate measured under perturbations at or above round-off scale (§27.5), and that measurement can
be made on the tier where the failure happened.

*Why it is admissible.* FACT arithmetic on the exponent quoted in §27.9, 0.16 per control step: the growth factor
e^(0.16·n) is 24.5 at n = 20, 602 at n = 40 and 3.6 × 10⁵ at n = 80. Single-precision round-off of 6 × 10⁻⁸
therefore reaches 1.5 × 10⁻⁶ of state scale after 20 steps, 3.6 × 10⁻⁵ after 40 and 2% after 80; at that
benchmark's 25 ms period these are fork windows of 0.5 s, 1 s and 2 s. A verdict that moves under a relative
change of 10⁻⁵ in state also moves under sensor noise and friction scatter two orders larger. It is marginal in
any arithmetic, and the right output is the label `marginal`, not more digits. HYPOTHESIS: the exponent of our
closed loops is of the same order. It was measured on walker and cheetah benchmarks under learned policies, and
the gate below measures ours.

*Procedure* for a failure recorded on a single-precision tier.

1. The null fork on the originating profile must give identical digests (unchanged, INV-AUTOPSY-01).
2. R₀ placebo forks at a relative 10⁻⁷ on the originating tier over the fork window W (DESIGN default R₀ = 32).
   Record the placebo flip rate ρ₀ and the measured growth G(W) of the separation between placebo forks and parent.
3. *Admission.* ρ₀ ≤ 0.1 and G(W)·u ≤ 10⁻⁴ of state scale, with u = 6 × 10⁻⁸. Attribution then runs on the
   originating tier in single precision with at least 16 replicates per intervention at 10⁻⁷, contrasts tested
   against the placebo as in §27.6, and the record carries `tier: <backend>, precision: f32`.
4. *Not admitted.* Shorten W to the longest window that passes, within the bound the first-divergence algorithm of
   §27.10 gives on how late a fork may start, or escalate to double precision as in §27.9.
5. *A failure that double precision does not reproduce* is no longer refused outright. It is attributed in this
   lane with the numerical-variant interventions first: half step, doubled solver iterations, the alternative
   contact law, the stricter step profile. A rescue by one of them gives the label `tier-specific: <variant>` and
   passes the world to the artifact guard of §26.6. Only when the lane is also not admitted is the failure
   labelled `precision-sensitive` and attribution refused.

*A cross-check that can fail.* One attribution in k (DESIGN default k = 8), and every attribution that enters a
report, is repeated in double precision on `batch-cpu`; the top factor, its label and the sign of each contrast
are compared, and the agreement rate is a ledger figure.

*Known answers.* (i) The linear map x ← 1.1735·x has exponent ln 1.1735 = 0.16 per step: after 40 steps a
perturbation has grown by 602, and the measured G must match within 1%. (ii) Negative control: a pendulum released
5 × 10⁻⁸ rad from upright with no control, with the verdict "falls to the positive side". A placebo of 10⁻⁷ rad
flips the side whenever its sign is negative, so ρ₀ is about one half; the lane must not admit the case, and the
label is `marginal`. At a placebo of 10⁻¹² the side is stable, which is why the 10⁻¹² series alone would have
hidden the problem.

*Cost and ceiling.* One failure with ten factors and 16 replicates is 160 forks of 2 s: 320 world-seconds,
seconds on either tier, and the lane saves nothing. A cluster of 200 failures with pair interactions (55
interventions × 32 replicates × 2 s) is 7.0 × 10⁵ world-seconds: about 3 minutes on a device producing 4,000
world-seconds per second, against 12 minutes to 2 hours on `batch-cpu` at 1,000 to 100. Ceiling: the wall time of
bulk attribution, by the ratio of device to CPU world-seconds; and attribution of tier-specific failures, which
the double-precision rule could not attribute at all.

*Owner and verb.* `frob-autopsy`. `autopsy.attribute --lane {f64, tier-f32, auto}`; `auto` applies the admission
rule and records which lane ran and why.

| Gate | Claim | Threshold (TARGET) | First milestone |
|---|---|---|---|
| GATE-AUTOPSY-09 | Known answer; Design comparison | The linear map and the pendulum control behave as stated. G(W) is recorded for the reference quadruped and humanoid policies at 0.5 s, 1 s and 2 s. On the planted-cause suite of GATE-AUTOPSY-03 with windows of at most 1 s, the lane names the same top factor as double precision in at least 95% of admitted cases. A planted solver artifact that double precision does not reproduce is labelled `tier-specific` with the right variant. Bulk attribution of 200 failures is at least 3 times faster in wall time than on `batch-cpu` | M3 |

| Kill gate | Trigger | Fallback |
|---|---|---|
| ✖ KILL-ENSEMBLE | Agreement with double precision below 90%; or fewer than half of the reference failures admitted at any window of 0.5 s or more; or a bulk speedup below 3 | ADR-AUTOPSY-04 as first written: attribution in double precision only, and a failure not reproduced there goes to the artifact guard unattributed |

## 28. Atelier: the studio loop, analyses, comparison, lineage, cascade, decision cores

### 28.1 What Atelier owns

Atelier is the design studio: the loop in which a design is checked, given a controller, simulated, explained, edited
and compared, and every rule that decides how evaluation effort is spent inside that loop. It is two crates.
`frob-analyze` holds the analyses A-01 to A-26, each of which returns a typed finding with ranked repairs. `frob-opt`
holds comparison, lineage queries, optimization, the evaluation ladder and its allocation rules, the co-design
cascade, revalidation, experiment suggestion, registered predictions, reports, and the compiler for the decision-core
tables of §28.19.

| Atelier owns | Atelier uses and does not own |
|---|---|
| The order of the studio loop and the right of each stage to refuse the next | Design terms, typed edits and the model compiler (§14) |
| Analyses A-01 to A-26 and the aggregate verb `design.check` | The three tiers, the trust ladder and effort profiles (§16) |
| Paired comparison in two declared study types | Family batches and campaign deduplication (§17) |
| Lineage queries: diff, blame, bisect, merge | Baseline controllers, gait orbits and skills (§22); family policies and inheritance (§23) |
| The ladder of evaluation rungs, its allocation rule and the rank-agreement policy | Tasks, requirements, batteries and the blinded qualification lane (§24) |
| The six-stage co-design cascade and its screening audits | Mission queries and family certificates (§25) |
| Revalidation of verdicts after an edit (`result.revalidate`) | Adversarial worlds and rare-failure estimation (§26); interventional attribution (§27) |
| The memo policy: what may be served from the memo graph, and when | Every ledger and the memo store, which are tables of Chronicle (§29) |
| Experiment suggestion, registered predictions, reports | Calibration against reality (§30); the daemon and its queue (§32) |
| The decision-core contract and the eleven decision rules DC-01 to DC-11 | The mechanisms those rules govern, each in its own chapter |

Where a decision core governs a mechanism that another chapter owns, this chapter fixes the decision rule (the table,
its loss model, its obligations, its fallback) and the owning chapter fixes the mechanism.

The mechanisms of this chapter at a glance. Every Frontier row has its pilot, its ceiling and its kill gate in the
section named.

### 28.2 Decisions

- **ADR-ATEL-01: the order of the loop is a rule.** Check before you simulate, simulate before you train, train before
  you claim. Reason: each stage is cheaper than the next by roughly an order of magnitude (HYPOTHESIS; settled by the
  phase ledger of §39) and each can refuse the next.
- **ADR-ATEL-02: two study types, never mixed inside one study.** A comparison is declared either as an anytime-valid
  e-process study or as a fixed-n exact study with a pre-analysis of which verdicts are reachable at that n. Reason:
  time-uniform inference and a sealed fixed-n rule compute different decisions; data collected under one is not
  re-read under the other.
- **ADR-ATEL-03: successive halving is the fixed baseline and the fallback of the ladder.** Every adaptive allocation
  rule ships in shadow behind it and reverts to it on a named trigger. Reason: an adaptive rule can fail in a way that
  costs validity or the best design; the fixed table can only cost compute. One asymmetry governs every rule in this
  chapter: reporting an artifact-dependent result as established, or eliminating the best design, costs far more than
  a wasted higher-rung episode.
- **ADR-ATEL-04: a cheap rung discards; it does not select.** A rung may choose finalists only in the strata where the
  rank-agreement ledger (§28.10) has measured that it can. Reason: no published measurement of rank agreement between
  a shared policy and trained specialists exists, and the nearest neighbours are weak (§28.10).
- **ADR-ATEL-05: a hash identifies; only an implication licenses skipping a recheck.** A content hash says that an
  input or a result is the same object. It says nothing about whether a verdict survives a different input. Reuse of a
  verdict needs a dependency argument or an implication argument, recorded and independently checkable (§28.13).
- **ADR-ATEL-06: decision rules are compiled to tables.** Every adaptive decision in the studio is compiled ahead of
  time into an integer guard table, an automaton or a monitor with a version, stored under `registries/cores/`,
  regenerated in continuous integration and diffed. The runtime evaluates tables. No decision reads the wall clock,
  device load or arrival order. Reason: replay, audit, and a rollback that is a configuration flag.
- **ADR-ATEL-07: parametric models rank experiments; distribution-free tests issue verdicts.** The
  value-of-information model of DC-05 never issues a verdict, so a wrong model costs efficiency and never validity.
- **ADR-ATEL-08: agents are the discrete optimizer.** Agents choose topology, leg count and actuator families. The
  studio supplies fast continuous optimization, population evaluation and honest comparison underneath.
- **ADR-ATEL-09: the controller gate.** No adaptive controller is enabled by default without a replay scenario,
  evidence records, a calibration report and a demonstrated fallback. Adoption is always shadow (report both rules,
  act on the old), then canary, then default; the incumbent in each shadow run is the plan's own reference path.
- **ADR-ATEL-10: two planes.** Kernels, step plans and physics never depend on the dispatcher, the memo policy or any
  estimator. The decision plane reads results and writes requests; it cannot change what a world computes.
- **ADR-ATEL-11: decision cores are named DC-01 to DC-11.** Reason: the letter D already names determinism classes (D0
  to D4) and doctrine rules; a second meaning would make "D2" ambiguous in exactly the sentences where both appear.

### 28.3 The loop

```
 design ──► check ──► synth controller ──► simulate ──► explain ──► edit ──► compare ──┐
   ▲        (static,   (seconds)           (batch or     (telemetry,  (typed)  (anytime-  │
   │         seconds)                       GPU)          energy,              valid or   │
   │                                                      forks)               fixed-n)   │
   └── revalidate ◄── lineage, archive, ladder, cascade, optimize, train ◄────────────────┘
```

The order is a rule, not a suggestion: check before you simulate, simulate before you train, train before you claim.
Each stage is cheaper than the next by roughly an order of magnitude, and each can refuse the next. Two things are
added to the loop of the first studio milestone. An edit does not only produce a new design; it produces an
invalidation set, the verdicts and derived assets that the edit puts in question, and `result.revalidate` says which
survive (§28.13). And a population of designs does not walk the loop one at a time; it climbs the ladder of §28.9
together, in mixed batches (§17), with the cascade of §28.11 deciding who climbs.

The loop is measured, not assumed. Every verb records its phase (authoring, check, synthesis, simulation, training,
promotion, review) and its cost in the phase ledger that the ten-fold test reads (§39). A phase that accounts for less
than nine tenths of elapsed time cannot deliver a ten-fold improvement alone even if its cost falls to zero, so the
ledger is read before any speed claim is made about a stage.

### 28.4 Analyses

A-01 to A-18 and A-20 to A-25 need no batch simulation; the orbit solve of A-04 is a small CPU computation. A-19 and
A-26 read runs. `frob design check` runs the ones marked ✓ and returns in under two seconds for a template-sized
design (TARGET). An analysis marked "✓ when bound" joins `check` only when the request names the scene, budget or
skill it needs.

| ID | Analysis | Question it answers | Mathematics | In `check` | Tier |

Which subgroup also preserves the sensors, the payload and the task? | C-09; two nested groups, the mechanical group and its observation-preserving subgroup (§13, §20). Only the subgroup may be used for weight sharing, deduplication and gait orbits | ✓ | [S] |

Does a periodic orbit exist under the baseline controller, and how does it move with a design parameter? | C-10; periodic orbits by shooting on the compliant tier, full-space Floquet multipliers, continuation in design parameters (§22). Labelled a screening signal | | [F] |

Are there two admitted worlds with the same observation history that need different actions? | Rank and conditioning of the observability Gramian along nominal motions; an alias witness as an explicit pair of worlds (§20) | ✓ (structural rank) | [S] / [F] |

Can the body deliver more energy into a contact than the safety budget allows? | A lower bound on mandatory work (potential rise, unavoidable dissipation) against stored, injected and approach kinetic energy under the `.fenergy` budget; port quantities of C-12 | ✓ when bound | [S] / [F] |

| A-26 | Regime atlas | In which contact modes, slip states and saturation states did the design operate, where is a gradient trustworthy, and where does a ranking change? | A partition of recorded operation by mode, slip, saturation and derivative validity; per region a local model, an error estimate and the shortest replayable failure | | [F] |

Every analysis returns its result with an evidence class, the model identity, and, when it finds a problem, ranked
repairs as typed edits. Four rules are added.

1. **A bound says which side it is on.** A feasibility result is typed `exact`, `inner` (everything reported feasible
   is feasible) or `outer` (everything reported infeasible is infeasible), and it names the authority model it
   assumed. DESIGN, because the same body gives different answers under different load-sharing models: under
   independent foot forces a stance needs 155 N at the worst foot, and under equal passive springs the forces are
   (175, 115, 85, 25) N against a 160 N cap (FACT, executed stance enumeration; source register).
2. **An exclusion encloses every state and every energy source.** A static or energy argument may exclude a design
   only for a model whose states and energy sources it encloses. A-20 therefore always includes approach kinetic
   energy.
3. **An analysis is a memo node.** Its key is the model identity restricted to the fields it reads, its own version
   and its parameters; its determinism class is D0 for the exact analyses. An edit that does not touch those fields
   recomputes nothing (§28.14).
4. **A screening analysis is labelled as one.** A-04 orbit results, A-17 Gramian conditioning and A-26 regions are
   screening signals. They may discard under the rules of §28.9 and may not establish a comparison.

**Frontier analyses and their pilots.** A-04, A-17's alias witness, A-18, A-24's witness and A-25 are piloted and
gated in the chapters that own their mathematics (§22, §20, §19, §22, §30); A-15 in §31; A-09 remains among the first
items to be cut if its payoff is not measured. A-26 is piloted here. Ceiling: the atlas computes nothing new about the
robot; its whole value is fewer wrong gradient steps and fewer misread rankings. Pilot: on recorded runs of the
reference quadruped, test whether a region's validity label predicts the sign agreement between a smoothed gradient
estimate and a specialist-checked finite difference. Kill gate KILL-ATLAS: the label predicts no better than "trust
nowhere" at a 95% lower bound; fallback: A-26 is a descriptive report with no validity label.

**Shortcuts that are wrong.** Each row is a hand-checkable case in which a plausible analysis gives the wrong answer.
They are seeds of the negative-control registry (§38).

| Shortcut | Smallest case that breaks it | What the analysis does instead |
|---|---|---|
| Support polygon plus total actuator capacity as a stance screen (A-08) | In an exhaustive stance enumeration of 11,520 body and load cases the screen accepts 1,596 bodies that the exact classifier rejects (FACT, executed; source register) | Per-contact force limits enter the cone program; the result is typed and names its load-sharing model |
| Adding peak currents on a shared bus (A-23) | Two fingers each need one powered tick; the bus powers one finger per tick. With a one-tick deadline no joint schedule exists; with two ticks exactly two exist. A rule that adds both peaks rejects the two-tick design, which is feasible | The joint time-indexed contract is kept; a prune is rejected if any discarded design is feasible under the same mission |
| Connection curvature as a test for a misaligned mecanum roller (A-09) | A base with misaligned rollers still has spanning curvature, as a differential drive does | The defect is a rank drop in the connection, which the growth vector of A-07 reports |
| The mechanical symmetry group as the policy's symmetry (A-03) | A quadruped with one forward lidar has the four-element group mechanically and a two-element group in closed loop | Both groups are stored on each robot-and-task pair; only the observation-preserving subgroup is used |
| A quasi-static energy exclusion without approach energy (A-20) | An 8 kg body on a 12 mm rise needs 8 × 9.81 × 0.012 = 0.94176 J; a 0.90 J budget excludes the passive crossing; 0.05 J of approach kinetic energy removes the exclusion | The budget includes kinetic energy at the start of the segment; the result is `outer` only for the enclosed model |
| Per-reading accuracy as the value of sensor redundancy (A-17) | Seven independent readings, each right with probability 0.75, give a majority success of 3807/4096 ≈ 0.929; seven readings with a perfectly shared error stay at 0.75 | The alias analysis reads the declared error dependence of the cards, not the per-reading accuracy |
| An instantaneous-current model of the drive loop (A-22) | For a 75 mm wheel with total reflected inertia 0.00107890625 kg·m² and a current target held for 10 ms, the one-tick spectral radius is 1.4820 with target-current feedforward and 0.9207 with measured-current feedforward; the instantaneous model gives 2.6917 for both with the fixture's shaft damping (2.7075 without it) and misses the stable case (FACT, executed pilot; re-derived from the fixture before it is pinned) | The hold is modelled exactly over the control period |
| Identifying friction from a convenient run (A-25) | With drawbar force F = min(k_t·I/r, μ·N), k_t = 0.2 N·m/A and r = 0.06 m, runs at 1 A and 2 A under 30 N and 40 N give 3.33 N and 6.67 N for μ = 0.4 and for μ = 0.8; at 3 A under 10 N they give 4 N and 8 N | The analysis reports zero sensitivity to μ for the first two runs and asks for an excitation in the traction-limited regime |
| A late observation with the right content (A-21) | A packet that arrives at tick 1 serves decisions that commit at ticks 2 and 4; delayed to tick 3 it still serves the second and no longer serves the first | Arrival instants are compared with decision instants per decision, in rational time |

### 28.5 Explain

After a simulation, `frob explain <run>` assembles: the failure taxonomy with first-cause ordering (§29.10); the
energy ledger (§29.9); the saturation report by joint; friction utilization and slip; the gap between estimated and
privileged state; and a ranked list of typed edits predicted to help, computed from A-16. The list is the envelope's
`next_actions`.

Four additions make the explanation harder to misread.

- **Description and cause are different outputs.** The first-cause ordering is a description: it orders anomalies by
  time and is labelled `Estimated`. A causal statement ("torque saturation caused the fall") comes only from a
  controlled intervention, which is the fork machinery of §27 under decision core DC-06. `explain` offers that as a
  `next_action`; it does not imply it.
- **Explaining a comparison.** `frob explain compare <comparison>` clusters the paired-episode differences by contact
  signature and scene region and names the two or three regimes in which the candidate gained or regressed, within a
  token budget. A paired difference is attributed to a regime only if both arms' traces for that world address are
  present; the address-keyed sample of §29.6 guarantees that the same worlds were traced for both arms.
- **Gait by symmetry mode.** Joint trajectories are projected onto the isotypic components of the
  observation-preserving subgroup (A-03) and the energy per component is reported. One line tells the agent which gait
  emerged and how far a payload or a sensor broke the symmetry. It is a readability aid and makes no claim about
  performance.
- **The first physical consequence of an edit.** When a run follows an edit, `explain` leads with the change the agent
  made, the first event at which the two lineages' traces part (the first-divergence algorithm of §29.8), and the
  evidence for the comparison.

### 28.6 Comparing designs honestly (C-15)

`frob eval compare A B --task T` pairs episodes by world address, so both designs meet the same scenes, the same
disturbances and the same randomization draws. A comparison declares its study type before it draws an episode.

**Study type `anytime`.** A betting e-process runs per metric. The comparison stops when a threshold is crossed or the
budget ends, cancels the unfinished episodes, and returns a verdict with the e-value, the confidence sequence for the
effect, the number of pairs used, and the tier. Episodes are consumed in address order, never in completion order, so
preemption and reordering by the daemon leave the e-value unchanged. A metric enters an e-process only with a bound on
its paired difference that was fixed before the first observation (FACT: `frankensim/crates/fs-eproc` requires an
explicit `LossSpan`, which "must not be estimated from the race data"); the span comes from the task definition (§24),
and a metric without one is refused for this study type.

**Study type `fixed-n`.** The rule is frozen before sampling: n pairs, the counts b (candidate succeeds, baseline
fails) and a (the reverse), the effect (b − a)/n, and exact Clopper–Pearson intervals on the two discordant
probabilities at 97.5% two-sided each, with opposite endpoints subtracted, which gives at least 95% simultaneous
coverage. The candidate is promoted if the lower endpoint exceeds the margin and hard feasibility holds; the verdict
is a practical tie if the interval lies inside ±margin, inferior if the upper endpoint is below −margin, and otherwise
inconclusive. Two rules attach.

- *Reachability pre-analysis.* `eval.preanalyze` enumerates every outcome the frozen rule can produce at the
  declared n and margin and reports which verdicts are reachable. A study whose declared verdict set contains an
  unreachable verdict is refused unless the request acknowledges it. Known answer: at n = 64 with a five-point margin
  there are 2,145 count pairs, of which 521 promote, 521 are inferior, 1,103 are inconclusive and none is a practical
  tie, because perfect concordance gives [−0.0662, +0.0662]; promotion with a = 0 needs b ≥ 15; a tie first becomes
  reachable at n = 86, and only for (0, 0) among 3,828 pairs (FACT, executed enumeration; the endpoint
  1 − 0.0125^(1/64) = 0.0662 and the counts C(66, 2) and C(88, 2) are reproduced by hand).
- *Exact curtailment.* A fixed-n study may stop early only when every admissible completion of the unresolved labels
  yields the same verdict. No e-process may stop it.

**Pairing rules.** These are requirements on every paired study; violating one is a refusal, not a warning.

1. Pair by (world, replicate). A counter that depends on training progress is not part of an address. Counterexample:
   seeds keyed by (world, epoch) on a 64-wide batch pair only morphologies whose indices agree modulo 64.
2. Exogenous fields are indexed by physical coordinate, not by event order. Two robots on different paths must read
   one space-indexed material field at their own contact points; two tires on different paths need not receive equal
   friction samples at corresponding ticks, and a comparison that pairs "the k-th friction draw" has paired nothing.
3. Each design is settled separately. The settled equilibrium is recomputed per design; a design that starts in
   penetration makes the pair `unscored`; a buildable design that stalls is a failed trial, not a missing one.
4. Pairing imposes no minimum number of episodes per design.
5. The accounting identity holds: a_only + b_only + both + neither + unscored = planned, each an integer, and the
   verdict states its denominator. An agent cannot optimize failures out of the denominator.
6. Paired statistics are refused under an uncontrolled determinism class (§35). Both arms run at D2 or better on one
   backend, or at D3 with decision-level equivalence recorded for the task. A D4 run never enters a comparison.

**Several metrics.** The average of the per-metric e-values is an e-value under arbitrary dependence and tests the
global null that the candidate is no better on any listed metric (FACT: `fs-eproc::combine_average`; the product is
valid only for independent comparisons, `combine_product`). A claim about one named metric uses that metric's own
e-process, with the e-value form of the Benjamini–Hochberg rule across metrics when several are claimed (FACT:
`fs-eproc::e_benjamini_hochberg`, false discovery rate at most α under arbitrary dependence).

**Several designs.** A race over N candidates uses the mixture construction of `fs-race::race_field`: rounds are the
only clock, every survivor consumes one observation per round in index order, a candidate's elimination evidence is
the average of the pairwise e-processes against all original opponents, and an elimination needs that mixture to reach
at least 1/α, so the true best is eliminated with probability at most α (FACT:
`frankensim/crates/fs-race/CONTRACT.md`). An implementation that eliminates on any single pairwise crossing runs each
comparison at α/(N − 1) instead.

**What a comparison returns.** The verdict (`settled`, `tied`, `inconclusive`, `incomparable` or `infeasible`, all
legitimate dispositions); the statistic of its study type; the pairs used with the accounting identity; the tier; the
first divergent event between the arms when one exists; each design's absolute hard-limit verdict beside the paired
verdict, because a relative result does not establish that either design meets the mission; and a rank-robustness
field (`model-robust`, `model-conditional` or `unchecked`, from A-19). A verdict from a fast tier is `provisional`
until promoted (the trust ladder of §16, decision core DC-01); a promoted verdict also carries the estimate at referee
fidelity from the tier-correction ledger (§29.11).

**What a comparison does not control.** One comparison is valid under optional stopping. It does nothing about an
agent that submits fifty candidates to the same held-out worlds until one passes. That is the job of the blinded
qualification lane of §24, with its fresh sealed world clusters and its error budget α_i = α / [i·(i+1)] for the i-th
submission. A design comparison that is to be reported as a claim (§8) goes through that lane; `eval.compare` on
discovery worlds is a development result.

**A relation, not two scores [F].** "Can this replacement make a formerly successful delivery fail?" is a question
about the pair, and the statistical comparison answers it only in distribution. The exact form, reachability of the
outcome pair (success, failure) in the product of the two closed loops driven by the same exogenous inputs, is a
mission query (§25). Atelier's part is the pairing discipline above, without which neither form means anything.

### 28.7 Lineage: diff, blame, bisect, merge

Design versions form a content-addressed graph whose edges are typed edits. `design diff` lowers the difference of two
terms to a list of edits. `design blame` names the edit that introduced a parameter value. `design bisect --predicate
"<task> succeeds"` walks a lineage path by binary search, deciding each step with the anytime-valid comparison, and
returns the edit that changed the outcome (NS-06).

- **An edit returns its invalidation set.** `design.edit` takes the expected parent and an idempotency key, refuses a
  stale parent, and returns the new immutable version, the structural and parameter diff, the symmetry effect, and the
  set of derived assets and stored verdicts whose dependency support the edit touches (§28.13). The agent sees what
  its change put in question before it spends anything.
- **Bisect is honest about non-monotone lineages.** Binary search is correct only for a predicate that is monotone
  along the path. Counterexample: outcomes along six versions are pass, fail, pass, pass, pass, fail. The midpoint
  passes, the search goes right and reports the last edit, while the first edit also changed the outcome and the
  second changed it back. `design bisect` therefore returns a pair of adjacent versions with different decided
  outcomes, which is always a true statement, labelled `a-change`. It labels the result `first-change` only after the
  prefix has been scanned (every earlier version decided) or when the caller declares the predicate monotone, which is
  recorded as an assumption on the result.
- **Bisect controls its own error.** Each probe is an e-process at α / ⌈log₂ L⌉ for a path of L edits, so the whole
  search errs with probability at most α by the union bound. An inconclusive probe ends the search with the bracket
  reached and the evidence so far.
- **Merge is order-independent.** Lineages and archives from several agents merge as grow-only sets of versions and
  per-cell maxima under a total order (fitness, then `DesignId`). The merge is commutative, associative and
  idempotent, so the result does not depend on who synchronized first. FACT: `fs-archive::MapElites::add` replaces an
  elite only on strict improvement, so equal fitness keeps the first arrival; the total order removes that dependence
  on arrival.
- **Migration keeps old replay possible.** A schema migration reads the old object and writes a new one with migration
  provenance. The old version stays addressable and replayable with the worker version that produced it.

### 28.8 Optimization

Agents are the discrete optimizer: they choose topology, leg count and actuator families. The studio supplies fast
continuous optimization and honest evaluation underneath.

- **Continuous parameters.** CMA-ES with restarts, Bayesian optimization with trust regions and multiple fidelities,
  and Riemannian quasi-Newton for static objectives on manifold-valued parameters, all from FrankenSim (FACT: `fs-dfo`
  with restart schedules, `fs-bo` with `turbo` and `mf` modules, `fs-ascent::riemann`), reached through the airlock.
- **Racing.** Candidates in a generation are compared by e-processes and the dominated ones are cancelled
  mid-evaluation, so compute follows the survivors. The benefit depends on separation: the sibling's own battery
  asserts a saving of at least 2 on a separated field and below 1.5 on an inseparable one, with 11.7 and 1.03 measured
  on its fixtures (FACT: `frankensim/crates/fs-race/tests/battery.rs`, `CONTRACT.md`). The plan therefore expects two
  to five times fewer evaluations when candidates are separated and nothing otherwise (HYPOTHESIS; settled per
  campaign by the saving the race ledger records).
- **Quality-diversity.** A MAP-Elites archive (`fs-archive`, FACT) over behaviour descriptors such as mass, speed,
  energy per metre and footprint. `frob opt archive show` gives an agent a map of different good designs instead of
  one optimum. Mutations are typed edits, including adding and removing a limb, and one generation is one mixed batch
  (§17) under the class's family policy (§23).
- **The fidelity ladder.** Static analyses, then a shared family policy on a fast tier, then a fine-tuned policy, then
  a specialist, then promotion on the referee, then a rare-failure estimate for finalists. Each rung certifies or
  escalates. §28.9 specifies it.
- **Co-design with control.** The inner loop is a controller that needs no per-design training: the synthesized
  baseline controller, which costs seconds, or the family policy of the design's morphology class. Policy fine-tuning
  is spent only on survivors and specialist training only on finalists.
- **A family per dispatch [F].** A neighbourhood of designs (a sweep, a finite-difference stencil with common random
  numbers, an evolutionary generation) is evaluated in one mixed batch, which cuts sequential agent rounds. A
  20-parameter central stencil with 64 addresses per design is 41 × 64 = 2,624 worlds and fits one device. The ceiling
  is stated before any test: published population co-design reports compute gains of about three to four times, not
  ten (FACT, source register), and parameter sweeps inside one topology are something incumbents batch today. Paired
  finite-difference design gradients are used only over short horizons and smooth metrics, because paired worlds
  decouple under contact (a perturbation of 5 × 10⁻⁴ degrees is reported to diverge after 50 steps; FACT, source
  register). The pilot, its falsifier and the kill gate KILL-FDGRAD are specified in §17.13, which owns them: on one
  quadruped with 12 design parameters, the variance ratio of paired against independent central differences at
  horizons of 25 to 500 steps and the sign agreement over 20 replicate batches. The gate fires on a variance ratio
  below 2 at every horizon of 50 steps or more, on sign agreement below 70%, or when no end point is confirmed by a
  specialist; its fallback is rank-based search (CMA-ES, racing) with the stencil kept as a sensitivity report.
- **One verb for the whole campaign.** `frob opt cascade --spec <mission or task> --budget …` runs the cascade of
  §28.11 from a specification to a ranked, typed result set, streaming progress with denominators. It is orchestration
  over the verbs of this chapter and is judged as such. The agent-facing orchestration verb is `solve.run` (§32.6.2),
  which calls `opt.cascade` and adds no mechanism. There is one A/B, not two: the one-verb arm of GATE-ATEL-03 is the
  second arm of GATE-TETHER-13, and KILL-SOLVE is decided on it. If agents with the one-verb form do no better than
  agents driving the verbs by hand in that A/B, it stays a convenience and is not counted as a lever.

### 28.9 The ladder of evaluation rungs

A design is never scored by the most expensive method first. Six rungs, each about an order of magnitude dearer than
the one below, each allowed to decide only what its evidence supports.

| Rung | What scores the design | Cost per design | What it may decide |
|---|---|---|---|
| R0 Static | `design.check` and the bound analyses | Seconds of CPU; under 2 s for `check` (TARGET) | Refuse a design; exclude with a typed bound. It never ranks survivors |
| R1 Shared policy | The family policy of the design's morphology class, zero-shot, on a fast tier (§23); the synthesized baseline controller where the class has no family policy (§22) | Tens of GPU-seconds (HYPOTHESIS; the phase ledger records it) | Discard, under §28.10. Select only in strata where rank agreement has been measured |
| R2 Fine-tuned | The family policy fine-tuned to the design at a declared fraction of specialist steps. Each fraction is its own rung for calibration | Minutes | Discard, and select among survivors |
| R3 Specialist | A policy trained or inherited for this design alone | One training run. The leading incumbent trains a quadruped velocity policy in about 410 s on one RTX 4090 and humanoids in under 30 minutes (FACT, source register) | Rank finalists, as `provisional` |
| R4 Referee | Paired re-evaluation on the referee at the same world addresses (DC-01), with the tier-correction estimate (§29.11) | Referee episodes: 16 / 64 / 256 at the 50th / 95th / 99th percentile per established verdict (TARGET, unmeasured) | Establish, or label `tier-sensitive` |
| R5 Rare failure | A failure-rate bound for finalists (DC-04, §26) | n = ⌈ln(1/δ)/p*⌉ nominal episodes for a bound p* at confidence 1 − δ | Certify, refute or exhaust the bound, scoped to its tier |

A sampling-based controller that needs no training is admitted as an R1 scorer and as an out-of-distribution fallback.
It never stands in for a trained policy as the evaluator of record: at about 0.33 and 1 GPU-minutes per 20 s episode
(quadruped, humanoid) at a 20 ms planning step, and about 1.7 and 5.2 at 4 ms (§22.8), a few hundred episodes cost
